ideas.title: Sweep: the SEC marketing sweep, run on yourself
ideas.one_liner: A free scanner that crawls a small advisor's public footprint (website, microsites, YouTube, public social, review sites), cross-checks claims against their own Form ADV and IAPD/BrokerCheck record, and returns a ranked punch list for their compliance reviewer; paid tiers add change monitoring and an exam-ready binder.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators of small RIAs (1-20 people) with no marketing-review software, where the owner is usually the CCO. Phase-2 second buyer: RIA acquirers doing diligence on targets.
ideas.who_pays: The RIA owner/CCO, from the compliance or marketing budget: free scan, then $99-199/mo monitoring and a $495-1,500 one-time Exam-Ready Binder (dated snapshots, claim inventory, remediation log). Anchors: FMG about $178/mo plus $994 setup, Archive Intel $99/mo platform plus $500/mo AI marketing review, outsourced CCO retainers $8k+/yr, and small-firm Marketing Rule penalties of $20k-$430k (2023-2025 cases). Acquirer diligence at $2-5k per target is my estimate.
ideas.problem: The SEC's Marketing Rule sweeps were built from advisers' public websites. Draft-review tools only see content someone submits, and nobody checks the live site against what the firm has filed. Typical hits: 'no conflicts' claims versus Form ADV disclosures (the Meridian pattern, Sept 2025), unsubstantiated superlatives, undisclosed testimonials, stale awards and third-party ratings, hypothetical performance on public pages, AUM figures that disagree with Form ADV, and 'AI-powered' claims. The Dec 16, 2025 SEC Risk Alert on testimonials, endorsements and ratings raised exam attention, and about 16.4k state RIAs (84% with 0-2 employees) plus thousands of small SEC RIAs have no compliance department or tool.
ideas.solution: Crawl, extract claims, map each to the rule section, cross-check against Form ADV/IAPD data, rank by exam risk, suggest redlines, and send a weekly diff when pages change. One-click PDF to the firm's compliance consultant. Publish accuracy on a labeled test set of violating and clean pages (he did the same with his AI-text detector). Positioned strictly as flags for a qualified reviewer, never as legal advice or a 'compliant' stamp. Public pages only; no LinkedIn scraping or logged-in areas.
ideas.why_now: Dec 2025 SEC Risk Alert; Jan 15, 2026 staff FAQs; Sept 2025 Meridian case proved the Atkins-era SEC still brings small technical Marketing Rule cases; AI-written site copy is multiplying; Reg S-P is a FY2026 exam priority; Hadrius raised $27M (July 2026), so awareness is high while the long tail is unserved. Caveat: I found no 2026 off-channel fines, so do not pitch fear of those.
ideas.founder_edge: Fast crawler plus LLM pipeline build; benchmark-first habit from the AI-text detector; Ron's 24 years of advisor relationships plus MFA's CCO (Kevin Condon, per an old Gust profile) as the named human reviewer; MFA advisors as the first live scans and pilot customers. Ask Ron in week 1 what MFA's compliance tech does today to avoid overlap.
ideas.first_10_customers: Week 1: Ron introduces 5 advisors plus Kevin Condon; run live 20-minute scans on their sites for free. Weeks 2-6: pull newly registered RIAs from the SEC's public Form ADV bulk data (1,478 SEC registrants in 2025 alone), scan about 300 sites, and email each owner a one-page 'three things an examiner would ask about' note (accurate, polite, opt-out, never implying he is a regulator). Weeks 4-8: 30-day pilots with about 15; convert on the $495 binder or $99/mo monitoring. Parallel: plain-English breakdowns of each new SEC/FINRA action, and a Ron intro to a state IAA or FPA chapter call. Expect 3-5 paying by day 75, about 10 by day 120.
ideas.path_to_big: Reachable long tail is about 25k firms with no marketing-review tool; 20% adoption at about $1,500/yr is roughly $7.5M. Add broker-dealer reps (639,723 FINRA reps, 331,802 dual-registered) via firm deals at $10-30 per rep per year, insurance agencies (FMG alone claims 3,500 P&C agencies), and acquirer diligence. Standalone ceiling about $15-30M ARR; $100M needs horizontal expansion to any regulated marketing claim or a strategic sale (comps: Yext paid $125M plus up to $95M for Hearsay in 2024; GTCR bought FMG in 2025, price undisclosed; Hadrius $27M raised). $10M ARR does not need heroic share.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Hadrius (YC W23, $27M led by CRV July 2026; reviews website changes, social, video; quote-priced), Sedric ($22M raised; enterprise), Saifr (Fidelity-born; per-user or enterprise quote), Archive Intel (scans website content; AI review add-on from $500/mo), FMG Overwatch (inside FMG), Red Oak (workflow plus review service; Slashdot lists $749/user/yr, unverified), Smarsh Web Archive (captures but does not judge), Wealthtender plus Hadrius testimonial scanner (testimonials only, free to Wealthtender clients through year-end), and consultants doing manual reviews. I found no free outside-in scan that joins public claims to the firm's own Form ADV. A funded rival could copy it in a sprint, so the moat must be the labeled violation dataset, the Form ADV join, and MFA/association distribution. Kill test: if fewer than 3 of 10 advisors say the scan found something they would fix, stop within 14 days.

ideas.title: Reviewer Cockpit: review software sold to the consultants who sign off
ideas.one_liner: A multi-client workspace for outsourced CCOs and small compliance firms with intake from clients, AI first-pass redlines from each client's approved disclosure library, a rule checklist, version-hashed approvals and a monthly exam log, so the same billable hours cover 3-5x more clients.
ideas.customer: Independent compliance consultants and small compliance firms serving 20-200 RIAs each. Secondary seat: the advisors who submit content.
ideas.who_pays: The consultancy, at $200-500/mo per reviewer plus $5-15 per client seat, funded from margin on retainers and hourly work, because their binding constraint is reviewer capacity. Option: advisors pay a $29/mo submit-and-track seat resold by the consultant. Anchors: SmartAsset, citing Schwab's 2025 benchmarking, says 83% of advisors outsource compliance activities (second-hand figure); outsourced retainers run roughly $8k-15k/yr (older consultant figure) up to $12k-100k+/yr.
ideas.problem: Reviews happen over email and Word with no consistent record of what was reviewed, which disclosures were required, or which version posted. The SEC's April 2024 Risk Alert found advisers lacking copies of social posts, rating questionnaires and support for performance claims. Advisors complain compliance takes days; consultants cannot add clients without adding people.
ideas.solution: Intake by email, Slack and a Chrome extension; auto-classify the piece type and rule set (206(4)-1 versus FINRA 2210 for dual registrants); pre-fill redlines from the client's disclosure library; reviewer approves or edits; auto-archive with a hash and approval stamp; export the exam log. Anonymized cross-client patterns improve suggestions over time. Software only: the consultant remains the accountable reviewer.
ideas.why_now: AI is multiplying the number of drafts per advisor; FINRA Notice 26-14 (July 2026) pushes documented, risk-based review and says the firm is responsible whether a human or AI wrote it; the funded players (Hadrius, Sedric, Saifr) aim at firms with compliance departments, not at the consultant channel.
ideas.founder_edge: He cannot pass as a compliance expert, so he sells picks and shovels to experts. Ron and Kevin Condon likely know outsourced CCOs and law firms (the old Gust page lists a law firm and an accountant, status unconfirmed). A named reviewer from MFA lends credibility.
ideas.first_10_customers: Ask Ron for 5 introductions to consultants he has used or whose clients he knows. First discovery question to all five: 'What do you review client content in today?' Offer 2 of them a free 30-day custom intake-and-redline portal if each brings 10 clients, then charge from month 2. Add NSCP events and LinkedIn after the first logos.
ideas.path_to_big: About 33k RIA firms (16.4k SEC plus about 16.4k state). If 40% are served through consultants and 2,000 consultancies pay $400/mo, that is about $10M; client seats at $15/mo across 13k firms add about $2.3M. The larger prize is becoming the system of record where small-firm compliance work flows (marketing, annual review, Reg S-P, AI governance) with a 15-20% take rate on a consultant marketplace, a bit like pharma's promotional-review software. Honest ceiling $10-25M; $100M is heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Red Oak (software plus a review service, the closest incumbent), Smarsh, Saifr's SaifrReview, Hadrius, Sedric, COMPLY (sells outsourced support), plus consultants' own email and spreadsheets. My searches found no white-label multi-client tool for consultants, but that is absence of evidence from thin searching; confirm in week 1. Kill test: if five consultants say Red Oak or email is fine, or will not put client content into a tool built by an 18-year-old, stop. Trust is the risk, not technology.

ideas.title: Third-Party Marketing Ledger: promoters, ratings and influencers (MFA as customer zero)
ideas.one_liner: One system for every outside party an advisor pays or relies on in marketing: written-agreement templates with e-sign, standard disclosure blocks, recurring disqualification screening, a payment ledger that flags the $1,000 threshold, and a diligence file for third-party ratings and awards, with verified promoter profiles any advisor can adopt.
ideas.customer: RIAs that pay anyone for referrals, testimonials or lead generation, or that display 'Top Advisor' style awards; plus the promoters themselves (lead-gen sites, directories, CPAs, podcasts, creators) who want to be easy to pay.
ideas.who_pays: Advisors at $49-99/mo; promoters $500-2,500/yr for verification. Adjacent budgets already exist: advisors pay roughly $90-190 per lead historically or about $5k/mo (Wealthtender's cited example) for lead gen, and pay rating providers.
ideas.problem: The Marketing Rule requires a written agreement when a promoter is paid over $1,000 in 12 months (non-cash counts), clear and prominent disclosure, and a disqualification screen under a 'reasonably should know' standard, which means ongoing monitoring. The Dec 2025 Risk Alert targeted exactly this, the Jan 2026 SRO-order FAQ made eligibility more nuanced, and GeaSphere was cited for missing agreements with compensated endorsers. Advisers must also keep rating questionnaires and have a reasonable basis for any rating. Today it is Word templates and memory.
ideas.solution: Registry plus checker plus generator: a promoter profile with disclosure text and an e-signed agreement; the advisor connects; payments import by CSV, Stripe or QuickBooks; threshold alerts; monthly re-screen of IAPD, BrokerCheck and SEC orders; a ratings file with methodology, date, criteria and disclosure plus expiry reminders; a records binder for exams; an API so a lead-gen site can inject the correct disclosure automatically.
ideas.why_now: The Dec 16, 2025 Risk Alert is squarely about testimonials, endorsements and third-party ratings, and Mintz names referral networks and influencer partnerships as exam focus; Jan 2026 FAQs changed eligibility analysis.
ideas.founder_edge: By the brief, MFA connects consumers with advisors, so MFA is itself a promoter and its advisors are the advertisers: customer zero and the first registry entry. Ron can introduce peer directories and networks; Asher's Gen Z network supplies creator-promoters. Verify MFA's current business model with Ron first.
ideas.first_10_customers: Day 1: build MFA's own promoter pack (agreement, disclosure, screening log) free as the case study. Then Ron introduces 3 peer platforms or associations for verification at about $1,000 each, and 10 MFA advisors onboard at $49/mo. Revenue by day 60 is roughly $500/mo plus 2 verifications.
ideas.path_to_big: Standalone about 10k firms at $600/yr is about $6M. It grows by becoming the standard that lead-gen platforms embed (they are paid per lead, so they want to be easy to pay), extending to private fund placement agents and the 6,389 exempt reporting advisers with bigger budgets, and merging as the third-party module of Idea 1 or 2. $100M is not credible alone; honest standalone ceiling $5-10M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No dedicated registry found. Compliance consultants and law-firm templates, generic CRMs (referral tracking in Salesforce), and lead-gen platforms' own boilerplate (SmartAsset, Zoe Financial, Wealthtender). Kill test: if MFA and five advisors cannot name a single promoter they currently pay, the ledger has no payers, so ask first.

ideas.title: Shadow-AI Ledger: record what advisors ask chatbots and send clients
ideas.one_liner: A browser extension and vault that logs prompts and outputs on approved AI sites into a tamper-evident archive, warns and redacts client identifiers before they are pasted, tags outputs that become client communications, and generates the AI-tool inventory and vendor-diligence file.
ideas.customer: Small and mid RIAs (1-50 staff) whose people already use ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and the CCO who must answer for it.
ideas.who_pays: The firm at about $29/user/mo plus $99/firm. Anchors: Archive Intel charges $99/mo platform, $40/user/mo for text capture and $12/user/mo per connector; its Zocks integration is listed at $12/user/mo.
ideas.problem: Consumer chatbots leave no firm-side record. FINRA's 2026 oversight report has a GenAI section and Notice 26-14 reaffirms firm responsibility for AI-generated communications. The Reg S-P small-entity compliance date (June 3, 2026, advisers under $1.5B AUM) has passed and covers incident response, service-provider oversight and records; the SEC lists it as a FY2026 exam priority. AI meeting-note output is likely Rule 204-2 books and records per law-firm commentary (no formal SEC guidance), and auto-emailed notes trigger archiving. Staff paste client details into chatbots today.
ideas.solution: Extension plus admin console: daily digest, per-user policy, client-identifier detection with local redaction, 'became a client communication' tagging, AI-tool inventory, vendor questionnaire, and export to a WORM archive partner or object-lock storage. Optional: sample outbound client emails with his AI-text detector as a CCO sampling aid only, never as proof.
ideas.why_now: Reg S-P exam priority just after the deadline; FINRA GenAI emphasis; the records status of AI output is unresolved and commentary expects stricter guidance, so firms want a defensible default.
ideas.founder_edge: An extension plus vault is a 2-3 week build for him; he already built an AI-text detector that beat commercial tools in his blind tests. MFA advisors are beta users. Possible cross-over: a HIPAA-flavored build (PHI detection, local processing) could be piloted at MHC Healthcare, only after counsel review and a BAA.
ideas.first_10_customers: Beta with 8-10 advisors via Ron, free for 30 days; the hook is 'your team pasted N client identifiers into ChatGPT last week.' Charge from month 2. Ask the consultants from Idea 2 to recommend it, since the vendor-oversight file is something they must produce for Reg S-P anyway.
ideas.path_to_big: Vertical wedge into a horizontal problem: about 33k RIA firms plus 639,723 FINRA reps; 5% of reps at $300/yr is about $9.6M, then CPA firms, insurance agencies, mortgage and healthcare practices. Horizontal AI governance is crowded (enterprise DLP vendors, from memory, unverified), so rule-mapped templates and the advisor channel are the wedge. SOC 2 ($10-30k) will gate larger firms. $100M is a stretch; $10M is plausible.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Archive Intel (chat archiving, Zocks integration, FINRA 2026 AI recordkeeping content), Smarsh and Global Relay (capture integrations), the AI tools' own logs (Zocks, Jump), and enterprise DLP and AI-governance tools aimed at large companies. I found no advisor-specific browser-capture product, though my search was thin here. Kill test: if advisors will not install an extension that reads their chats, or two CCOs say holding the content creates more liability than it removes, stop.

ideas.title: Creator-Advisor Desk: the compliance layer for advisors who post short video
ideas.one_liner: A $49-79/mo desk where an advisor pastes a script or video link and gets disclosures and risky claims flagged, required captions or disclaimers burned in, a dated archive (including TikTok, historically a capture gap) and an approval packet for their firm or consultant.
ideas.customer: Independent RIAs and next-gen advisors building audiences, dual registrants at small broker-dealers, and advisor-creators.
ideas.who_pays: The advisor personally or from marketing spend. Anchors: Wealthtender about $49-59/mo, FMG about $178/mo, and lead gen at roughly $5k/mo in one cited case, so social is the cheaper channel.
ideas.problem: Public video is generally an advertisement or retail communication; influencer programs are named exam topics (Dec 2025 Risk Alert, FINRA). Archiving TikTok has been manual per a 2020 article (current vendor support unverified). Existing tools are sold to firms, not to the creator.
ideas.solution: Web app and phone share sheet; AI first pass on transcript and caption; disclosure overlay; archive via export, API or screen-record fallback; approval packet that drops into Smarsh, Hearsay or a consultant's queue.
ideas.why_now: Finfluencer scrutiny; Notice 26-14 would treat all social media alike (removing the static versus interactive split); consumers increasingly discover advisors on social.
ideas.founder_edge: Gen Z native who knows what hooks work and can build the content side too. Per the old Gust profile, MFA's historical product is social-media training for advisors, so this is the software layer for that training and Ron can co-brand it.
ideas.first_10_customers: MFA's roster for the first 10; Asher DMs 100 advisor-creators on public profiles with a free clip review; convert at $49/mo after a live demo.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest weak point: advisor-creators number in the thousands and a broker-dealer rep cannot adopt a tool without firm approval; 1% of 639,723 reps at $300/yr is under $2M. It only gets bigger if sold to firms and networks as an approved-creator program at $10-40 per rep per month. Ceiling $5-15M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Hearsay, Smarsh, Archive Intel (YouTube archiving), Global Relay, Saifr and Hadrius (video review), PerformLine (finfluencer monitoring for firms), and Marky-style schedulers that have no archiving. Nothing found built for the individual creator. Kill test: if 20 creator-advisors will not pay $49 after a live demo, stop.

ideas.title: Roll-up Marketing Integration Desk for RIA acquirers and aggregators
ideas.one_liner: Marketing-claims diligence and clean-up for acquirers: scan a target's sites, microsites, social, testimonials and awards before close, then keep every acquired firm's distributed marketing under one ledger afterward.
ideas.customer: Chief compliance officers and integration leads at RIA aggregators and acquisitive mid-size RIAs; also breakaway-advisor transition teams.
ideas.who_pays: The acquirer, from deal and integration budget: $2-5k per target for diligence (my estimate), then $200-500 per firm per month for portfolio monitoring; an enterprise contract across 50-400 affiliated firms could be $100-500k/yr (my estimate, unverified).
ideas.problem: Mintz (Feb 2026) names buyers and breakaways as higher-risk Marketing Rule groups: acquired firms bring dated testimonials, stale awards, branch advisors posting independently and alternative trade-name microsites. Aggregators inherit all of it at once.
ideas.solution: Idea 1's scanner run in bulk with an acquirer-specific report, plus the Idea 3 ledger across all affiliated firms and a standard set of marketing policies deployed centrally.
ideas.why_now: The Dec 2025 Risk Alert and commentary explicitly name these groups; RIA M&A pace is high (deal counts not verified in this research).
ideas.founder_edge: Ron's 24 years of peer relationships are the only way in; enterprise buyers will not take an 18-year-old seriously cold.
ideas.first_10_customers: This will not produce 10 customers in 90 days. Realistic: 1-2 diligence jobs via Ron's introductions, then a pilot. Do not start here; build it as a phase-2 expansion of Idea 1.
ideas.path_to_big: Aggregators are the large payers and one enterprise logo equals dozens of small RIAs, which is how a small-firm product reaches $10M+ faster. Honest drawbacks: slow sales cycle, few buyers, high concentration, and heavy reliance on Ron's relationships.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Law-firm and consulting diligence (manual), Smarsh and Hearsay enterprise suites for distributed marketing, and Hadrius and Sedric for large firms. Kill test: if Ron cannot get two introductions to aggregator CCOs, park it.

ideas.title: Backtest Audit and Gated Delivery (from his Strategy Lab)
ideas.one_liner: Upload a model portfolio or strategy; an independent engine reproduces the backtest from raw data, produces net-of-fee results and the required assumptions and risk disclosures, and delivers them behind a gate (qualified viewer, attestation, audit log) with the policy text the SEC fined firms for lacking.
ideas.customer: RIAs, strategists, TAMP model providers and newsletter publishers who show model or backtested performance.
ideas.who_pays: The owner or CCO at $149-399/mo or $1,500-3,000 per audited strategy. Penalty anchors: Atlas $175k, Pacific Financial $430k (Aug 2024), and $50k-175k each in the Sept 2023 nine-adviser sweep.
ideas.problem: Hypothetical performance includes model, backtested and projected returns, and the SEC's position is that it generally cannot go to a mass audience, yet firms still post it. The 2023 cases alleged no wrong numbers, only missing audience-relevance procedures. Atlas claimed Morningstar verified numbers it had not, and its models did not follow its advertised formulas.
ideas.solution: Reproducibility report, net-of-fee computation, disclosure pack, gated page, audit log and a template policy for the CCO to adopt. It does not make content legal; it produces the evidence the CCO needs and reduces mass-audience exposure.
ideas.why_now: Continued sweeps and a rising volume of AI-generated 'strategies'; the March 2024 AI-washing cases cost two advisers $400k combined.
ideas.founder_edge: His Strategy Lab (25 pre-registered strategies, 1927-2025, with holdouts where early winners flopped) is exactly the reproducibility discipline this needs.
ideas.first_10_customers: Find advisors in Ron's network who show model portfolios; give one a free audit as a case study; approach 5 newsletter and model providers at $1,500 per audit.
ideas.path_to_big: Weak: about 3,000 firms at $2,400/yr is roughly $7M and the true market may be smaller. This is the idea most at risk of being a boutique. Venture-scale only if repositioned as claims verification for TAMPs and model marketplaces that must vet hundreds of strategists; otherwise keep it as a module of Idea 1.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Performance systems (Orion, Black Diamond, Morningstar) compute numbers; GIPS verifiers serve large managers; Hadrius and Saifr flag language but do not reproduce numbers; law firms write checklists. I found no vendor that audits and gates backtests for small RIAs. Kill test: if five advisors who post model performance would rather delete it than pay, the demand is just avoidance.

ideas.title: Cleared Claims API: pre-substantiated facts for AI-written content
ideas.one_liner: A licensed library and API of atomic, cited, dated, rule-tagged facts (tax limits, historical market statistics, fee benchmarks, product facts) so AI drafts cite cleared facts instead of hallucinated numbers, with every use writing a substantiation record.
ideas.customer: AI writing and meeting tools serving advisors, content platforms, and advisors directly.
ideas.who_pays: Vendors at $500-5,000/mo API licenses; advisors direct at $29/mo. A budget line exists: advisors and firms already pay for content libraries (FMG at roughly $178-$1,044/mo).
ideas.problem: The Marketing Rule requires a reasonable basis to substantiate material facts on demand and firms must keep the support; AI invents numbers, and reviewers re-verify by hand. One AI scheduler reviewed admits it has no built-in archiving.
ideas.solution: Agents keep about 5,000 atomic facts fresh from primary sources (IRS notices, SSA, Fed, BLS); a credentialed reviewer verifies each; every fact has a citation, as-of date and expiry; the API returns facts plus disclosure snippets and logs usage as the substantiation file.
ideas.why_now: AI-written content volume; the Dec 2025 Risk Alert and commentary stress substantiation files; distribution partners (FMG, Hearsay, note-takers) already exist.
ideas.founder_edge: His multi-agent research pipelines and his own lesson that search snippets have returned fabricated quotes, so verification is built in; Kevin Condon's CFP and PhD as reviewer credibility.
ideas.first_10_customers: MFA's own content as customer zero; 10 advisors at $29/mo; 1-2 small AI-tool vendors through Ron (Hadrius's investors include founders of Altruist, Jump AI and FINNY, so those founders are reachable).
ideas.path_to_big: If it works: API licenses to thousands of financial AI vendors at $1-5k/mo, roughly $10-30M, and a real data asset. Biggest risk is that LLMs with live search commoditize facts and incumbents' pre-approved libraries already cover common ones. Unproven; ranked last for risk, not size.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FMG and Hearsay pre-approved content and AI coaches, Advisor Perspectives and Kitces content, Morningstar. I found no atomic-fact API aimed at AI drafts but could not confirm either way. Kill test: if no AI-tool vendor pays or signs an LOI within 45 days, stop.

ideas.title: MA Rate Truth: Medicare Advantage contract repricing plus peer rate benchmark for post-acute providers
ideas.one_liner: Reprice every Medicare Advantage payment an agency receives against its contract (his freight-audit engine, pointed at remits), then show owners how their MA rates rank against peers.
ideas.customer: Owner, CEO or MA-contracting lead of a Florida home health agency or hospice (1-20 agencies); later SNFs, therapy groups, DME suppliers and clinics.
ideas.who_pays: The owner or CFO. Two budget lines: (1) recovered underpayments, 20-25% contingency with nothing upfront; (2) MA contract negotiation: $2,500 flat diagnostic, then $12-24k a year for the peer benchmark.
ideas.problem: An 835 remit shows what a plan paid, not what the contract said it owed, and contract rate versions change. Florida is about 60% Medicare Advantage (roughly 3.1M of 5.2M beneficiaries) and has the most 2027 plan discontinuations in the US (offerings 611 to 560; about 81k South Florida members in plans that end or merge), so owners must re-contract with no market-rate information. No public dataset of negotiated MA home health rates exists; the NAHC/HHFMA MA survey results are not public. MedPAC says fee-for-service margin is 21.2% while industry says MA margins are low or negative, so MA is where margin leaks.
ideas.solution: Monday: ask MHC for 12 months of 835/ERA files and the MA rate exhibits for its top 3 plans under a BAA with minimum-necessary fields. Use Claude to parse contracts into structured terms (percent of PDGM base, per-visit and LUPA rates, auth rules, timely filing, sequestration). Reprice every remit line deterministically with the freight-audit rating engine; output a variance list with contract citations and a dispute-letter pack. Phase 2: an opt-in co-op showing each member its percent-of-Medicare by payer versus the peer median.
ideas.why_now: Florida leads the nation in 2027 MA plan exits; the CY2027 proposed rule keeps a 3% temporary Medicare cut (about $4.9B recoupment, possibly about 10 years) and MedPAC wants a further 7% cut, so every agency is hunting for MA margin. CMS-0057-F decision-time rules (72h/7d, in effect 2026) and payer API deadlines (Jan 2027) are reshuffling payer provider operations.
ideas.founder_edge: It is the freight-audit playbook (flat diagnostic plus contingency, repricing invoices against a tariff) transplanted onto remits and contracts, and he has already built that service but not sold it. His blind-test habit yields a proof artifact ('found $X in 90 days at MHC, verified by their billing lead'). MHC supplies real contracts and remits; his mother sees AR; the grandfather knows peer owners. Works even if MHC is a clinic or pharmacy rather than home health, because it rests on contracts and remits.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1: MHC (three or more LLCs means three or more MA contract sets). 2-5: the grandfather's peer owners, offered a free 'MA contract X-ray' on one payer in exchange for contributing anonymized percent-of-Medicare figures to the benchmark. 6-10: healthcare CPAs and billing companies serving Florida agencies, offered white-label audits for a rev share. Contingency pricing means the buyer risks nothing.
ideas.path_to_big: About 12,234 Medicare-certified agencies (MedPAC 2024) plus hospices and SNFs. At $15-25k average (subscription plus recoveries), 500 customers is $7.5-12.5M; $100M needs about 4,000 customers or a second layer: the data becomes the post-acute MA rate standard sold to PE buyers (diligence), lenders, plans' network teams and other provider types (the hospital rate-transparency model). Biggest risks: MA contracts often carry confidentiality clauses (design so owners enter percent-of-Medicare figures they control, not documents; counsel to confirm); the 1996 DOJ/FTC health care safety zones were withdrawn in 2023 so the benchmark needs an antitrust-counsel design; per-agency recoveries under about $15k a year would make the audit alone a boutique.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Remit-versus-contract underpayment tools exist for hospitals and physician practices (Lido, Rivet Health, RecoveAR). I found no post-acute-specific one: Axxess plus Texas Capital only does payment matching, Healthware is billing, and REVA on Microsoft Marketplace is generic. Hospital rate-transparency firms (Turquoise Health, Serif; not searched) show the data model works but cover hospitals. Inside the agency, the incumbent is its own biller and RCM firms like SimiTree.

ideas.title: StuckCash: the order-to-cash desk for home health and hospice
ideas.one_liner: Show an agency in dollars which claims are blocked and by whom (unsigned certifications, missing face-to-face, RCD holds, ADRs, MA auths) and run the chase automatically.
ideas.customer: Administrator, CFO or billing manager of a Medicare-certified home health agency or hospice; owner signs.
ideas.who_pays: The owner. Budget lines: billing staff payroll (outsourced billing commonly 3-6% of collections, unverified) and the cost of working capital. Flat $1.5-4k a month with a first-60-days 'cash release' guarantee.
ideas.problem: Final Medicare claims cannot be billed until the physician-signed certification and plan of care are in; one unsigned order can hold a period's payment, and billing without signatures creates overpayment liability. Florida is in the Review Choice Demonstration (extended 5 years from June 2024); pre-claim affirmations fell nationally from 96.2% to 85.5% (FY22-FY23), and the 90% affirmation threshold decides whether an agency gets lighter review. Staff chase by fax, and nobody ranks blocked dollars by cause.
ideas.solution: Start with read-only report exports from the EHR (HCHB, Axxess, WellSky), no integration. Produce a daily stuck-cash worklist ranked by dollars blocked, root cause and age. Automate the chase with e-sign links, fax and a voice agent to physician offices. At referral, verify the certifying physician is Medicare-enrolled and the face-to-face is valid so claims don't deny later. Later, size a working-capital facility off the same data through partner lenders (Medicare receivables cannot be assigned, so structure matters).
ideas.why_now: A 3% temporary cut plus a possible further 7% MedPAC cut leave no margin to waste on slow cash; the nationwide moratorium (2026-05-13) removes new competitors so cash discipline is the main lever left; RCD affirmation requirements are live in Florida.
ideas.founder_edge: Same instinct as the freight audit ('money stuck in paperwork') and he builds browser and portal agents fast. MHC's staff can show a real aging report and the real chase process on day one; the family company is a pilot with real stakes. Needs MHC to be a home health or hospice operator.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1: MHC, run in shadow mode for 30 days first. 2-5: peer agencies via the grandfather, offered a free 90-day 'stuck cash X-ray' built from an aging report alone. 6-10: state trade association members and events (Florida Hospices and Palliative Care Association runs documentation webinars; exact association names to confirm), then EHR user groups.
ideas.path_to_big: About 12,234 agencies plus hospices. $30k a year times 350 customers is about $10.5M; $100M needs about 3,300 customers or the financing layer: receivables lending against agency cashflow with the data as the underwriting edge, built through partner lenders first (capital-intensive). Biggest risks: EHR vendors (Axxess, HCHB/Trella, WellSky) bolt on similar order management and can block export access; a voice agent calling physicians raises HIPAA and TCPA questions.
ideas.who_does_it_today: EHR order modules plus staff (Axxess even lets agencies mark orders as not needing a signature to stop false chases); Parachute Health (e-ordering for home medical equipment); Claim Health (authorization automation for home health and hospice); Brellium (documentation compliance, not cash); generic voice-AI vendors such as Simbo. I found no startup that combines blocked-dollar ranking with an automated chase for home health.

ideas.title: Certified Agency Exchange: moratorium-era diligence and matching for Medicare-certified agencies
ideas.one_liner: With new agencies frozen out of Medicare, the only way in is to buy a certified one; sell buyers a data-driven 'Medicare agency X-ray' first and a marketplace later.
ideas.customer: Buyers (regional operators, PE-backed platforms, clinician-owners locked out by the freeze) and the brokers and healthcare attorneys who serve them.
ideas.who_pays: The buyer or broker: $5-15k per diligence report; a success fee later only if counsel clears the licensing question. Signer is the buyer's corp-dev lead or the owner.
ideas.problem: CMS imposed a nationwide moratorium on new Medicare enrollment of home health agencies (and hospices, per Mintz and JD Supra) on 2026-05-13, six months and renewable, including new branches. A majority ownership change inside the 36-month window requires re-enrollment and is blocked. Buyers get broker marketing (BizQuest lists a Tampa Bay certified agency 'with 12 MA contracts'), not independent risk data, while valuations are high (Kinderhook-Enhabit implies about 10.7x on $103.1M EBITDA; broker guides say 6-12x).
ideas.solution: Build the agency X-ray from public data: Care Compare, claims utilization, enrollment dates (to compute the 36-month clock), OIG exclusions, AHCA licensing and survey history, referral concentration. Then use AI to read the seller's data room (cost reports, remits, MA contracts and assignability, aging) and output red flags, a valuation range and a closing checklist.
ideas.why_now: The freeze began 2026-05-13 and the first term lapses around 2026-11-13 unless renewed; the CY2027 proposed rule adds a 10-year revocation bar that makes inherited enrollment errors an acquirer's problem.
ideas.founder_edge: The grandfather is an owner who knows peer owners and brokers; his mentor rolled up an AV integrator and teaches entrepreneurship (real M&A credibility); family investment connections reach buyers. Needs MHC to be a certified home health or hospice operator for the owner network to apply.
ideas.first_10_customers: Cold-email brokers listing certified agencies on BizQuest and BizBuySell with a free sample X-ray built from public data on their own listing. Mentor and family introduce 2-3 healthcare M&A attorneys who want cheap first-pass screening; customers 6-10 are buyers those attorneys refer.
ideas.path_to_big: About 12,234 agencies. If 5% change hands yearly at $5M average enterprise value and a 2% fee, the fee pool is about $30M a year; reaching $10M needs about a third of it, which is heroic. Biggest risks: if CMS lets the freeze lapse in mid-November the scarcity premium fades and the why-now is used up (check the Federal Register before building); success fees may trigger broker or securities rules so sell diligence reports only until counsel says otherwise; M&A buyers will not hire an 18-year-old, so white-label through a CPA or attorney.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Brokers and M&A advisers (valuation guides such as Ad Astra Equity; listing sites BizQuest and BizBuySell); Definitive Healthcare and Trella Health sell market data. I found no AI diligence product for home health or hospice.

ideas.title: Storm Desk: continuity-of-care outreach for power-dependent and homebound patients
ideas.one_liner: Before landfall, text and call every homebound patient by acuity and zone, confirm shelter and evacuation plans, and after landfall tell the agency whom to visit first, with audit-ready proof.
ideas.customer: Administrators and DONs at home health agencies and hospices, home oxygen and DME suppliers, assisted living facilities; later county emergency management, utilities and MA plans.
ideas.who_pays: The operating budget; Medicare home health emergency preparedness rules (42 CFR 484.102, from my recollection, to verify) require a plan, patient-specific risk assessment and testing. About $25-40 per census patient per year, so $8-16k for a 400-patient agency.
ideas.problem: Florida counties must keep a special-needs registry (F.S. 252.355) but registration is voluntary and renews yearly. After Hurricane Irma, tens of thousands of elderly Floridians relied on power-dependent equipment, and Hillsborough County's registry (about 2,800) was far smaller than the federal emPOWER count. Agencies do outreach by hand, one patient at a time.
ideas.solution: Pull census and acuity from the EHR export; run an AI voice and text cadence at 72, 48 and 24 hours with a short triage script, escalate to a human and update the county registry; produce a post-storm re-establishment-of-care queue and a surveyor-ready log.
ideas.why_now: The 2024 hurricanes (Helene, Milton) made the risk concrete; the December-to-May off-season is the time to sell and build before the season starts 2027-06-01.
ideas.founder_edge: Voice and text agents are what he ships fastest; the family company is a real Florida pilot with a real census; he can finish well before the season.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC's agencies, then oxygen and DME suppliers and ALFs they know, sold January-April 2027 as annual contracts before the season.
ideas.path_to_big: Agency price points are low; a big outcome needs a second payer: utilities with medical-priority obligations, counties, and MA plans protecting at-risk members across hurricane, wildfire and grid-outage states. That second payer is unproven. Biggest risks: seasonal revenue; outbound calls to patients raise TCPA and HIPAA issues; one serious failure in a real storm is an existential liability.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Mass-notification vendors for hospitals and governments (Everbridge, Rave, Juvare; not searched), federal emPOWER data for officials, and county voluntary registries. My search found no agency-level patient outreach product.

ideas.title: Referral Radar: referral-source intelligence for independent agencies
ideas.one_liner: Weekly ranked list of physicians and facilities worth a liaison visit, built from CMS public data plus the agency's own referral-to-revenue history, with AI-written visit briefs.
ideas.customer: Owner or VP of business development at an independent home health or hospice agency or small chain.
ideas.who_pays: The marketing and liaison budget (liaisons cost an estimated $60-100k each, unverified). $500-1,500 a month.
ideas.problem: With the freeze blocking entrants and supply flat outside California, growth means capturing share. Definitive Healthcare is priced for enterprises and small agencies guess; the 2027 PPO-to-HMO shift in MA plans changes who can refer to whom.
ideas.solution: Ingest CMS public files (physician utilization, home health provider data) plus the agency's referral and admission history by source and payer. Rank by expected admissions and margin (MA versus fee-for-service), auto-brief the liaison before each visit and track follow-up.
ideas.why_now: The moratorium shields incumbents from new entrants, margins are squeezed, and 2027 MA network changes reshuffle referral flows.
ideas.founder_edge: He builds data products fast, and MHC's referral data is a real test set. Needs MHC to be a home health or hospice operator.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC, then the grandfather's peer owners, with a free 'who refers to my competitor' report as the hook.
ideas.path_to_big: About 12,234 agencies at $12k is roughly a $147M ceiling, plus hospices and DME. Biggest risks: Definitive Healthcare (public) and Trella Health (Homecare Homebase's analytics arm, with the Excel Health referral partnership) already sell this and the independent-chain price point is the only gap; it is the least AI-native and most replicable idea in this set.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Definitive Healthcare, Trella Health/Homecare Homebase with Excel Health referral data, and EHR referral modules.

ideas.title: Enrollment Sentinel: continuous Medicare enrollment and ownership compliance monitor
ideas.one_liner: Keep a multi-entity operator out of a 10-year revocation bar by tracking every ownership, managing-employee and licence change deadline and screening every person monthly.
ideas.customer: Owners of multi-entity home health agencies, hospices and DME suppliers (MHC appears to run several 'Area N' LLCs).
ideas.who_pays: Compliance budget and outside counsel (hundreds of dollars an hour). $3-6k a year per organization.
ideas.problem: The CY2027 proposed rule expands disclosure, makes enrollment errors easier to revoke, and bars re-enrollment for 10 years with knock-on effects on the company's other provider numbers. The 36-month rule and the freeze make an error uncurable. Multi-LLC owners track this in spreadsheets.
ideas.solution: Build an ownership and managing-employee register across entities; calendar the 30-day and 90-day change-reporting deadlines, revalidation dates, licence and accreditation expiry; run monthly exclusion screening across OIG, SAM and Florida Medicaid; compare the CMS 855 on file with the real org chart.
ideas.why_now: The final CY2027 rule is expected within weeks, the freeze is live, and the 10-year bar is new.
ideas.founder_edge: The family company is a multi-entity operator and a live test; low build effort. Needs MHC to be a Medicare-enrolled provider.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC, peer multi-entity owners, and healthcare attorneys who want to resell a monitor.
ideas.path_to_big: About 12k agencies plus hospices and 10k+ DME suppliers at about $4k is a plausible $100M ceiling but with small budgets. Biggest risks: exclusion screening is a commodity (credentialing vendors such as Verisys and Streamline Verify, not searched); honest rating: this one risks the tiny-boutique failure mode and only works if it becomes the compliance operating system for every Medicare-enrolled organization.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Exclusion and credentialing vendors, healthcare attorneys and consultants, and EHR vendors' moratorium explainers (Axxess ebook). I did not find a monitor built specifically around ownership disclosure and the 36-month clock.

ideas.title: PBM Contract Reader: underwater-claim alarm and audit shield for independent pharmacies
ideas.one_liner: Read PBM provider manuals, network change notices and MAC lists with AI, flag every claim paid below acquisition cost, and generate the appeal.
ideas.customer: Owner-pharmacist of an independent or small-chain pharmacy, including long-term-care, specialty and infusion pharmacies (applies only if MHC owns or knows a pharmacy).
ideas.who_pays: The owner. $199-499 a month plus 20% of recovered appeals.
ideas.problem: Major PBMs have released specialty-network pricing below acquisition cost for many pharmacies (Frier Levitt alert) and 'cost-plus' networks may become 'cost-minus'; pharmacies are closing faster. Florida's AG issued a civil investigative demand to CVS Caremark in June 2026 and sued Express Scripts and Prime Therapeutics in August 2026. Federal PBM reform was signed 2026-02-03 but most of it takes effect in 2028.
ideas.solution: Per-claim underwater detection against the pharmacy's actual invoice cost; a contract and manual reader that quantifies the profit impact of each change notice and audit risk; appeal packets; later an opt-in claims data pool for litigation support (de-identified, HIPAA reviewed with counsel).
ideas.why_now: Florida AG actions, the 2026 federal law and rising closures.
ideas.founder_edge: Long-document reading and repricing are what he builds; weak family fit unless MHC has a pharmacy.
ideas.first_10_customers: Through MHC's pharmacy contacts if any, the state pharmacy association and PSAOs.
ideas.path_to_big: About 19,000 independent pharmacies (my recollection, unverified) at $1.2-6k a year is $23-115M. Biggest risks: crowded (Pharmacy Marketplace sells underwater-claim recovery as a feature, PharmaPulse is $99 a month, Tideline RCM is a 2025 startup, Frier Levitt sells legal services); federal reform may fix part of the problem by 2028; weak family fit.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Pharmacy Marketplace, PharmaPulse, Tideline RCM, PSAOs, and law firms such as Frier Levitt.

ideas.title: Care Bench: a Gen Z pre-health workforce channel for home health aides and hospice volunteers
ideas.one_liner: Recruit, screen and train college pre-health students into per-visit aide roles and hospice volunteers, and prove the hours.
ideas.customer: Administrator or volunteer coordinator at a home health agency or hospice.
ideas.who_pays: Recruiting and volunteer-coordinator budget. $500-1,500 per placed aide, or $300-600 a month for a hospice volunteer program with hours tracking.
ideas.problem: Hospices must have volunteers provide at least 5% of patient-care hours, and over-counting hours is an audit risk. Pre-health students want clinical hours and listings exist but there is no organized pipeline. Aide turnover and shortages block growth.
ideas.solution: A Gen Z-facing funnel (short video, campus partners), an AI screener, document and background-screen checks, a placement or volunteer scheduler, and eligible-hour logging mapped to what CMS counts. Adults only (18+).
ideas.why_now: With the freeze, labor is the main way incumbents can grow, and workforce funding is flowing into the sector (Abby Care raised $82M on 2026-10-19).
ideas.founder_edge: This is where his Gen Z network actually helps, and the family company can host the first cohort.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC, local hospices, and a few Florida campuses.
ideas.path_to_big: Weak by itself; it scales only if it becomes a national pre-health clinical-experience marketplace. Biggest risks: crowded supply side (Carefam $14.5M, MochaCare, Abby Care, Papa); Florida employment agency or staffing rules to check; guardrails exclude minors.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Carefam, MochaCare, Abby Care, Papa (not searched), volunteer-management modules in hospice EHRs, and campus pre-health programs.

ideas.title: StatusGuard: work-authorization and credential continuity desk for home-based care
ideas.one_liner: A PHI-free system that tracks every aide's work-authorization, license, screening, TB, CPR and in-service dates, maps each expiry onto the client schedule (which patients lose care, how much weekly revenue is at risk), runs counsel-approved reverification workflows, and keeps survey-ready personnel files.
ideas.customer: Owner, administrator or HR lead of a home health, home care or assisted-living operator in Florida (MHC's Area entities first), then multi-site operators nationally.
ideas.who_pays: The agency, from its HR/compliance budget, where I-9 and HRIS tools already cost roughly $3-10 per employee per month. Pricing: $149/mo base + $3 per worker per month, plus a one-time Survey-Ready Personnel File Audit at $1,500-4,000 (about $4.5k/yr for a 75-aide agency). At MHC the signers are the founder-grandfather and Mom's team.
ideas.problem: Authorization cliffs (Haitian TPS, parole, EAD changes) hit an agency all at once. Owners either keep workers who may no longer be authorized or fire authorized ones out of fear (discrimination risk), and the AP reported Florida agencies terminating 17-18 aides at a time. Today it runs on spreadsheets, and nothing connects an expiring document to 'which clients lose their aide and what revenue is at risk'.
ideas.solution: OCR/LLM intake of documents the employee already presented (I-9 docs, EADs, licenses, TB, CPR, screening receipts). The expiry engine follows Form I-9 reverification rules exactly: it flags only documents carrying an expiry date and never infers status from name or origin. It adds an exposure-to-coverage map, pre-drafted worker notices in English/Spanish/Creole, and an audit-gap report. An employment-immigration attorney approves the logic and nothing is reported to any government body. Data is employment records, which HIPAA excludes from PHI, so no BAA is needed.
ideas.why_now: Supreme Court allowed Haitian TPS termination on June 25, 2026; about 158,000 Haitian TPS holders live in Florida (about 404,000 TPS holders total) and immigrants are 46% of Florida's direct care workforce (PHI, June 2026). Court dates and EAD auto-extension rules are in flux, and Florida already mandates E-Verify for employers with 25+ employees.
ideas.founder_edge: Ships documents-to-structured-data pipelines fast. MHC looks like a multi-agency operator (directory listings show MHC Area 6 and Area 10 LLCs, so at least ten Area entities; UNVERIFIED), giving one customer with many sites. He can shadow MHC HR for a week and build against consented real files, with no PHI hurdle. The mentor can pressure-test the managed-services upsell.
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) MHC's Area entities as one deal (audit plus monitoring pilot, priced low but real). (2-4) Three peer owners introduced by the grandfather. (5-7) Agencies met via Florida at Home / HCAOA Florida chapter using a free TPS exposure scan (upload a roster of expiry dates, get a one-page report in 24 hours). (8-10) ALFs and nursing homes through the same associations; the Florida Health Care Association has already lobbied DHS on caregivers.
ideas.path_to_big: Subscription is the base: 12,000 Medicare HHAs x $4.5k is about $54M, and adding non-medical home care, ALFs and nursing homes (counts UNVERIFIED) makes the pool plausibly $130M+; $10M ARR needs about 2,200 agencies, which is a high share on its own. The real upside is the flywheel: each flagged gap becomes a Day-One Desk onboarding or Surge Bench transaction, and the compliance record becomes the system of record for the home-care workforce.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Generic I-9 vendors: Equifax I-9 Management, Mitratech Tracker I-9 (its own guide says TPS reverification dates do not auto-calculate), Experian, Lookout i9 Intelligence, EmpTrust. Home care EMRs (AxisCare, WellSky, Axxess, AlayaCare) likely have basic credential-expiry tracking (assumed, not verified). I found no product tying work authorization to client coverage or producing survey-ready files for home care.

ideas.title: Day-One Desk: done-for-you trilingual onboarding with a 5-day speed guarantee
ideas.one_liner: An onboarding back office (AI plus a few bilingual coordinators) that takes an accepted offer to shift-ready in 5 business days: document chasing, I-9 scheduling with the employer's rep, Level 2 screening, TB, CPR, training, EVV and payroll setup, by text and WhatsApp in English, Spanish and Creole.
ideas.customer: Multi-site home health and home care operators (3+ sites), PE-backed roll-ups and growing independents, starting with MHC's Area entities.
ideas.who_pays: Operations/HR budget that already pays admin time, recruiter time and sign-on bonuses. $350 per aide onboarded (or $1,200/mo + $200 per hire), with the fee waived if the 5-day SLA is missed. Value assumption to validate with MHC: an aide bills about 25 hrs/wk, so each day saved is about $100-150 of revenue and a 7-day cut is $700-1,000 per hire.
ideas.problem: Time-to-first-shift is long because HR staff chase documents, appointments and signatures by phone. Candidates ghost during the gap, wasting the $561+ median recruiting spend, and with 65-79% annual turnover an agency onboards roughly 65-80 aides a year per 100 aides.
ideas.solution: Workflow engine + three-language messaging agent + a small exception desk, producing a complete audit-ready file that feeds StatusGuard. Sold on outcomes: days saved and files that pass survey.
ideas.why_now: The TPS cliff adds a forced replacement wave on top of 65-79% baseline churn, while the 2026 Medicare rate cut (-1.3% aggregate) pushes agencies to cut admin cost.
ideas.founder_edge: The mentor built a roughly $1B company on managed services, so the recurring-service model is home turf. MHC's multi-entity structure supplies volume on day one and real metrics as proof. Asher builds the workflow software in weeks, in school-year hours.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC (pilot at near cost for the first 30 hires, tracking their own time-to-shift-ready), then three owners from the grandfather's circle, then association members through a 20-minute '5-day onboarding' demo, then the mentor's channel contacts.
ideas.path_to_big: Average Medicare HHA hires about 45 aides a year, so $350 x 45 is about $15.7k per agency per year. $10M revenue is about 29,000 onboardings, or roughly 640 agencies, or six to ten PE-backed groups. Every onboarding builds the consented candidate database that powers the Retained-Hire Network and Surge Bench. Gross margin reaches 60-70% only once AI handles most exceptions.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Software only: EngineHire (ATS plus AI agents), Hireology ($60.5M raised as of 2019), Apploi, Nevvon TrainOnce (portable training), Phoebe and Zingage (scheduling/call-outs), plus generic virtual-assistant/BPO firms. I found no one selling a tri-lingual, SLA-priced onboarding service for home care.

ideas.title: Retained-Hire Network: bilingual aide recruiting priced per 90-day retained hire
ideas.one_liner: Pay-on-retention recruiting ($300 at start, $600 at day 90, free replacement if the aide leaves early), sourced through Creole and Spanish community channels (WhatsApp, Facebook groups, churches, radio) and short-form video produced by Gen Z creators.
ideas.customer: Home health and home care agencies in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach that struggle to hire aides, especially Creole- or Spanish-speaking ones.
ideas.who_pays: The recruiting budget. Indeed's median cost per hire is $561 and referral programs $837 (Home Care Pulse, older data); at about 60% 90-day survival the real cost per retained aide is near $900, so $900 with a guarantee is parity that moves the risk to us.
ideas.problem: Postings go unanswered in the languages candidates actually use (some Miami postings still demand fluent English), and cheap sourcing is not cheap when early dropouts never recover their cost.
ideas.solution: Own the channel and a consented candidate list, pre-screen at the document level for work authorization (never by origin), then hand off to Day-One Desk. Referral rewards plus creator content in Creole and Spanish.
ideas.why_now: Authorized-worker supply just shrank, so agencies are bidding for the same smaller pool; community and short-video channels are the cheapest unsaturated sources.
ideas.founder_edge: Gen Z content production at AI speed; MHC staff as the first referral network; his father built a pre-screened, compliance-monitored marketplace (MyFinancialAdvice), the same architecture applied to caregivers.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC's agencies (some Miami agencies already post for Creole-speaking aides), five peers via the grandfather and association introductions, then agencies whose postings seek Creole or Spanish speakers.
ideas.path_to_big: Florida hires of roughly 80k a year x $900 is about $72M; 10% share is $7M. The long-term asset is the opted-in candidate base that feeds Surge Bench and Day-One Desk (a 'Handshake for aides'). Honest weakness: aides skew older than Gen Z, so community channels, not TikTok, will carry volume.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Indeed (the strongest channel per Home Care Pulse), Facebook groups, myCNAjobs, EngineHire, Hireology, Apploi and local recruiters. I found none pricing on 90-day retention with a bilingual community channel.

ideas.title: Surge Bench: AHCA-registered health care services pool for aides and CNAs
ideas.one_liner: A registered pool of pre-cleared W-2 aides and CNAs that agencies, ALFs and nursing homes can call for 2-8 week gaps from TPS departures, hurricanes, mass call-outs or new-contract ramp-ups, sold as prepaid surge blocks.
ideas.customer: Director of nursing or administrator at home health agencies, ALFs and nursing homes in South Florida.
ideas.who_pays: The temporary-labor line. Bill roughly $27-32/hr against $18-19 wages (35-45% markup, an assumption to check against local quotes). Medicaid-funded agencies also lose margin on every unfilled authorized hour.
ideas.problem: When a cohort of aides disappears, the agency either turns away patients or pays emergency premiums.
ideas.solution: Register the LLC as a health care services pool with AHCA (registration about $616, Level 2 screening of the administrator and financial officer, a designated representative who knows the disciplines supplied, so use an MHC or family clinician), employ the bench through StatusGuard-verified files, and sell storm-season and TPS-gap blocks.
ideas.why_now: TPS cliff plus Florida hurricane season, and CMS emergency-preparedness expectations make surge capacity a recurring need.
ideas.founder_edge: MHC can be the anchor customer and the clinical oversight; the vetted-network model comes from his father's company; the bench inherits StatusGuard and Day-One Desk data.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC, three peers, two ALFs, and association contacts.
ideas.path_to_big: Revenue is hours x bill rate: 400k hours a year at $27 is about $10.8M, gross margin about 25-35%. Venture scale only if it becomes an app-based aide marketplace. This is the most cash-hungry idea (payroll float, workers' comp); factoring or a family partner may be needed.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Gento (home health per diem, $5M Series A 2020), Nursa ($80M 2023), CareRev ($50M 2021), ConnectRN, FleetNurse, local staffing agencies; Diem Health (home health per diem) looks like a cautionary tale. I did not find nurse-registry rules, and AHCA requirements must be confirmed directly.

ideas.title: The Ladder: registered-apprenticeship sponsor for home-based care (aide to CNA to LPN to RN)
ideas.one_liner: An intermediary that registers and runs a home health aide to nurse apprenticeship, handles on-the-job hour logs, related instruction and wage steps with AI, and pulls in state workforce dollars, with a track for internationally trained clinicians already in South Florida.
ideas.customer: Employers as sponsors (home health agencies, ALFs), with a Florida college or school district as the grant partner.
ideas.who_pays: Employer admin fee ($1,200-2,000 per apprentice per year, assumption) plus training dollars from Florida's Pathways to Career Opportunities Grant (a $14.6M recent round that has funded an EMT apprenticeship) and CareerSource programs.
ideas.problem: RN and LPN vacancies cost agencies five-figure recruiter fees while 79% aide turnover wastes training spend.
ideas.solution: Register the program, standardize wage steps and instruction with a partner college, and run all tracking and reporting in software; add NCLEX and credential-pathway coaching for internationally trained clinicians who already hold work authorization.
ideas.why_now: Apprenticeship funding is bipartisan and growing; WES counts 165,000-263,000 underemployed immigrants with health degrees; Massachusetts shows a home health aide apprenticeship working through an intermediary (12 of 12 apprentices active).
ideas.founder_edge: Documentation-heavy compliance is exactly what AI builds well; MHC can be the lead sponsor with a shadowable training program.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC as lead sponsor, a partner college (Miami Dade College or FIU, by introduction), and peers from associations.
ideas.path_to_big: A national apprenticeship operating system for care work. Caveats: this is a longer fuse (first cash likely after 90 days), and DOL's July 2026 $162M awards covered non-healthcare sectors while the only per-apprentice payment I found ($3,500) was for manufacturing, so a federal healthcare money path is UNVERIFIED.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No Florida home health aide apprenticeship intermediary found. Massachusetts programs, PHI, Nevvon's mentorship (funded by a $971,600 state workforce grant), college LPN-to-RN bridges, WES Global Talent Bridge and Upwardly Global-type nonprofits.

ideas.title: Wage Radar: pay, bonus and turnover benchmarks for home care by ZIP
ideas.one_liner: Weekly pay and benefit benchmarks built from licensed job-posting data plus anonymized contributions from member agencies, with a sign-on and referral bonus optimizer.
ideas.customer: Agency owners, PE firms and lenders in home care, and state Medicaid agencies and MCOs doing rate studies.
ideas.who_pays: Agency owners $149-499/mo, PE firms and lenders $10-50k a year for data feeds, state Medicaid agencies/MCOs $25-100k per rate study.
ideas.problem: Owners set pay blind, and a pay mistake means a hiring crisis or margin loss.
ideas.solution: Licensed job-posting data plus anonymized payroll contributions, aggregated by ZIP and role, with a recommended pay and bonus range and a retention forecast.
ideas.why_now: Florida's minimum wage should have reached $15.00 on Sept 30, 2026 (from memory of Amendment 2, UNVERIFIED), compressing the ladder when Miami aides earn about $16-24/hr; Medicare rates fell 1.3% in 2026; the Medicaid 80/20 pass-through (effective 2030 per LeadingAge) will eventually require wage documentation.
ideas.founder_edge: Data pipelines and scraping skills; MHC as the first contributor.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC, five association members, and two PE or lender contacts through family.
ideas.path_to_big: Small on its own (probably a $2-6M ceiling); valuable as the data layer of the stack and as a lead magnet for ideas 1-4.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Activated Insights (formerly Home Care Pulse) benchmarking surveys, Lightcast, Indeed and Glassdoor salary pages, BLS OEWS (free but lagged and not by ZIP). Antitrust caution: competitor wage sharing needs aggregation, anonymization and lag, and scraping must respect site terms.

ideas.title: Campus Corps: pre-health students as W-2 home health aides
ideas.one_liner: Recruit pre-nursing and pre-med undergrads (18+ only) at FIU, UM, FAU, Nova and Miami Dade College, train them to the 75-hour aide standard through the employer, and place them part-time with MHC and peers, with a clinical-hours reference letter as the perk.
ideas.customer: Home health agencies and ALFs in South Florida that need part-time, work-authorized aides.
ideas.who_pays: Agencies pay a $500-800 placement fee plus a managed-bench margin on hours worked.
ideas.problem: Authorized-worker supply is shrinking while pre-health students need patient-contact hours and cannot find flexible, well-supervised aide work.
ideas.solution: Campus ambassadors, a cohort-based aide training track run through partner agencies, scheduling that respects class timetables, and a reference-letter and hours-verification program.
ideas.why_now: US-citizen and permanent-resident students are immune to authorization shocks, and pre-health clinical experience is in demand.
ideas.founder_edge: His college-applicant world is the same peer group, and he can recruit ambassadors directly. Weaknesses: part-time class schedules, semester churn, and fit with skilled home health visits.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC, three peers, and campus pre-health clubs as the supply side.
ideas.path_to_big: An early-career health workforce marketplace; ceiling unclear and likely below the first four ideas.
ideas.who_does_it_today: CareYaya (25,000+ enrolled students, grant-funded, non-medical, families pay $15+/hr) and Papa (Medicare-Advantage-funded companionship, still expanding as of Aug 2026). Neither places students as W-2 aides for Medicare HHAs.

ideas.title: Voz: voice-first visit notes for aides in Creole, Spanish and English
ideas.one_liner: Aides speak a note and the system returns a structured English visit note, incident report and timesheet note for the agency's EMR.
ideas.customer: Home health and home care agencies with many Creole- or Spanish-dominant aides.
ideas.who_pays: The agency at $3-5 per aide per month from the QA/operations budget, justified by fewer documentation denials and survey findings.
ideas.problem: Aides who are less fluent in written English produce thin or late notes, causing documentation errors and survey deficiencies.
ideas.solution: Voice or WhatsApp voice-note intake, transcription, structuring into the agency's note templates, and EMR export, built under a BAA at MHC first.
ideas.why_now: Speech models are cheap and good, and aides' languages are the bottleneck as the English-fluent pool shrinks.
ideas.founder_edge: Fast AI builds; MHC for real note formats and a BAA pilot. Risks: Haitian Creole accuracy is untested, PHI means a BAA is required, and buyer pain is weaker than in ideas 1-4.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC pilot, then association peers.
ideas.path_to_big: An embedded layer for EMRs and EVV vendors; low priority and small as a standalone.
ideas.who_does_it_today: EMR and EVV mobile apps (Spanish interfaces), clinician AI scribes, Nevvon (multilingual training). I did not find an aide-voice documentation product in Creole.

ideas.title: Payer Truth: contract-compliance audits of Medicare Advantage and managed-care pay for home-health agencies
ideas.one_liner: Port his freight-invoice audit engine to home health: compare every remittance (835) with the agency's payer contract, recover underpayments for 25% of what comes back, and pool the results into the first payer-performance benchmark for post-acute care.
ideas.customer: Owner or CFO of an independent Medicare-certified home-health agency (or small group) with $3M+ a year from Medicare Advantage, commercial and managed Medicaid; Florida first (1,079 agencies in 2023, MA about 57% of Florida Medicare).
ideas.who_pays: The agency, from found money never in its cash forecast: $2,500 flat diagnostic credited against 25% of recovered dollars. Benchmark: outsourced RCM costs about 5-10% of collections. Signer is the owner/CFO.
ideas.problem: MedPAC (Mar 2026): FFS Medicare margin 21.2% but all-payer margin only 5.0%, so the non-FFS book is where agencies bleed. MA now exceeds FFS in home-health volume and pays less. Plans pay by their own methods (percent of Medicare PDGM rate, per episode, per visit), re-group claims with their own logic, and (general knowledge, to test on real contracts) load new Medicare rates late each January. A remit that 'paid' is never re-checked against the contract, so shortfalls close as normal payments. Assumed leakage 2-4% of MA revenue (a vendor cites up to 4%); this is the number to test first.
ideas.solution: Ingest 835s plus contract PDFs (LLM extracts rate terms into a rules table); recompute expected payment per claim with CMS's public grouper/pricer or per-visit tables; file dispute packets citing contract sections inside each plan's window; run a 'January rate-reset watch' on the first 60 days of 2027 remits after the CY2027 final rule; add a payer P&L showing which plans to renegotiate or drop. Legal premise: cash must flow only to agency-owned accounts (Medicare/Medicaid billing-agent rules, 42 CFR 424.73/447.10, general knowledge, unverified); have a healthcare attorney confirm a percentage fee, with flat-per-dispute as fallback. BAA, minimum-necessary data, zero-retention model API.
ideas.why_now: MA is now the majority payer (55.4% nationally, about 57% in Florida). MedPAC recommends a 7% cut for 2027 while CMS says 2025 payments exceeded cost by about 34%, so owners are hunting margin. The CY2027 final rule lands about November and resets Medicare rates Jan 1, 2027, which falls inside his 90-day window. CMS-0057-F gives plans 72-hour and 7-day clocks, making plan behavior measurable.
ideas.founder_edge: The freight audit he already built is the same machine (invoice vs contract tariff becomes remit vs contract), so he is productizing something that exists. Blind-test habit for proving recovery rates. Family agency as pilot and proof, if the MHC identity checks out. Mentor and grandfather supply owner-to-owner trust he cannot buy.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Family agency: sign BAA, pull 12 months of 835s and MA contracts, free scan, fee only on recovery. 2-4) Three owner-peers through the grandfather's calls. 5-6) Two via state home care association and Alliance for Care at Home webinars. 7-8) Two via CPAs/healthcare attorneys serving agencies (no referral fees until counsel reviews). 9-10) Two via the mentor's network or cold outreach to Florida owners offering a free scan of 3 months of remits. Kill test: if the family's MA remits show shortfalls under 0.5% of MA revenue, drop it.
ideas.path_to_big: MA home-health revenue is roughly $12-16B (my estimate: FFS is $16.0B, MA volume now exceeds FFS but pays less). At 2% leakage the pool is about $280M a year, so the 25% fee pool is about $70M (about $140M at 4%). $10M a year is about 15% of the fee pool. $100M is NOT reachable in home health alone: it needs hospice, SNF and therapy contracts plus data licensing (payer benchmarks sold to associations, hospital systems and investors).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nobody found that models home-health case-mix contracts. Adjacent: HHAeXchange RCM (lists underpayment recovery, claims 97% payment success), Prochant, ASPR CMS Solutions (Florida home-health billing; underpayment case studies for physician groups), Claim Health (YC, $4.4M seed; payment reconciliation), and generic underpayment engines for physicians and hospitals (PMM, Lido, Contracto, RecoveAR, Genzeon REVA).

ideas.title: Documentation-to-Cash Desk: Review Choice packet QA and signed-order release
ideas.one_liner: An EHR-agnostic AI-plus-human desk that checks Review Choice Demonstration packets for the exact defects Palmetto denies (F2F unrelated to the primary diagnosis, missing notes or certifications) and chases unsigned physician orders so held claims release, billed per affirmed packet or released claim.
ideas.customer: Administrator or billing/compliance director at a Florida (then TX, IL, OH, NC, OK) Medicare home-health agency in pre-claim or postpayment review, or sitting on claims held for unsigned orders.
ideas.who_pays: The agency, from PCR-coordinator and order-chaser payroll (my estimate $45-60K loaded each). Flat per-item pricing, not percent of dollars (avoids the billing-agent percentage issue): about $12-20 per packet affirmed first time, $150 per overturned level 1 appeal, $15-25 per held claim released.
ideas.problem: FY2024 RCD approval was 84.4% against the 90% target that unlocks relief, and 51.6% of level 1 appeals were overturned, so many denials are fixable paperwork. Palmetto's top denial reasons: F2F not related to the primary reason or missing, no certification or plan of care, no order. Vendors call unsigned orders the top cause of held claims; Medicare cannot final-bill until every order is signed, and orders never signed become bad debt.
ideas.solution: (1) Pre-submission checker: F2F date window (within 90 days before or 30 days after start of care), encounter relevance to primary reason, homebound narrative, signatures and dates, pass/fix list. (2) Resubmission and level 1 appeal drafting. (3) Order chase by fax, SMS and e-sign links with a signature-turnaround scorecard per physician. (4) Dashboard of the 6-month cycle affirmation rate vs 90%. Documentation checks only, no clinical decisions; BAA; agency keeps its Palmetto portal credentials.
ideas.why_now: RCD was extended five years from June 2024 (to about May 2029) and the 25%-reduction option was removed, pushing more agencies into PCR or postpayment. CMS's July 2026 proposal cuts the OASIS deadline from 4.5 months to 45 days, tightening back-office timing. The nationwide moratorium on new agencies and branches means incumbents must defend margin rather than expand.
ideas.founder_edge: His multi-agent research pipelines and detector work are document judgement at scale; Palmetto's checklists are public. If Mom works inside the company she can walk him through real packets. Family agency is the live test bed and first reference.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Family agency: PCR packets plus a held-claims aging report. 2-4) Three peers via the grandfather. 5-8) Four more Florida administrators via Palmetto-region webinars and association events. 9-10) Two via EHR user groups. Pilot offer: the first 30 days priced only on packets that affirm first time.
ideas.path_to_big: Six RCD states likely hold about 4,000-5,000 agencies (my estimate; Florida alone 1,079). At about $35K per agency a year the pool is about $150M; agencies that hit 90% need less, so assume 40% stay: about $60M, and $10M is about 16% of it. The RCD sunsets around May 2029. The durable second act is an orders and F2F release network that works in all 50 states: 12,000+ agencies at about $20K is a $240M pool with physician-side network effects.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Enzo Health ($26M raised; agentic EHR with intake, QA, order tracking, claim prep), EHR modules (Axxess, HCHB), SimiTree (order-management consulting, SARA chart review), in-house PCR coordinators, Axxess RCD webinars. No outsourced, per-result, EHR-agnostic desk found. Biggest risk: it works itself out of a job at each client, and Enzo or the EHRs absorb it.

ideas.title: Chart Integrity Radar: audit-defensibility scoring for the AI-scribe era
ideas.one_liner: Use his AI-text and similarity detection to find cloned, copy-forward and templated visit notes and F2F narratives, so the agency fixes them before a Medicare auditor flags them.
ideas.customer: Compliance officer, director of nursing or QA director at a home-health agency adopting AI scribes (hospices later).
ideas.who_pays: The agency's QA and audit-response budget: $0.60-1.25 per note reviewed with a $500 a month minimum, or $100 per ADR (record request) pre-check; entry product is a $2,500 baseline report.
ideas.problem: AI scribes cut charting time sharply (Enzo claims 75%), producing uniform language. Medicare contractor notices (NGS, 2012) treat cloned or template-worded notes as failing medical necessity regardless of source, and 2026 compliance commentary says AI-generated notes carry the same risk. Palmetto still denies for documentation that does not show skilled need (40 of 942 denials in one quarter) and for F2F narratives. No agency has a tool that measures its own sameness. Gap: I found no current CMS or MAC guidance specific to AI-written home-health notes.
ideas.solution: Embedding and n-gram clustering across patients, clinicians and time; copy-forward detection within one patient's chart; narrative vs structured-data consistency (vitals, diagnoses, visit times); ranked fix list for QA staff; weekly score by clinician and discipline; ADR packet pre-check. It only flags for human review and never edits a clinical record or helps hide AI use. BAA or de-identified batches for the demo.
ideas.why_now: Ambient AI scribes are shipping into home health now (Enzo Scribe), CMS's July 2026 proposal pushes program integrity, and the shorter OASIS deadline pushes agencies toward faster, more templated documentation.
ideas.founder_edge: His detect-ai-writing skill and a detector that beat commercial tools in blind tests, plus a draft-comparison method. A 90-second demo on 500 de-identified notes ('14 clusters of near-identical narratives') sells itself.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Family agency (de-identified 500-note batch). 2-4) Three peers via the grandfather. 5-6) Two via audit-defense and compliance consultants who want a tool. 7-10) Four via owner groups and EHR user communities. Demo first, price after the first report.
ideas.path_to_big: About 12,000 home-health agencies plus roughly 6,000 hospices (general knowledge) at about $12K a year is about $216M, so $10M is about 5%. Distribution through EHR marketplaces, audit-defense firms and regulatory-liability insurers; the score could become something buyers, lenders and insurers ask for.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Enzo QA (clinical and regulatory accuracy), Olli Health and SimiTree SARA (coding and OASIS), MAC/UPIC analytics. No clone-detection product found, but I searched only once, so verify. Biggest risk: demand may be latent until audits bite, and Enzo could add a similarity check quickly.

ideas.title: Triple-Match: authorization, EVV and claim reconciliation for Florida Medicaid home care
ideas.one_liner: Move the freight three-way match (contract, receipt, invoice) to Florida Medicaid home care (authorization, EVV visit, claim) and chase every delivered visit that went unpaid, using the state's claim-dispute program.
ideas.customer: Owner or billing manager of a Florida skilled home-health agency, personal care or homemaker agency, or nurse registry paid by Statewide Medicaid Managed Care plans. If the family agency is Medicare-only, it needs a different pilot.
ideas.who_pays: The agency: 15-20% of recovered dollars, or $8-15 per resolved visit if percentage pay is barred (Medicaid billing-agent rule, 42 CFR 447.10, general knowledge, verify).
ideas.problem: Florida plans deny home health and personal care claims that are not EVV-verified through HHAeXchange. Molina returns code N821 ('visit not found'); manual claims are denied (Molina from July 1, 2024, Sunshine from Jan 30, 2025); edited visit times hurt the compliance rate; disputes need electronic clinical notes plus ticket numbers, and time sheets do not count. Agencies write off visits that were actually delivered.
ideas.solution: Nightly pull of schedules, EVV visits, authorizations, claims and remits. Flags: delivered but unbilled, billed with no EVV, open exceptions, units beyond authorization, claims nearing timely filing. Builds each appeal packet to that plan's rules, escalates unresolved items to AHCA's claim-dispute program (Fla. Stat. 408.7057 covers Medicaid prepaid plans and HMOs; interest-only disputes are excluded), and tracks late-pay days for interest claims (verify which prompt-pay statute reaches SMMC plans).
ideas.why_now: EVV mandates are in force; 2024-25 plan notices tightened denials; AHCA has enforced prompt-pay against plans (2022 letter to Sunshine); a class action alleges SMMC plans withheld interest on late payments.
