ideas.founder_edge: The freight three-way match is the same logic, already built. Florida-based, so he can walk into agencies and knows the plans. Dad's regulated-industry world adds credibility.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Family agency if it has a Medicaid book. 2-5) Florida nurse registries and homemaker/companion agencies through owner groups. 6-8) Skilled agencies with SMMC contracts via grandfather introductions. 9-10) Billing firms that want a recovery partner. Start with a free scan of 90 days of denied claims.
ideas.path_to_big: I did NOT size Florida Medicaid home-care spend; that is the first task (AHCA data). EVV is federally mandated, so the match generalizes state by state with aggregator data. My guess is $5-15M a year if multistate; I do not see a $100M business.
ideas.who_does_it_today: HHAeXchange (the EVV aggregator, which also sells RCM and is the gatekeeper), plan portals, billing firms (ASPR CMS Solutions lists Florida home-health billing), law firms recovering prompt-pay interest (Frier Levitt). Biggest risks: depends on MHC's service mix, HHAeXchange can block or copy it, and tickets are small.

ideas.title: Auth Clock: prior-authorization tracking, appeals and a plan scorecard for Medicare Advantage home health
ideas.one_liner: Log every Medicare Advantage authorization against the new 72-hour and 7-day decision clocks, auto-draft appeals on denials and short approvals, and publish the first home-health-level MA denial index.
ideas.customer: Intake or authorization coordinator and administrator at a home-health agency with a heavy MA census.
ideas.who_pays: The agency: $40-60 per appeal packet plus 20-25% of overturned dollars (flat-fee fallback if percentage pay is risky). Budget is the authorization and denial staff line.
ideas.problem: MA plans denied 12% of prior-authorization requests in 2025 and 67% of appealed standard denials were overturned, yet denials are rarely appealed (KFF, Aug 2026). Home-health-specific rates are not published because the data are aggregated across services. Since Jan 1, 2026 plans owe 72-hour (expedited) and 7-day (standard) decisions with specific denial reasons, but agencies do not track which plans miss the clock.
ideas.solution: Track submit time, decision time, visits requested vs approved and denial reasons; draft reconsiderations using the plan's own stated reason and the clinical record; plug into plans' FHIR prior-authorization APIs when they go live Jan 1, 2027; produce quarterly anonymized scorecards by plan for contract renewals, and sell them to hospital systems, ACOs and investors. Provider-side only; never act as a beneficiary's representative.
ideas.why_now: CMS-0057-F clocks took effect Jan 1, 2026, first public plan metrics were due Mar 31, 2026, prior-authorization APIs are due Jan 1, 2027, and MA now exceeds FFS in home-health volume.
ideas.founder_edge: Pre-registered, methodology-first indexes from his strategy lab make a defensible scorecard. Fast document assembly and plan-policy research pipelines.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Family agency. 2-4) Three peers via the grandfather. 5-8) Four MA-heavy Florida owners via the association. 9-10) Two via the mentor's network. Free 30-day clock audit of the last 90 days of authorizations as the opener.
ideas.path_to_big: If 3% of MA home-health revenue (about $14B, my estimate) is reversible authorization loss, that is about $420M and the 25% fee pool is about $105M; $10M is about 10% of it. Shares its data layer with Payer Truth, and the scorecard is the data asset.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Crowded. Claim Health (YC, $4.4M seed; authorization management plus appeals), HHAeXchange RCM (appeals within 72 hours), Prochant, Enzo (intake, eligibility), Availity and clearinghouses. It ranks fifth because it is the first idea anyone would have.

ideas.title: Revenue Clock Sentinel: the alarm system for deadlines that can zero out home-health cash
ideas.one_liner: One dashboard for the clocks that silently destroy home-health revenue: the 5-day NOA, OASIS submission, certifying-physician enrollment and exclusion status, 855A revalidation, state license, RCD cycle dates and MA authorization expirations.
ideas.customer: Administrator or compliance officer at a Medicare-certified home-health agency.
ideas.who_pays: The agency's compliance budget: SaaS at $249-799 a month by census.
ideas.problem: A late Notice of Admission cuts payment by 1/30 per day on the final claim (CMS manual). CMS proposes shrinking the OASIS deadline to 45 days and clawing back payments to the date of noncompliance for ALL enrollment revocations, and with the new-enrollment moratorium a revoked or deactivated agency cannot simply re-enroll. An unenrolled certifying physician can cause denials and employing an excluded person brings penalties (both general knowledge, verify).
ideas.solution: Read EHR exports plus free public files (exclusion list, ordering/referring file, opt-out list; general knowledge), apply clock rules, send SMS and email alerts, publish a monthly clock report. No clinical data beyond dates and identifiers needed, so lighter HIPAA exposure.
ideas.why_now: The May 13, 2026 nationwide moratorium raises the cost of losing billing privileges; July 2026 proposals tighten enrollment and OASIS timing.
ideas.founder_edge: Public-data plumbing plus fast shipping, with no regulated-data wall. The easiest first sale of the eight.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Family agency. 2-4) Three peers via the grandfather. 5-8) Four via accreditation and compliance consultants as resellers. 9-10) Two via association newsletters.
ideas.path_to_big: 12,000 agencies at $3-5K a year is $36-60M, so $10M is 15-25% share, which is heroic. Treat it as a wedge into Payer Truth and the Documentation Desk, not a standalone company.
ideas.who_does_it_today: EHR alert modules (Axxess, HCHB), exclusion-screening vendors and accreditation bodies (names from general knowledge, unverified), compliance consultants. Not exhaustively searched.

ideas.title: Certified-Agency Readiness Dossier: moratorium-era sell-side Medicare integrity report
ideas.one_liner: Because CMS froze new agency and branch enrollments nationwide in May 2026, existing Medicare numbers are scarce; sell owners an AI-assisted, buyer-ready Medicare-integrity binder before they sell.
ideas.customer: Owner of a certified home-health agency considering a sale or capital raise within 12-24 months, with brokers and PE buyers as channel.
ideas.who_pays: The seller, flat $15-40K from sale-prep budget; no success fees (broker rules).
ideas.problem: Buyers inherit liabilities; a change of ownership takes 4-9 months; diligence centers on PDGM and HHVBP performance, payer mix and post-close CMS audits, and earnouts tie to ratings and audits. Sellers do not know their own exposure, so price gets chipped. Certified home-health deals are on pace for 48 in 2026, up 41%.
ideas.solution: Two-week report: 3-year claims sweep for overpayment exposure, outlier and PEPPER-style analysis from public data, RCD history, HHVBP score, enrollment and license status, exclusion checks, and a payer-contract-vs-Medicare summary. A healthcare CPA or attorney signs off; it is not an audit opinion or legal advice.
ideas.why_now: The nationwide moratorium began May 13, 2026 (six months, renewal expected), deal volume is recovering, and CMS proposes broader clawbacks that raise buyer caution.
ideas.founder_edge: Grandfather is an owner-operator with peers who may sell or buy; the mentor built and sold a roughly $1B company and knows exits; family finance contacts reach brokers and PE.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Family agency as a pre-sale health check. 2-4) Three peers via the grandfather. 5-6) Two broker partners (Braff, Mertz Taggart style). 7-8) Two healthcare CPAs. 9-10) Two PE-backed platforms via the mentor.
ideas.path_to_big: Weak. About 48 certified deals a year at $25K is about $1.2M even at 100% share. It becomes big only as an annual 'Medicare Integrity Score' for about 1,000 agencies at $10K (about $10M) sold to lenders, insurers and buyers; otherwise it is a $1-3M services niche and should be called that.
ideas.who_does_it_today: M&A advisors (Braff, Mertz Taggart, Lincoln International), accounting-firm quality-of-earnings teams, compliance consultants (SimiTree), data vendors such as Definitive Healthcare (general knowledge). No standardized AI-assisted dossier found.

ideas.title: HHVBP Score-to-Cash: audit the CMS scorecard and share the payment uplift
ideas.one_liner: Audit each agency's Home Health Value-Based Purchasing annual performance report, fix the OASIS and claims data that drive it, and take a share of the payment improvement.
ideas.customer: Administrator or QA director at a Medicare home-health agency with $3M+ in FFS revenue.
ideas.who_pays: The agency: flat $2.5-4K report audit, then 15-20% of first-year HHVBP adjustment improvement (a consulting performance fee, not billing; confirm with counsel).
ideas.problem: HHVBP moves up to +/-5% of FFS payment (weights OASIS 40, claims 40, survey 20); a $5M-FFS agency swings up to $250K. It is budget-neutral, so gains come from peers. Most agencies never check CMS's math in the short recalculation window (Aug 20-Sep 4, 2026), and the two-year lag hides cause and effect.
ideas.solution: Compare the iQIES report with the agency's own data, flag missing OASIS functional items, build a performance-year-2026 early-warning dashboard (it sets CY2028 payments), improve survey response, and file the August 2027 recalculation request.
ideas.why_now: Final 2027 adjustments publish in January 2027, and performance year 2026 decides CY2028 pay. Other payers may reuse the public scores.
ideas.founder_edge: Pre-registered, data-hygiene discipline. Honestly the weakest fit for his speed edge.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Family agency, then 2-4) peers from the grandfather, 5-6) two via QA consultants, 7-10) four from association events. Flat audit is the opener since performance fees pay late.
ideas.path_to_big: Weak. Realistically 1-2% of FFS ($160-320M) is redistributed a year; a 15% fee on a minority of it is $3-5M at best. Big only if MA plans adopt HHVBP-style adjustments and he sells them the scoring layer.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Forvis Mazars guidance, vendor glossary content (Enzo), consultants, EHR analytics, Olli for OASIS quality. Slowest to cash of the eight, so ranked last.

ideas.title: PayerProof: contract-compliance audit of Medicare Advantage and Medicaid-MCO payments
ideas.one_liner: Upload 12 months of remittances (835s) plus the plan contract rate exhibits; the engine recomputes what each claim should have paid, returns a variance list and ready-to-file payment disputes, then monitors monthly.
ideas.customer: Owner or CFO of independent Florida home-health agencies and multi-LLC operators (MHC first) where MA plus Medicaid managed care is roughly 35%+ of revenue.
ideas.who_pays: The agency owner/CFO. There is usually no underpayment budget line, so a contingency (20-25% of recovered MA/MCO/commercial underpayments) removes the budget objection; also a $1,500-$2,500 flat diagnostic credited against fees, or $750-$1,250/month monitoring.
ideas.problem: Agencies chase denials but nobody reconciles paid versus contract, because rate terms live in PDFs. Florida MA penetration is about 57-60%, the home-health denial rate is about 13% with 52 days in A/R (vendor benchmark), plans' automated claim review is rising, and Florida Medicaid MCOs add EVV denials (Sunshine denies unverified EVV claims without an exception code; Molina denies manual home-health claims with N821). KFF: 67% of appealed MA denials were overturned (all services).
ideas.solution: Week 1: LLC, BAA, contingency agreement; get MHC's top-5 payer contracts and 12 months of 835s. Weeks 1-2: contract extractor (PDF to rate-rule JSON, human-checked), 835 parser, expected-versus-paid engine reusing his freight-audit variance logic. Week 3: variance report and dispute letters. Week 4: MHC files the first disputes. Later: an anonymized MA-rate benchmark across customers.
ideas.why_now: MA is 57-60% of Florida Medicare, the temporary 3% PDGM cut continues in 2027 (about $500M recouped), fraud-driven payment pressure tightens cash, and contract-PDF extraction is now cheap. CenterWell/Humana is buying Florida agencies, squeezing independents on cash.
ideas.founder_edge: He already built a freight-invoice audit with a flat diagnostic plus contingency; this is the same contract-versus-invoice engine pointed at remits. MHC's several Area LLCs give multiple real payer contract sets as the validation data, and the family company is customer zero.
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) MHC diagnostic on its remits. (2) Three owner peers the grandfather knows personally, via a dinner he hosts. (3) Two or three through the Home Care Association of Florida. (4) Two billing companies as resellers. (5) Two through accountants in his father's MyFinancialAdvice network who serve agency owners. Lead with a free one-quarter variance preview. Kill test at day 30: if realized short-pay on MA/MCO revenue is under 0.5% of that revenue (the 1% figure is my assumption), stop. Legal: keep contingency off Medicare FFS claims (42 CFR 424.73, verify), check contract confidentiality, and sign a BAA.
ideas.path_to_big: At an assumed $15k per agency per year ($9k monitoring plus $6k contingency), $10M needs about 670 agencies, 5.6% of the 11,925 US agencies; Florida alone (1,079 agencies) caps near $16M at 100% share, so it must go national. The same engine extends to hospice, SNF, DME and physician groups, where payer-underpayment recovery is an established category. The biggest unverified assumption is the short-pay rate; the MHC scan tests it in 30 days.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Claim Health (YC; denial prevention and appeals for post-acute), Amperos ($16M Series A, April 2026; agentic denial management), Prochant PulseIQ (RCM services), Enzo, and ordinary billing companies. My search found no home-health-specific MA contract-compliance auditor, but the query returned nothing on the topic at all, so that is absence of evidence, not proof of a gap. The sibling healthcare_ops lens has a similar 'MA Rate Truth' idea.

ideas.title: Clean-Agency Shield: proof-of-visit and note-authenticity forensics
ideas.one_liner: For every billed visit, build an evidence bundle (note originality score, timestamps, GPS, mileage, signature timing, duration versus note length) so a legitimate Florida agency can prove its visits happened when pre-claim review, ADR, TPE or UPIC requests land; add a pre-admission check on the referring physician.
ideas.customer: Administrator, compliance officer or DON at Florida home-health agencies and hospices (MHC first).
ideas.who_pays: Agency owner, from the compliance and audit-defense budget; about $0.30-$0.60 per visit (roughly $16k/year for an agency with about 3,000 visits a month; assumption), with a free retro scan of 500 notes as the opener.
ideas.problem: Regulators now treat Florida home health as a fraud market (CMS nationwide enrollment moratorium from 2026-05-13; Oz letter to DeSantis 2026-03-17; Florida is a Review Choice Demonstration state). ADR responses are due in 30-45 days and a missed deadline is an automatic denial. Auditors read identical notes across dates as inauthentic or written after the fact. AI scribes will make notes more uniform, adding a new audit risk. Existing QA tools ask whether the note supports the code, not whether the note is authentic.
ideas.solution: Ingest EMR note exports; embeddings and similarity per clinician, patient and time with per-agency template baselines so legitimate templates are not flagged; authorship-style scoring using the gestalt method from his detector; anomaly rules (impossible travel, same-minute notes, duration versus note length, late signatures); a per-claim audit-ready proof-packet PDF; and an admission gate checking the referring physician against the CMS Ordering and Referring file (updated twice weekly), OIG exclusions and volume outliers. Output is a needs-review queue, never an accusation.
ideas.why_now: The moratorium and fraud letter make proof the thing every legitimate Florida operator needs. Brellium raised $23M on 2026-10-14, showing buyers pay for documentation audit; forensics is adjacent to that, not the same.
ideas.founder_edge: His AI-text detector beat commercial detectors in his own blind tests, and his strategy lab taught pre-registered testing and false-positive control, which matters because wrongly flagging a clinician is costly. MHC's DON can label 200 known-good and known-problem notes as ground truth.
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) MHC retro scan. (2) Owner peers through the grandfather. (3) Home Care Association of Florida members. (4) Two or three Florida healthcare fraud-defense and compliance law firms, who refer clients under audit. (5) Billing companies. (6) Hospice owners via the same network. Kill test: flag precision under 70% on MHC's labeled set, or the DON calls the queue noise. Technical risk: clinical notes are templated by nature, so per-agency baselines are the whole game.
ideas.path_to_big: At $16k per agency per year (assumption), $10M needs about 625 agencies, 5.2% of US home-health agencies; adding about 6,000 hospices (unverified count) roughly doubles the pool. Honest risk: Brellium or Enzo could add similarity checks, so the moat must be the cross-agency originality corpus and calibrated false-positive rates. Longer term, payers and auditors want the same engine from the other side, but that is a different business.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Brellium ($23M; audits 100% of notes against payer rules; customers include Gentiva), Enzo QA, SimiTree SARA (OASIS and coding), generic similarity tools used by auditors and payers, and PEPPER (a free billing-pattern report that few states' agencies download). I found no provider-side clone and authenticity product with proof-of-visit packets, but I could not rule out that one exists.

ideas.title: FieldPay Audit: per-visit pay, mileage and overtime integrity for field clinicians
ideas.one_liner: Recompute weekly regular-rate overtime, unpaid drive and charting time, and mileage from the EMR payroll export; open with a mileage-savings audit that pays for itself and sell the wage-hour module only through the agency's employment counsel.
ideas.customer: Owner or CFO of home-health agencies and hospices, plus the agency's employment counsel for the wage-hour module (MHC first, if it pays per visit).
ideas.who_pays: Owner/CFO from payroll and legal-risk budget: 25% of verified first-year mileage savings, or $12-$20 per field clinician per month for continuous monitoring (assumption).
ideas.problem: Per-visit pay for non-exempt clinicians is a recurring FLSA target: Amedisys settled for $8M (2016), Guardian Home Care and Hospice for $3M, Franciscan VNS for $3.65M. Fisher Phillips guidance says the DOL will make an employer recalculate overtime on a weighted regular rate. Axxess already exports auto-calculated mileage, travel hours and EVV hours, so the data exists, but I found no tool that audits regular-rate overtime on it (only EVV-to-payroll validators and GPS mileage apps).
ideas.solution: Ingest the EMR payroll export and payroll register; recompute regular rate and overtime per workweek; flag mixed hourly and per-visit pay (the Amedisys/Guardian theory), after-hours charting with no paid time, and visit-rate-card drift; compare claimed miles with route-computed miles from visit addresses (overpayment equals savings). The wage-hour analysis is commissioned by the agency's employment attorney so it stays privileged; he supplies software, not legal advice.
ideas.why_now: Fraud scrutiny and the 3% cut push owners to find cost; the nurse shortage drives turnover and wage claims; the EMR already holds the data and models make the analysis cheap.
ideas.founder_edge: He ships data pipelines quickly and MHC supplies real payroll exports. Family sensitivity: do this only if the grandfather wants to know, and structure it through counsel so findings are not an un-privileged liability number (the earlier-rounds trap of selling a privileged number that defeats its own privilege).
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) MHC, mileage module first. (2) Owner peers. (3) Employment-law firms that defend home-care employers, who sell the privileged module. (4) Payroll and PEO firms serving home care. (5) Home Care Association of Florida pay-practice sessions. Kill test: MHC pays all field staff hourly or salaried (wage module moot, mileage still works), or the grandfather declines.
ideas.path_to_big: At $14k per agency per year (80 clinicians x $15 x 12; assumption), $10M needs about 700 agencies, 5.9% of US agencies. The same engine extends to hospice and private-duty aides; BLS projects about 765,000 home health and personal care aide openings a year, a far larger worker pool. Open legal question I could not source: whether mileage reimbursement belongs in the regular rate (counsel must answer).
ideas.who_does_it_today: No home-health regular-rate overtime auditor found. Adjacent: EMR payroll exports into ADP and Paychex, EVV-to-payroll validators such as ShiftCare (vendor claim), GPS mileage apps such as Timeero, and employment law firms. The sibling mhc_workforce lens covers pay benchmarks (Wage Radar), not FLSA recompute.

ideas.title: CCN Guardian: regulatory back office for multi-CCN operators
ideas.one_liner: One system that tracks and drafts every filing, renewal, revalidation, change report, payer credentialing packet and cost report for operators who run several separately enrolled agencies.
ideas.customer: Owner or compliance director of Florida operators with 3 to 30 CCNs (MHC's 'Area N, LLC' structure suggests it is one).
ideas.who_pays: The operator, from compliance staff, enrollment-consultant and CPA budgets: about $400-$600 per CCN per month plus $2k-$5k per payer credentialing package (assumption).
ideas.problem: Each LLC and CCN has its own CMS-855A enrollment (ownership/control changes reportable within about 30 days and most other changes within 90; verify in 42 CFR 424.516), state license, accreditation, cost report (Form CMS-1728-20 per CCN) and credentialing with every MA plan and MCO. Under the moratorium a lost or revoked enrollment cannot be replaced, so a paperwork slip becomes asset loss. CMS revised the cost-report chapter and electronic specifications on 2026-05-28, and the form's OMB approval expires 2027-01-31.
ideas.solution: Per-CCN calendar built from PECOS and state license data; AI-drafted 855A change forms and payer packets from one master data room per operator; a weekly 'what could cost us a CCN' list; later, cost-report workpapers for CPA review.
ideas.why_now: The moratorium makes every existing Medicare number a scarce asset; fraud scrutiny raises the cost of administrative slips; AI document drafting is now reliable enough for first drafts.
ideas.founder_edge: MHC literally runs multiple Area LLCs, so the pain is real and customer zero is family. He has built multi-agent document pipelines.
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) MHC. (2) Owner peers who run multi-LLC groups. (3) Florida healthcare M&A attorneys, whose clients arrive with messy records. (4) CPAs who prepare home-health cost reports (white-label). (5) Hospice operators. Kill test: MHC runs a single CCN or its compliance team already has this under control.
ideas.path_to_big: Provider-paid alone is heroic: at $6k per CCN per year (assumption), $10M needs about 1,670 CCNs, 14% of US agencies. It gets big only if the verified 'organization passport' becomes a network that MA plans, health systems and ACOs pay to query; at $50-100k a year per buyer, 100-200 buyers is $5-20M. If payers do not adopt it, this is a $3-5M services business, which is why it is ranked fourth.
ideas.who_does_it_today: AI form-fillers for the 855A (Instafill, vendor), general credentialing platforms (Medallion, Verifiable, CertifyOS, Modio, symplr, MedTrainer; none confirmed to handle 855A or PECOS revalidation), enrollment consultants and CPAs. I found no product built for multi-CCN home-health operators. The sibling healthcare_ops lens has a related 'Enrollment Sentinel' monitor.

ideas.title: Referral Ledger: kickback-safe marketing supervision for referral-driven agencies
ideas.one_liner: Every meal, gift, event, free in-service and hour of free staff time given to a referral source is logged, checked against the agency's written policy and Florida plus federal law, routed to supervisory review and attested monthly, reusing the books-and-records architecture of his father's advisor social-media compliance tech.
ideas.customer: Compliance officer or owner of Florida home-health agencies and hospices, plus the marketing/liaison team they supervise.
ideas.who_pays: Owner or compliance budget: about $400-$900 per month per agency (assumption).
ideas.problem: Florida's Patient Brokering Act (Fla. Stat. 817.505) applies to all payers, not just federal programs; it is a felony with reported penalties of $50,000-$500,000 per violation, and a 2019 appellate decision held that advice of counsel is not a defense (law-firm summaries; verify current text). Hospice compliance counsel say marketing is often divorced from compliance and somebody must track what marketers hand out. I found referral CRMs but no product that logs gifts and meals against AKS and Patient Brokering thresholds.
ideas.solution: Expense feed from corporate cards plus calendar and CRM entries; policy engine with per-source annual caps set by the client's counsel; flags for 'free staffing' and other in-kind support; a supervisory review queue; monthly attestation; an archive documenting intent. He sells software, not legal advice.
ideas.why_now: Fraud crackdown on Florida, a nationwide moratorium and the CMS letter to Florida raise enforcement attention on referral practices; the moratorium also makes each agency's Medicare number too valuable to risk.
ideas.founder_edge: His father spent about 24 years in financial services and built technology that keeps advisors compliant on social media (archive, lexicon flags, supervisory sign-off). This is the same workflow in a new vertical, and he can borrow the playbook with his father's blessing.
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) MHC's marketing team. (2) The Florida Hospice and Palliative Care Association (it ran a 'Create & Maintain a Compliant Marketing Strategy' event; propose a co-presented webinar). (3) Healthcare compliance attorneys. (4) Owner peers. (5) Hospices. Never give free tools or services to referral sources: that is the same remuneration problem the product exists to prevent. Kill test: marketers will not log, or a referral CRM ships this as a feature.
ideas.path_to_big: At $9k per organization per year (assumption), $10M needs about 1,100 organizations. The eligible pool is about 11,925 home-health agencies plus hospices, DME, labs, ABA and senior living; call it 25,000 organizations (assumption), so about 4%. Weakness: standalone it is a feature of a referral CRM, so it needs the supervision and archive layer to be the product.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Referral CRMs (Trella CRM, Playmaker and similar) track referral volume and activity, not gifts versus thresholds. Pharma and device spend trackers exist outside this vertical (from my background knowledge, not searched). No home-health tool that logs inducements against AKS and Patient Brokering thresholds was found.

ideas.title: CHOW Desk: moratorium-era diligence report and change-of-ownership closing engine
ideas.one_liner: A public-data diligence report on any Medicare home-health agency (ownership history, 36-month-rule status, survey history, quality, outlier flags, litigation, exclusions) plus a change-of-ownership closing checklist engine (855A CHOW, state license CHOW, payer notices and re-credentialing, EMR transfer).
ideas.customer: M&A attorneys, business brokers, PE add-on teams, individual buyers and lenders evaluating Medicare-certified home-health agencies.
ideas.who_pays: The buyer side, from diligence budgets: $750-$2,500 per report, about $1,500/month to monitor a 50-agency watch-list, and a flat closing-desk fee per deal. Definitive Healthcare's median contract is reported around $50k a year, so the budget exists.
ideas.problem: Under the moratorium the only way into Medicare home health is to buy an existing CCN. Multiples are reported at 5-12x EBITDA (broker pages, indicative), referral concentration above 25% from one source is often a deal-breaker, and the 36-month rule makes some structures unworkable. Definitive's coverage reportedly lags during consolidation and I found no diligence workflow in it.
ideas.solution: Public-data pipeline (CMS enrollment and ownership data, quality and HHCAHPS, 2567 survey history, state corporate records, exclusion lists, litigation) producing a standard report; later a closing-checklist engine that drafts the filings. Flat-fee data and software only, no success fees.
ideas.why_now: The moratorium took effect 2026-05-13 for six months and can be extended. Date risk: if CMS lets it lapse around mid-November 2026, the scarcity premium fades and demand shifts back to new-agency start-up kits.
ideas.founder_edge: His grandfather is a founder-owner who sees buyers and sellers; his father's advisor network reaches people who want cash-flowing businesses; his mentor knows M&A. His research pipelines suit public-record assembly.
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) Five brokers and M&A attorneys at a flat $750 with resale rights. (2) Three individual buyers from his father's network. (3) MHC's own acquisition team, if any. (4) Two lenders. Legal: take no success fees (Florida's real-estate licensing statute, Ch. 475, covers brokering business opportunities; verify) and avoid finder-fee securities issues. Kill test: brokers will not pay over $300 per report, or the moratorium ends.
ideas.path_to_big: Stand-alone diligence is a $2-6M niche (assumption; I found no deal count). It becomes big only as a subscription post-acute provider integrity score sold to payers, systems and lenders: at a Definitive-like $25-50k a year, 200 contracts is $10M. I would call it dead if it stays a diligence-report shop.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Definitive Healthcare ($25-50k a year, over 100K post-acute records, reported data lag), Trella, and brokers' own research. The sibling healthcare_ops lens has a related 'Certified Agency Exchange' diligence-and-matching idea.

ideas.title: Survey Ready: public CMS-2567 corpus, AI mock survey and plan-of-correction engine
ideas.one_liner: Learn from every public CMS-2567 home-health survey report to show an agency what surveyors are citing in its state this quarter, run an AI mock survey against its policies and a chart sample, and draft the plan of correction inside the roughly 10-day window.
ideas.customer: Administrator or DON at Medicare-certified home-health agencies, then hospices and nursing homes.
ideas.who_pays: Agency owner from compliance-consulting and accreditation-prep budgets: about $3k a year subscription plus about $2.5k for an emergency plan of correction (assumption).
ideas.problem: A plan of correction is generally due within about 10 calendar days of the 2567. Condition-level findings start an enforcement clock of 90 days to termination, or 23 days with immediate jeopardy (vendor-sourced; check the State Operations Manual). Repeat condition-level findings can bar an agency from running an aide training program for two years (seen in Indiana 2567s). I found no AI survey-readiness product.
ideas.solution: Ingest the public 2567 corpus (CMS QCOR and state sites); tag deficiencies by condition of participation; per-state frequency dashboard; map an agency's uploaded policies and QAPI documents to 42 CFR 484 sections and flag gaps; sample-chart mock survey; draft the plan of correction (correction, others affected, systemic fix, monitoring in QAPI). No PHI in the public data.
ideas.why_now: Fraud scrutiny and a nationwide enrollment freeze make survey failure and termination the worst case for a scarce Medicare number; the corpus is public and large-document analysis is now cheap.
ideas.founder_edge: His multi-agent research pipelines are built for large document corpora, and the data is public, so he can build it before any family-company data access.
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) MHC. (2) Owner peers. (3) Accreditation consultants who would resell. (4) Agencies that have just been cited, which public 2567s identify (outreach is sensitive and must be respectful). Kill test: the DON says mock surveys are not a budgeted purchase, or accredited (deemed) agencies see state surveys too rarely to care.
ideas.path_to_big: At $4k per agency per year (assumption), $10M needs about 2,500 agencies, 21% of the US, which is heroic; home-health-only is therefore dead. It lives only as a multi-provider survey-intelligence product, where the nursing-home 2567 corpus is much larger and contracts are bigger. That is why it ranks seventh.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Human consultants, accreditors' consulting arms, and vendor glossary pages (Enzo explains plans of correction). My search found no AI survey-readiness or mock-survey product for home health.

ideas.title: Florida Independent Operators Alliance: benchmark co-op, group purchasing and a contracting vehicle
ideas.one_liner: A grandfather-chaired roundtable of independent Florida owners that starts as a free quarterly meeting, grows into an anonymized KPI and MA-rate benchmark and a group purchasing program, and eventually a counsel-built contracting vehicle for MA and Medicaid plans.
ideas.customer: Owners of independent Florida home-health agencies facing scale competitors such as CenterWell (350 branches in 37 states, bought Trilogy's 11 Florida locations).
ideas.who_pays: Members pay dues ($3-6k a year, assumption), vendors pay admin fees (up to 3% under the group-purchasing safe harbor, 42 CFR 1001.952(j); verify), and data licensing comes later.
ideas.problem: Independents lack scale, nobody publishes MA home-health rates, and Humana's own leaders describe the market as fragmented (top 10 providers under 30% share). Precedent: the California Association for Health Services at Home runs a group purchasing program with vendor royalties. I found no independent home-health alliance contracting with MA plans.
ideas.solution: Month 1: a roundtable and a shared, anonymized KPI sheet (A/R days, denial rate, clinician pay, MA rates). Next: a benchmark pipeline built on the idea-1 engine. Then vendor purchasing deals. Eventually a clinically integrated or messenger-model contracting vehicle, only with antitrust counsel.
ideas.why_now: The moratorium blocks new branches and de novo entry, so owners must grow by contracts and conversion; the 3% cut and MA slow-pay raise the value of peer benchmarks and purchasing scale.
ideas.founder_edge: The grandfather's convening power is the one asset no competitor can copy. This is the only idea where the family is a distribution moat, not just a pilot customer.
ideas.first_10_customers: Six owners from the grandfather's personal network and four from the Home Care Association of Florida as founding members. Legal: use the retired DOJ/FTC safety-zone conditions as a floor for information exchange (third-party managed, at least 5 contributors, no contributor over 25% of any statistic, data at least 3 months old; DOJ withdrew those statements in 2023, so hire antitrust counsel before the first data exchange). Kill test: fewer than six owners agree to share data in the first quarter.
ideas.path_to_big: At an assumed $12k per member per year ($6k dues plus $6k vendor fees), $10M needs about 830 members across five or six states, 7% of US agencies; Florida alone caps near $13M at 100% share. A national alliance that payers contract with could be venture-sized, but it needs a clinical-integration program, years and counsel, the lowest-probability path for an 18-year-old. Without payer contracting it is an association-sized $3-8M business.
ideas.who_does_it_today: The California association's group purchasing program, home-medical-equipment buying groups, and the Independent Home Care Alliance (purchasing and shared services). Benchmarking vendors such as SHP exist (seen only as an HCAF exhibitor). I found no independent home-health alliance or clinically integrated network contracting directly with MA plans.

ideas.title: Heir Bridge: Gen Z-run next-gen onboarding for advisory firms
ideas.one_liner: A white-label, mobile-first 'money moves' path that advisors send to their clients' 18-30-year-old kids, hosted by a Gen Z team, so the advisor knows the heir before the inheritance arrives.
ideas.customer: Owners and managing partners of AUM-model RIAs and wealth teams with roughly $100M-$1B in assets and mostly 55+ clients (SEC RIAs: 16,544, median AUM about $447M, per IAA 2026).
ideas.who_pays: The advisory firm pays from its client-experience and marketing budget, $299-$999 a month by firm size (pilot $1,200 flat for 90 days). At $500 a month a $1M-revenue firm spends 0.6% of revenue. The owner signs. Kitces data puts median cost to acquire a client at about $3,800, so retention of heirs is a clear budget argument.
ideas.problem: Advisors assume they will keep the heirs but barely know them (Cerulli/Everplans: 92% of advisors unacquainted or only quasi-acquainted with clients' grandchildren, 2016). Cerulli finds 52% of affluent heirs will not keep the benefactor's advisor; Harris 2025 says 43% plan to switch and 26% of leavers never personally knew the advisor. About $68T moves over 25 years. Heirs ignore advisor email and awkward family dinners.
ideas.solution: The advisor sends a branded link. Heirs get 8-10 short paths (first W-2 and 401(k)/Roth, credit and loans, rent vs buy, 'what your parents' plan means for you', scams, how to sanity-check AI money answers) in short Gen Z-hosted video plus checklists, a '15 minutes with [Advisor]' button, and an engagement report to the advisor with heir consent. Education only, from a pre-approved content library built with Ron's compliance workflow; no personalized advice or performance claims. Flat SaaS fee, not per converted client, which avoids Marketing Rule promoter-compensation problems. Legal premise is mild but get a lawyer to review disclaimers and the heir-consent flow.
ideas.why_now: Wealth transfer is under way and the leave rates are measured. 2026 surveys show Gen Z wants a human to check AI: NY Life says 40% of Gen Z feel a greater need for a human, SIFMA/KPMG (19 Oct 2026) says Gen Z trust in AI-only advice fell from 20% to 10%, and Gallup/Edward Jones says only 14% of Gen Z who sought guidance used a professional adviser, so heirs start from zero relationship. SEC Marketing Rule scrutiny (Dec 2025 risk alert) also pushes firms toward pre-approved content libraries.
ideas.founder_edge: He IS the persona and can run 50 peer interviews in a week; he ships a mobile web app plus content engine fast with AI agents; Ron brings 24 years of advisor trust and a rolodex of peers who can supply real heirs for pilots; MFA's compliance workflow gives the content a pre-approval backbone. A 40-year-old vendor cannot credibly host this.
ideas.first_10_customers: Week 1: Ron hand-picks 25 RIA owners he has known for years and joins 20-minute calls. Pilot 1 free for case-study rights; pilots 2-4 at $1,200 for 90 days, each with 10-20 real heirs. Month 4: convert to $500 a month and ask each for 3 peer intros. Then FPA chapter talks (start with the Colorado chapter near MFA's Boulder base) and the NAPFA/XYPN member groups. Customers 6-10 come from those intros.
ideas.path_to_big: Bottom-up: about 8,000 individual-focused SEC RIAs x 40% adoption x $6k a year is roughly $19M. Add state RIAs and IBD teams, enterprise tiers for TAMPs, trust companies and bank wealth arms at $50k-$200k, and a paid heir tier that hands off to flat-fee planners. Honest ceiling is $20-50M a year; reaching $100M needs a custodian or TAMP distribution deal (Schwab/Altruist/Orion-type) because it would take over half of all RIAs at $10k.
ideas.who_does_it_today: EverFi NEXT (older advisor-delivered financial education), Everplans Network Amplifier (a 'deputy' model that invites family members), HeirWealth (Australia), SS&C Black Diamond next-gen client portal segment, custodian next-gen programs (TD/Schwab), and advisors hosting events by hand. None is Gen Z-native or sold as a managed program. Consumer apps (Frich, which raised $2.8M, sells to institutions) are not advisor-paid.

ideas.title: CFP-Checked: the human validation layer for AI money answers
ideas.one_liner: A $29-$79 async second opinion: a young adult pastes a ChatGPT money plan into a structured intake and a vetted CFP replies within 48 hours with fix, risk and next steps.
ideas.customer: 18-34-year-olds (and parents buying for adult kids) who use AI for money questions; later neobanks, credit unions, employers and AI finance apps that need compliant human escalation.
ideas.who_pays: The consumer pays by card now ($29-$79 per review). Later B2B customers pay $15-$40 per validation or a per-seat fee from customer-service and compliance budgets. CFPs earn $18-$30 per review for 15-20 minutes of work.
ideas.problem: Gallup/Edward Jones (Aug 2026): about 1 in 5 who sought advice used AI, about a quarter of Gen Z and millennials, yet only 14% of Gen Z used a professional. NY Life: only 23% act on AI advice without validating it. CFP Board: nearly 1 in 5 who took AI advice lost at least $100. Choices today are a sales pitch, a $150-$400 session, or nothing.
ideas.solution: An intake converts the AI transcript plus basic facts into a one-page brief. The CFP works a checklist (wrong assumptions, taxes, fees, missing risks) and replies in writing with an optional 20-minute call. The platform runs the queue, a second-CFP spot check, disclosures and record retention. Legal premise to clear first: each CFP contracts with the consumer through their own RIA and the platform is software plus billing (Ron's MFA ran a pre-screened fee-for-service model since 2004); counsel decides whether the platform is a promoter or needs state registration (Zoe registered as an RIA for this reason). Budget $2-4k of securities-lawyer time before the first dollar.
ideas.why_now: Three 2026 surveys (Gallup, NY Life, SIFMA/KPMG) show heavy AI use and falling trust in AI-only advice at the same moment. CFP Board is messaging 'an accountable human'. A record 6,709 new CFPs joined in 2025 (3,964 under 35) and 11,037 sat the exam, so there is eager supply of young planners who need clients.
ideas.founder_edge: Gen Z distribution through school and college group chats, gaming and sports communities; AI building and QA (his detector work helps flag weak or invented numbers); Ron's pre-screened advisor model and CFP network. Asher gives no advice himself.
ideas.first_10_customers: Recruit 5 CFPs via Ron plus XYPN and FPA NexGen groups. Run 30 free reviews with friends and classmates to tune the brief. Then price at $29 and sell to 10 paying customers in 30 days through 3 high-school and 3 college group chats and one gaming Discord; parents buy for adult kids. Target 100 paid reviews by day 90.
ideas.path_to_big: B2C alone: about 45M US adults aged 18-29; 0.3% buying 1.5 reviews a year at $49 is about $10M GMV and $3-4M take at 35%. Venture scale needs the embedded B2B2C layer where banks, apps and employers pay per validation and qualified intros flow to flat-fee advisors. Heroic share is required in B2C alone, so be honest that the upside depends on B2B2C.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No exact match found. Adjacent: Ellevest one-time sessions from $199, American Century $150 session, Ask Dolly (Your Rich BFF, CFP chats at $59 a month), Nest Egg (on-demand advice through institutions, 10,000+ clients), Uprise (embedded human + AI advice), Range ($60M raised Feb 2026, AI flat-fee planning for high earners), Fruitful ($33M, subscription planning), Origin's AI advisor, and free 'second opinions' from AUM advisors.

ideas.title: Launch Season: pre-warmed household acquisition for advisors, triggered by senior year
ideas.one_liner: Parents of college-bound seniors buy a $149 'Launch Session' with a vetted flat-fee planner, and advisors buy exclusive local seats because these households (45-58, high income, 20+ years of runway) are exactly the clients they want.
ideas.customer: Parents of juniors, seniors and freshmen with household income over $150k, and local flat-fee or fee-only advisors.
ideas.who_pays: Parents pay $99-$199 per session. Advisors pay $250-$500 a month for an exclusive territory seat (a flat seat fee, not contingent on conversion). Advisor budget line: the roughly $3,800 median cost to acquire a client and purchased leads at $25-$300 each.
ideas.problem: Standard advisor leads are intent-based, costly and convert at only about 5-10%. Parents of seniors face a dated, high-stakes decision: aid letters arrive March-April, and new Parent PLUS limits ($20k a year, $65k aggregate) apply to first disbursements on or after 1 July 2026, so families need a plan for the gap. Admissions consultants ($850-$10,000) do not plan the money.
ideas.solution: A 'what our family did' content funnel from a real applicant, a free net-price and award-letter comparison worksheet (education, not securities advice), then an upsell to a Launch Session. The advisor gets a structured intake the day before and covers college-cost reality, the 529, the student's first accounts, a Roth for summer-job income, scam defense and the Parent PLUS gap. Marketing goes to parents, never to minors. Legal premise: keep the advisor seat fee flat and non-contingent and have counsel confirm it is not a promoter arrangement.
ideas.why_now: The Class of 2027, which is Asher's class, is the first cohort to hit the Parent PLUS caps. Award letters land in March-April 2027, so selling from January fits his school-year hours.
ideas.founder_edge: He is living the process: classmates' parents, school newsletters and team parent groups are his distribution, and a real applicant's voice has credibility agencies lack. Ron staffs the planners. The timeline fits school-year hours.
ideas.first_10_customers: 10 parents of classmates and teammates by January at $149 (about $1,490). Ron or one of his picks takes the first territory seat. Then 18+ campus ambassadors in other schools plus PTA and counselor newsletters to reach parents elsewhere, and local advisors buy seats in those zip codes.
ideas.path_to_big: Senior year is only the beachhead: about 3.7M seniors a year, perhaps 900k households above $150k; 2% buying is about 18k sessions or $2.7M. Adding advisor seats (3,000 advisors x $400 x 8 months, about $9.6M) gets near $12M. The scalable version is a 'premium agent seat' model for other life events (new baby, home purchase, job change, inheritance, retirement date). Honest: venture scale only if two or three other events also work; otherwise a $3-12M seasonal business.
ideas.who_does_it_today: General lead-gen: SmartAsset ($25-$240 per lead), WiserAdvisor, Zoe Financial, Broadridge ($1,899 a month). A small niche of college-funding planners, admissions consultants ($850-$10,000, typical comprehensive about $6,500), and 529 vendors. No one found selling event-triggered, pre-paid, territory-exclusive households to advisors.

ideas.title: Graduation Desk: the Marketing-Rule-safe referral exchange for advisors
ideas.one_liner: AUM advisors 'graduate' sub-minimum clients and specialty cases to flat-fee or hourly planners and receive a compliant referral share, with the SEC promoter agreement, disclosures, disqualification screen and $1,000-a-year ledger built into every transfer.
ideas.customer: AUM-model RIAs with a tail of small clients (senders) and flat-fee or hourly planners hungry for clients (receivers, e.g. XYPN's 2,000+ members).
ideas.who_pays: The receiving planner pays a fee per accepted client from its client-acquisition budget (median cost per client about $3,800). Benchmarks: Facet pays about 1x annual revenue to the sender; Zoe takes about 10 bps of the client fee per year or a flat annual fee. The platform keeps 15-30% of referral value. The advisor owner signs.
ideas.problem: Small accounts drag AUM firms, and flat-fee planners cannot find clients at a sane cost. When advisors do refer, they trip on disclosures, ineligible persons and state registration; the SEC's 16 Dec 2025 risk alert found missing or non-prominent disclosures and misclassified lead-gen, influencer and refer-a-friend arrangements.
ideas.solution: A web app: sender uploads an anonymized profile (client consent) and is matched on fee model, niche and state; auto-generated promoter agreement and disclosure delivered at the moment of referral; disqualification check, compensation ledger and exam-ready archive; a send-back trigger when a client crosses the sender's minimum. Legal premise to clear first: state solicitor or IAR registration and whether the platform is an 'operator'. This needs a securities lawyer and possibly an RIA partner before launch.
ideas.why_now: The December 2025 SEC risk alert, a record class of young CFPs who need clients, and (my inference) PE roll-ups pruning small accounts as RIA deal-making accelerates.
ideas.founder_edge: Ron's compliance-product DNA (social-media compliance tech for advisors) and pre-screening practice; both sides of the exchange are in his network; Asher builds workflow software quickly.
ideas.first_10_customers: Ron's 10 closest peers: 5 AUM firms with a tail of small clients and 5 flat-fee planners. Senders pay $0; receivers pay $500 flat per accepted client at the start. Then XYPN, NAPFA and Garrett member communities.
ideas.path_to_big: About 16.5k SEC RIAs, assume 30% willing to send, each graduating about $30k of annual revenue, is about $150M of yearly referral value; at a 15% take, about $22M. That needs real sender penetration, so realistic is $10-30M. Receiving capacity is the constraint (XYPN is about 2,000 members serving about 100k households).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Facet Wealth (buys small books at about 1x revenue, paid 25/50/25), Zoe Financial ($45M raised, advisor-paid referrals, itself an SEC-registered adviser), Wealthtender and other compliance add-ons (about 450 advisors at about $49 a month, which shows compliance-only SaaS stays small), and advisor-to-advisor referral groups run by hand. No neutral exchange with compliance rails found.

ideas.title: Frontline Money Benefit: flat-fee advice for home-care workforces, piloting at MHC
ideas.one_liner: Home-health and home-care agencies add a 'paycheck clinic' benefit: two free sessions a year with a vetted flat-fee planner plus text Q&A, paid per employee per month, with MHC as the pilot.
ideas.customer: Owners, HR and COOs of home-health, home-care and hospice agencies, starting with MHC's own Florida entities (NPI registry shows MHC AREA 9 LLC dba Choice Health At Home in Boca Raton; exact type and Medicare certification still to confirm).
ideas.who_pays: The agency pays about $4-$6 per employee per month from its recruiting and retention budget (comparable coaching benefits run $3-$6; ServSafe's bundle is $6.99), about $24k a year for 400 staff. Retention math: aide turnover is 34.17% and the average sign-on bonus is $2,304, so one point fewer on 400 aides is about 4 hires or roughly $9,200 in bonuses alone. This is unproven, since pay drives turnover.
ideas.problem: Agencies compete in a narrow wage band ($18.75 average at for-profit agencies) and need non-wage differentiators. Most workers do not know what benefits exist (BofA: 71% unaware). The pitch they hear is earned-wage access.
ideas.solution: An opt-in program built on MFA's old workplace channel: a text line plus quarterly 20-minute clinics (401(k) enrollment, debt triage, withholding, scam defense), bilingual, with aggregate-only reporting to HR. Sessions carry no sales; advisors earn new households through hand-raise intros. Employee data falls under Reg S-P and state privacy rules, not HIPAA, and the program must never touch patient data or PHI.
ideas.why_now: The 2025 turnover improvement came from wages and bonuses, which squeezes margins and pushes owners to look for cheaper retention levers; the home-care labor crunch continues.
ideas.founder_edge: His grandfather owns MHC and his mother works there, so there is an internal sponsor and a real pilot population. Ron's MFA sold advice through plan-sponsor billing back in 2004. An owner-operator's network of other agency owners gives warm access to peers.
ideas.first_10_customers: 3-4 MHC entities (Area 6, 9, 10 and any others sharing ownership), then 6 peer agencies via state home-care associations and the grandfather's introductions.
ideas.path_to_big: The workforce is millions of direct-care workers (the exact BLS count is unverified here). Illustratively, 5M workers x $4 x 12 months is a $240M pool and 10% of it is $24M. It extends to nursing homes, hospital aides and staffing firms. Honest: crowded, and the retention evidence is thin.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Brightside (5,000-employee minimum), Origin, Enrich (500 minimum), SmartDollar (coaching add-on at $67 a session), Your Money Line (about $3-$6 per employee per month), LearnLux, ServSafe-style benefit bundles, and earned-wage-access vendors pitched through home-care software.

ideas.title: Continuity Pact: the 'if I get hit by a bus' network for solo and small advisors
ideas.one_liner: A members-only network of vetted peers who sign standard reciprocal continuity agreements, with an AI-maintained 'go-file' that keeps each practice transferable and a paid path to sale.
ideas.customer: Solo and small RIAs, especially the flat-fee and hourly world (XYPN 2,000+, NAPFA about 3,500 in 2018, Garrett about 325 in 2013 and now member-owned).
ideas.who_pays: The advisor pays $49-$149 a month plus a 3-5% success fee on matched sales. It replaces legal and consulting fees they would not otherwise buy.
ideas.problem: 44% of advisors have no succession plan (Janus Henderson) and 57% who want to sell lack a formal plan (AssetMark 2025). Kitces argues the real exposure is sudden death or disability, when fees stop and clients leave. Local buy-sell handshakes rarely work because buyers lack capacity.
ideas.solution: Standard reciprocal continuity agreements with e-sign; a 'go-file' where AI assembles and keeps current the client roster, fee schedules, recurring tasks and tech logins in a secure vault with a dead-man's switch; a registry of designated successors; a valuation estimator; buyer matching including young CFPs. Avoid funded buy-sell insurance, which has licensing implications.
ideas.why_now: Advisors 55+ are 42% of advisors and 57% of assets; Cerulli projects 109,000 advisors retiring 2024-2034, while 3,964 CFPs under 35 joined in 2025 alone, so there is a supply of potential buyers.
ideas.founder_edge: Trust is the product and Ron has 24 years of it; Asher builds the vault and matching quickly. Weaker fit than the top ideas because the buyers are cautious and low-priced.
ideas.first_10_customers: Pair 5 older and 5 younger advisors from Ron's circle; the first pact is the first paid membership at $99 a month. Then XYPN and NAPFA groups.
ideas.path_to_big: 5,000 members x $1,200 is about $6M, plus 300 matched deals a year at $700k x 4% is about $8M. Honest ceiling is $10-15M. Practices historically sell for about 2.1-2.7x recurring revenue (FP Transitions, 2011 data).
ideas.who_does_it_today: FP Transitions (about 9,000 valuations and 1,500+ transactions), Succession Resource Group, Advisor Transitions, custodian succession programs, outsourcing platforms that buy practices, and peer buddy arrangements run by hand.

ideas.title: Plan Factory: AI-drafted, advisor-signed plan production for solo flat-fee advisors
ideas.one_liner: Advisors upload the meeting transcript and planning-software export and get a client-ready plan draft, summary letter and action checklist within 24 hours, priced per plan.
ideas.customer: Solo and small flat-fee or hourly planners delivering 30-150 plans a year.
ideas.who_pays: The advisor pays $149-$349 per plan or $499-$1,499 a month, in place of a roughly $77,751 average paraplanner salary (SmartAsset, Sep 2025) or 6-15 hours of their own time.
ideas.problem: Notetakers (Jump, Zocks, Zeplyn) save meeting notes, but plan writing is still manual. Solos cannot afford a paraplanner.
ideas.solution: An AI pipeline drafts the plan from the exports, a human QA layer of CFP-track reviewers checks it, and the advisor signs off. A Reg S-P vendor due-diligence pack, NDAs and retention under the advisor's records policy are required. Asher does not give advice; the advisor signs every deliverable.
ideas.why_now: Notetakers are commoditized (Jump about $75-$175 per seat, Zocks $67-$184, Zeplyn $120), so the next workflow is plan writing. About 11,000 CFP candidates a year create trained part-time labor.
ideas.founder_edge: His multi-agent pipelines and QA experience. The trust barrier is high for a regulated buyer, so Ron's endorsement is essential.
ideas.first_10_customers: 5 flat-fee friends of Ron at $149 a plan for 3 plans each, then XYPN communities.
ideas.path_to_big: 7-10k reachable solos x $6k a year is $40-60M if all bought, so realistically $5-10M; labor leverage is needed to go further.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Valenta (US RIA virtual planning plus automation), Commonwealth's Virtual Paraplanning Program (captive), Vela and other virtual paraplanning firms, Holistiplan (tax-return analysis), and Jump, Zocks and Zeplyn, which are adding agentic features (Zeplyn Agent Nexus from $195 a month). Crowded and the notetaker vendors are moving into plan drafting.

ideas.title: Creator Desk: pre-cleared Gen Z finance creator campaigns for advisors
ideas.one_liner: A done-with-you service where advisors sponsor 18+ finance creators under Marketing-Rule paperwork, with disclosures baked into the video itself and an exam-ready archive.
ideas.customer: Growth-minded RIAs and flat-fee firms already spending on social media; creators are 18+ only.
ideas.who_pays: The advisor pays a campaign fee and the platform takes 15-20% of creator fees, funded from the 2-12% of revenue advisors spend on marketing.
ideas.problem: The SEC's Dec 2025 alert shows advisors already use creators and refer-a-friend programs without proper agreements or disclosures. Fundrise paid over $8M to over 200 creators and settled with the SEC.
ideas.solution: A vetted creator roster, templates with in-video disclosures, promoter agreements, bad-actor screening and a $1,000-a-year ledger, plus an archive for exams. Legal premise to clear first: whether paying creators for referrals needs IAR registration in each state versus pure advertising; a securities lawyer must decide before launch.
ideas.why_now: The December 2025 SEC alert, Gen Z's shift to video, and the Fundrise precedent that makes advisors nervous about doing it ad hoc.
ideas.founder_edge: A Gen Z creator network from his world; Ron's compliance workflow background. Weak on the buyer side, since Asher is also selling to skeptical regulated buyers.
ideas.first_10_customers: 3 of Ron's marketing-minded peers plus 3 young CFP creators.
ideas.path_to_big: The spend pool is unknown; assuming 5% of advisor direct marketing goes to creators gives a low-single-digit $M platform. Honest ceiling is $5-10M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Generic influencer compliance tools (HypeAuditor, Sedric), advisor marketing agencies (Twenty Over Ten, Snappy Kraken), and Wealthtender (reviews only). No advisor-specific creator marketplace found, but the legal fragility and thin pool mean this is a distant option.

ideas.title: Sponsor Proof: ROI receipts that renew sponsors, then a multi-festival sponsor network
ideas.one_liner: An AI-built proof-of-performance report for every sponsor of every independent festival, which becomes the trust and data layer for selling bundled circuit buys to brands.
ideas.customer: Festival directors and sponsorship chairs at independent festivals with $100k to $3M budgets, later brand and regional marketers who want tier-two festival reach.
ideas.who_pays: Festival pays $500-$1,500 per event for the report and renewal deck, out of its sponsorship-sales and marketing line. Later, brands pay a 15-20% commission on multi-festival buys and $10-50k a year for benchmark data. Signer: the festival director now, a brand partnerships manager later.
ideas.problem: Sponsors renew on proof, and small festivals hand over a few photos and a guess. Enterprise tools (Relo Metrics, Hookit) are quote-only and built for pro leagues. Eventeny tracks deliverables and invoices but I found no independent outcome measurement. Brands are shifting budget to tier-two festivals but cannot deal with hundreds of separate events.
ideas.solution: Ingest the festival's photos and video (AI logo detection and impression counts), ticket data (zip codes, party size), promo-code and QR redemptions, email and social reach, and a five-question attendee survey. Output a branded one-page-per-sponsor report with a renewal recommendation and a price benchmark. Phase 2: publish a rate-card network so one brand can buy 10-40 festivals in one contract, with a sponsor price index. Add cause-matched units (for Baygrass: oysters planted or trash removed per sponsor dollar via its Bay-nonprofit partners). No license needed; the festival owes the deliverables, not Asher.
ideas.why_now: Brands are moving to independent tier-two festivals (Gigmit citing EventMarketer), sponsors face ROI scrutiny (FestivalPro, June 2026), vision models make logo counting nearly free, and 2027 sponsor decks are written November through February.
ideas.founder_edge: He ships fast, built an AI detector and backtesting lab that he blind-tested against commercial tools (same habit applies to logo counting), Baygrass is a live design partner, and his father knows the sponsors and the IBMA promoter community.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Baygrass: build the 2026 report from its photos and data for free and use it in the 2027 renewals. 2) Ask Dad to introduce 9 directors from IBMA's event-production community and the Southeast and Florida festival associations; also email 100 festivals from the 283-festival bluegrass list. Offer a free teardown (30 photos turned into logo counts), then a $500 full report. Ten reports at $500 is $5k.
ideas.path_to_big: 1,000 festivals at an average of $40k sponsorship is $40M gross; 18% is about $7M, plus roughly $2-3M of benchmark subscriptions (100 brands at $25k) clears $10M. That is about 5% of a pool that IEG put at $853M for festivals, fairs and annual events in 2014 (larger now): hard, not heroic. Risk: Gigmit or Eventeny copies the report.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Relo Metrics and Hookit (enterprise sports, quote-only); Eventeny sponsor app (deliverables and invoicing, from $180/mo, vendor claim); Ticket Fairy sponsor-code tracking; Gigmit (Berlin, 1,000+ independent festivals, Europe-centric brand matching); SponsorSync (small US agency, unverified).

ideas.title: Impact Receipt: verified visitor-impact reports for lodging-tax grants
ideas.one_liner: The festival-level, ticket-data-based economic impact report that tourism boards require and small festivals cannot afford, produced in a day.
ideas.customer: Festivals (nonprofits, municipal and chamber events) applying for or reporting on hotel-tax and tourism grants, then the tourism boards and county commissions that award them.
ideas.who_pays: Festival pays $295-$995 per report. A tourism board pays $5-25k a year for a portfolio dashboard across all its grantees (anchor: one NC county's total Zartico contract was $20k). Budget line: lodging-tax event grants, where payment is often conditional on an impact report (Everett, WA requires one with the payment request). Signer: tourism board director or festival treasurer.
ideas.problem: Grantors want out-of-area share, overnight stays and spend. Applicants guess or hire a consultant. Destination analytics (Zartico, Datafy) measure whole destinations by geolocation, not one festival's gate.
ideas.solution: Read the ticket export (zip, add-ons, camping nights), run a 2-minute QR survey (lodging nights, party size, spend), and apply each jurisdiction's own definitions (50-mile rule, out-of-state, paid lodging) to produce a report with an audit trail and a ready-to-paste grant narrative. Tourism boards get a standard format across grantees and a county rollup. Label it an estimate, not a certified appraisal.
ideas.why_now: U.S. lodging taxes were about $21.5B in 2019 (HVS) and boards face ROI scrutiny; Zartico trained boards to expect data; AI collapses the cost per report; grant applications open in winter and spring for fall events.
ideas.founder_edge: Baygrass is a clean pilot (check whether it has ever applied for county or state support), he is a strong data builder, and his mentor teaches entrepreneurship at a university and can open tourism-board doors.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass 2026 is report #1. Then pull public hotel-tax award lists (Hilton Head, Spartanburg, Augusta, Everett and similar post them) and email the 200 grantee festivals a free sample made from their own public numbers; target 10 paying $400 for $4k. Ask one tourism board to endorse the format.
ideas.path_to_big: Sell a grantee-portfolio dashboard to tourism boards: 500 boards at $10-25k is $5-12M, plus festival fees. The same audited data makes idea 1 sponsors trust the audience. Risks: government sales cycles; Zartico or Datafy adds a festival module; boards demand their own methodology.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Zartico (about $24.5M raised, 180+ customers, destination-level data); Datafy (tourism analytics); consultants doing IMPLAN-style studies; Placer.ai foot traffic; festival spreadsheets.

ideas.title: Revenue Desk: success-fee ticket pricing and yield for independent festivals
ideas.one_liner: A pace-and-price analyst for festivals that only gets paid when ticket and camping revenue beats last year's curve.
ideas.customer: Festival directors who set ticket tiers once and rarely revisit them.
ideas.who_pays: A share (8-10%) of verified incremental ticket and add-on revenue, or $250 a month. It comes from the ticketing and marketing line and carries no cash risk for the buyer. Signer: the festival director.
ideas.problem: Early-bird windows, tier thresholds and camping and VIP add-ons are set by gut while artist, insurance and production costs are squeezing festivals (UK saw 78 fallen festivals in 2024 and 43 in 2025; Michelada Fest cancelled in 2026). Squeezing 5-10% more revenue per attendee matters more than any new feature.
ideas.solution: Connect read-only to Eventbrite, Etix, Ticket Tailor or Square exports; model sales pace against prior years; recommend price steps, the Black Friday early-bird design, camping yield rules and last-14-day pushes; generate the email and SMS copy; send a weekly one-page memo. Analysis only; never touches ticket money.
ideas.why_now: Black Friday is four weeks away, so a live test at Baygrass can start now; cost pressure makes revenue per attendee the lever; AI makes forecast-plus-copy cheap.
ideas.founder_edge: His strategy lab was built on pre-registered tests, so he can run honest A/B comparisons with Baygrass as the control, and Dad can approve pricing changes.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass Black Friday 2026 test. Then offer nine spring-season festivals a 'no uplift, no fee' deal through the same contact lists as idea 1. Revenue arrives after sales; first dollars likely December to January.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest answer: the success fee alone is small (1,500 festivals, $400k average ticket gross, 7% lift, 10% share is about $4M). Big only if the data becomes the ticketing or payments rail for tier-two festivals ($600M of gross at a 2% net take is about $12M) or sells cash-flow forecasts to lenders. That means fighting Eventbrite, Etix and Ticket Fairy.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Ticket Fairy dynamic pricing and its Capital advance product; Tixr, Dice and Ticketmaster for big events; Eventbrite and Etix static tiers for small ones; Easol, POSH and Peatix advances; consultants.

ideas.title: The Circuit: a consented fan audience network across independent festivals
ideas.one_liner: A genre-by-genre network that lets festivals keep their own email and SMS lists while brands and tourism boards buy sponsored reach across all of them, starting with bluegrass.
ideas.customer: Festivals (supply of attention) and brands, tourism boards, instrument and outdoor companies (demand).
ideas.who_pays: Brands and destinations pay $1,500-$5,000 per sponsored send to 50-200k opted-in fans; festivals earn a revenue share and an affiliate commission on tickets sold to other festivals' fans. Signer: brand or tourism-board marketing manager.
ideas.problem: Each festival has a few thousand loyal fans and no way to monetize or cross-sell them, and bluegrass fans follow many festivals. National brands cannot deal with 283 separate festivals.
ideas.solution: Festivals connect their email service or ticketing audience. The network sends approved sponsor and cross-festival offers through each festival's own account (no list handover), tracks clicks and ticket sales and splits revenue. Start with bluegrass (283 festivals in 45 states per Bluegrass Today), then Americana, folk, blues, jazz and craft circuits. Consent is the whole game: CAN-SPAM, TCPA written consent for SMS and state privacy laws (Maryland's is strict; have counsel check).
ideas.why_now: First-party consented data is the one durable advertising asset left, and tier-two festivals under cost pressure want new revenue.
ideas.founder_edge: Dad's IBMA standing opens the festival side, Asher builds SMS and short-form content quickly, and Baygrass is the seed list.
ideas.first_10_customers: Seed with Baygrass plus four or five friendly festivals (about 50k addresses). Sell the first three sponsored sends to a Maryland or Virginia tourism board, an instrument maker and an outdoor brand at $1,500 each. Ten paying sends is about $15k.
ideas.path_to_big: 1,000 festivals times 5,000 subscribers is 5M fans; at $2-4 a year of sponsorship and affiliate revenue per subscriber that is $10-20M. Risks: list owners hesitate, email-service terms, fan fatigue.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Bluegrass Today and Bluegrass Unlimited (media and ads); Bluegrass RoadTrip and FestivalNet (listings; FestivalNet claims 1.3M monthly visitors); Bandsintown and Songkick (artist-centric discovery). I found no consented festival-to-festival audience co-op.

ideas.title: High-LTV Sponsors: advisors, senior-services and big-ticket locals as festival sponsors
ideas.one_liner: Sell festival sponsorships to local businesses whose customers are worth thousands (independent advisors, elder-law, senior living, realtors, boat dealers), packaged with lead capture, compliant content and category exclusivity.
ideas.customer: Independent financial advisors first, via Dad's MyFinancialAdvice network of pre-screened flat-fee advisors and its social-media compliance technology; then other high-lifetime-value local services.
ideas.who_pays: The advisor or local business pays $2,500-$10,000 per festival-year or $100-$300 a month for the content and lead toolkit, out of client-acquisition marketing (the lifetime-value logic is my inference; verify with five advisors). Signer: the advisor-owner.
ideas.problem: Festivals under-price sponsorships to beer brands, while advisors and similar practices need warm local acquisition but struggle to run compliant event marketing (SEC marketing rule, recordkeeping, pre-approval of posts and materials).
ideas.solution: Category-exclusive sponsor slots (one advisor per region per festival), QR lead capture with opt-in, pre-cleared post templates, automatic archiving of event content and a lead report. The platform gives no financial advice and does not refer clients. Highest legal risk of the eight: seminar-style senior-targeted events, testimonials and paid referrals draw regulator attention; needs a securities-compliance attorney before the first sale; keep Medicare-marketed healthcare sponsors out of version one.
ideas.why_now: Advisors need warm local channels, festivals need higher-paying sponsor categories, and bluegrass and Americana audiences skew older and affluent (inference).
ideas.founder_edge: Dad has 24 years in financial services, an advisor network and compliance technology already built for advisor social media; Baygrass is the first slot.
ideas.first_10_customers: Ask Dad to introduce 10 advisors in his network; offer the first three a Baygrass 2027 category slot plus the content toolkit at a founder price of $2,500; sell seven more through the festivals recruited for idea 1.
ideas.path_to_big: About 15,000 SEC-registered advisers plus tens of thousands of other high-value local practices; 3,000 sponsors at $4k a year is $12M. Risks: depends on Dad's appetite and on whether advisors will pay festival prices per lead.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Each festival's own local sponsor sales; advisor marketing and seminar platforms; social-media archiving vendors (Smarsh, Global Relay and similar). I found no category-exclusive festival marketplace for advisors.

ideas.title: Settle: vendor commission settlement for small festivals
ideas.one_liner: Pull every food and craft vendor's sales from the POS they already use, compute the festival's 10-15% commission, and collect it by ACH the same night.
ideas.customer: Festival treasurers and vendor coordinators at festivals with 20-200 vendors.
ideas.who_pays: $149-$299 per event, or 0.5% of vendor sales if collected through the platform, from the finance and admin line plus recovered commission lost to under-reporting. Signer: festival treasurer.
ideas.problem: Vendor terms are typically $200-$800 plus 10-15% of gross, settled on paper tapes with a spreadsheet tab per vendor and formulas that carry errors (atVenu's own description). Cash and under-reporting leak revenue.
ideas.solution: Vendors connect read-only Square, Toast or Clover reports (or upload end-of-day totals); the system applies each vendor's terms, deducts agreed show costs, produces a signed settlement and sends an ACH invoice. Never hold funds: use Stripe Connect or direct vendor ACH and check Stripe platform terms to avoid money-transmitter rules.
ideas.why_now: Festivals under cost pressure need every commission dollar, and most vendors already run Square or similar so no hardware is needed.
ideas.founder_edge: He builds payments and in-app-economy logic quickly, and Baygrass has vendors including its oyster concession.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass first, then nine festivals that charge commissions (county fairs, food festivals, music festivals) found through FestivalNet listings and the Florida and Southeast festival associations.
ideas.path_to_big: Weakest here: small-festival vendor sales are small, so even a 1% take on $400M of vendor sales is $4M. This is a feature-and-data wedge for ideas 1 and 3, not a standalone $10M business.
ideas.who_does_it_today: atVenu (food and beverage settlements for festivals, fairs and rodeos; pricing not published); Eventeny vendor payments; Square, Toast and Stripe building blocks; spreadsheets.

ideas.title: Lineup Intel: pooled artist-fee benchmarks and a routing co-op
ideas.one_liner: An anonymized 'what did comparable festivals pay this artist' database plus demand signals, so bluegrass, Americana and folk buyers stop overpaying and can share routing to cut travel.
ideas.customer: Festival talent buyers who book 12-18 months ahead.
ideas.who_pays: Festival pays $29-$99 a month or a $400 annual plan from the talent budget, usually the largest cost line (Port Fairy Folk Festival reported artist costs up 65%). Signer: the festival's talent buyer.
ideas.problem: Pollstar-grade data covers arenas and big festivals, not a $6k bluegrass band, so buyers negotiate blind. Neighboring festivals could book the same act on adjacent weekends and split travel but cannot find each other.
ideas.solution: Give-to-get benchmark submissions (anonymous offers and settled fees) combined with streaming, social and ticket-lift signals, plus a routing board showing which acts are already booked nearby. Software only: Asher never negotiates for artists, which avoids talent-agency licensing (California, New York and others). Share only anonymized, aged data to stay clear of antitrust problems.
ideas.why_now: Costs are squeezing festivals, artists are now being asked to carry their own insurance, and buyers want data.
ideas.founder_edge: Dad's booking experience and the IBMA promoter network seed the give-to-get data, and Asher can build the models.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass plus nine festival directors who contribute last year's fee data in exchange for the benchmark report at $199 one-time; revenue about $2k.
ideas.path_to_big: Small for the buyer alone; venture-scale only if it grows into a booking marketplace, which needs licenses and a trust network. Ranked 7 on bigness.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Pollstar Boxoffice; Chartmetric and Viberate (estimated fees); Gigmit (booking platform, claims 150k artists and 11.5k organizers); Prism.fm; booking agents.

ideas.title: Risk File: weather action plans and underwriter-ready safety packets
ideas.one_liner: A one-day weather and safety plan with live lightning, heat and wind decision support, plus an insurer-ready risk file that can win better terms.
ideas.customer: Outdoor festivals, especially Florida winter-season events and fall Mid-Atlantic events.
ideas.who_pays: Festival pays $400-$1,500 per event from the insurance and safety line (weather cover runs about 1-3% of insured value); later insurers and program administrators pay for cleaner underwriting. Signer: festival director or its broker.
ideas.problem: DTN WeatherOps has no published price, the National Weather Service supports emergency managers rather than festival producers unless a threat is imminent, and a specialist broker says most small festivals do not know parametric cover exists.
ideas.solution: NWS lightning and heat-index feeds, an AI-drafted weather action plan with the festival's own thresholds, SMS alerts to producers, an incident log, and a packaged risk file (crowd, weather, medical, security) a broker can show a carrier. A certified meteorologist contractor reviews each plan. It is decision support, not a safety guarantee: the festival keeps the evacuate decision, with disclaimers and E&O cover. Selling insurance or acting as a managing general agent needs licenses and carrier capacity, so the only route is a data or referral partnership with a licensed program administrator.
ideas.why_now: Insurance premiums and cancellations are climbing and organizers want documented plans.
ideas.founder_edge: Baygrass sits on a state-park waterfront where weather is a real risk, and Asher builds data products fast.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass as the case study, then winter-season Florida festivals through the Florida festival association (the MHC Florida link is unverified) and spring fairs. First revenue likely March-April, so this misses the 60-90 day target.
ideas.path_to_big: If a licensed program administrator uses the risk files to underwrite a festival insurance program, a revenue share on a premium pool is possible, but that is a multi-year path with an external partner. Risk: DTN or an insurtech replicates it.
