ideas.who_does_it_today: DTN WeatherOps live-event services (no published price); National Weather Service decision support; University of Alabama in Huntsville lightning tool used at Rock the South; Beazley parametric rain product; independent event meteorologists.

ideas.title: Surcharge Clawback: tariff pass-through, contract-price and hidden-fee recovery for healthcare buyers
ideas.one_liner: Read two years of a provider's supplier invoices, find tariff surcharges, tariff-timed price steps and fee creep, match each to the contract clause that lets the buyer claim money back, and take 20% of what comes back.
ideas.customer: Owner or CFO of an owner-operated healthcare services company (MHC first), then other home-health agencies (about 12,200 Medicare-certified), DME suppliers (about 79,000 enrolled), labs and clinics.
ideas.who_pays: The provider pays 20% of net cash, credit or price reduction recovered; no recovery means no fee, so no budget line is needed. Later a roughly $2,000 a year ledger subscription.
ideas.problem: Buyers saw 'tariff surcharge' lines and quiet price increases in 2025. The Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA tariffs unlawful on Feb 20, 2026 (about $166B collected; refunds to importers of record via CBP's CAPE portal since Apr 20). Only the importer of record gets the refund; the buyer who paid gets nothing unless a surcharge, true-up or refund-sharing clause, or an unjust-enrichment theory, forces a share. Private disputes only surfaced in Sept 2026 and no court has decided pass-through claims on the merits. Most small buyers have not identified which invoice lines to claim.
ideas.solution: Ingest supplier invoices (PDF, email, CSV) into a ledger of every surcharge line and unit-price step; map suppliers to importer of record where known; quote the relevant contract clause and score claim strength; output an evidence pack plus a demand letter the client's own officer or counsel signs (he does not give legal advice). Same pass also checks contract/GPO price compliance and fee creep (fuel, environmental, regulatory, small-order, shipping and handling) in the pattern of the Stericycle case (class of 246,000+, $295M settlement, $608M alleged overcharges). Kill test first: two hours on 12 months of MHC's top-5 supply vendor invoices; if there are no surcharge lines, no tariff-month price steps and no fee creep, drop the tariff angle.
ideas.why_now: Refunds reached importers from April 2026 and supplier-buyer disputes began in September; the window where suppliers will still negotiate before positions harden is months. Law firms publish advice but nobody sells a low-ticket productized service to a 10-site home-health operator. Caveat: one firm says most serious refund seekers already have their money, so speed matters.
ideas.founder_edge: His mother works at MHC, so real invoices exist on day one; the freight engine already does 'billed line vs tariff or contract'; vendor invoices normally contain no PHI so no BAA in the first pass (strip patient identifiers if present); AI-speed ingestion and ledger building.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) MHC itself (12 months of supplier invoices via his mother). 2-4) Two or three other agencies or DME shops the grandfather or MHC administrators name when asked who they trade notes with. 5) A pharmacy or clinic in the family circle. 6) Annapolis Baygrass (equipment rental and merch invoices). 7-10) Intros from the state home-care association and an HME buying group such as VGM (about 3,500 member providers). Get an attorney's written answer first on unauthorized practice of law, state collection licensing for a contingency fee on a commercial claim, and lawyer fee-splitting.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest: the tariff pool is one-time and the law is unsettled. It only becomes big as a recurring vendor surcharge ledger with a clause database: 5,000 customers at about $2,000 a year is $10M, a heroic share of roughly 91,000 agencies and DME suppliers unless it expands to clinics, dental, vet and senior living.
ideas.who_does_it_today: RSK Supplier Recovery (consulting-led, pricing unpublished); law-firm advisories (Jones Walker, Covington, Baker Donelson); importer-side tariff refund shops (Tariff Recovery Group and similar); carriers refunding their own duty payers (FedEx, UPS, DHL); home-care GPOs (HPSI, IMCO, MED Group with 3-5% stated savings); Cass waste expense management for large healthcare accounts. No self-serve ledger for small multi-site providers found.

ideas.title: MedFreight Desk: freight audit plus damage claims for medical-device and medical-supply makers and distributors
ideas.one_liner: Point the finished LTL and parcel audit engine at one vertical (companies that make or distribute medical products), add a damage-claims desk, and reach them through MHC's suppliers and the manufacturing-extension network.
ideas.customer: Owner or operations lead at a 5-100 person medical-device maker, supply importer or distributor, starting in Florida (26,000+ manufacturers, 80% with 20 or fewer employees; roughly 400-1,000+ device makers by inconsistent old counts).
ideas.who_pays: The manufacturer pays 15% of recovered overcharges (free first look) plus 20% on filed damage claims.
ideas.problem: LTL accessorials, reclass and reweigh bills go unaudited at small shippers. Medical products ship high value per pallet and are handling-sensitive, so damage claims are bigger. The NMFC density rewrite effective July 19, 2025 is still producing reclass bills. Carmack gives at least 9 months to file claims and the statute does not shift a claims firm's fee to the carrier.
ideas.solution: Run the existing engine (22 checks, 2,266 tests, 187 callable prospects) with a medical pack: documentation for damage and temperature claims, serial/lot traceability fields, a claims-filing desk for small claims big shops ignore. Offer a free first look, then 15% contingency.
ideas.why_now: Density-class change and rising LTL accessorials; FloridaMakes (official NIST MEP representative in Florida) and the Florida SBDC network have an MOU, so a ready-made advisor channel exists; the engine is finished and idle with zero calls made since August.
ideas.founder_edge: The engine, the call sheet and the site already exist; the only missing input is calls. His mother can ask MHC procurement to introduce three suppliers, a warm door a cold call lacks.
ideas.first_10_customers: Three suppliers MHC's purchasing contact introduces; three FloridaMakes or SBDC introductions (offer a short talk for small manufacturers); four from the existing call sheet filtered to medical products. Later other states' MEP centers.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest math: a maker with $200k of LTL spend and a 4% error rate yields $8,000 recoverable, or $1,200-1,600 a year at 15-20%, so $10M needs 6,000-8,000 clients. Only big with claims automation, the event-evidence data asset (idea 3) and the MEP channel across states. Prior validation scored the generic version 3.33/10; this changes the door and claims upside, not the ceiling.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Eller Audit (free first audit at 15%), the freight-audit-and-payment field (Cass, nVision and others), freight claims shops such as TLI, Warp's free reweigh/reclass and accessorial audit tools, vMeasure and FreightSizer for dimensions.

ideas.title: Event Truth: independent evidence that a billed freight event actually happened
ideas.one_liner: For every accessorial on a freight bill (liftgate, inside delivery, residential, limited access, redelivery), assemble independent evidence from licensed address data, a 20-second consignee text and the delivery receipt, and file the dispute with the evidence attached.
ideas.customer: Small shippers with repeat consignees: medical makers shipping to clinics, DME shops delivering to homes, small distributors; later freight-audit firms and brokers via API.
ideas.who_pays: The shipper pays 20% of accessorials recovered (bundled with MedFreight), later $2-5 per verified shipment; audit firms and brokers pay per-shipment API fees.
ideas.problem: Carriers generally win accessorial disputes when the service was required and performed, and the burden of proof is on the shipper (dock photos, delivery receipt). Rate-file automation, which is what the big auditors run, cannot tell whether a liftgate was actually used. His own fact-check file states the same limit.
ideas.solution: Address truth from licensed map and parcel data (dock presence, commercial vs residential; do not scrape consumer map products, whose terms forbid it); an SMS to the consignee after delivery ('Was a liftgate used? Was a dock available?'); parse the signed receipt and driver photos; auto-compose the dispute within the carrier's window (some allow only 30 days). Kill test: on 30 real disputed accessorials, at least 40% withdrawn after an evidence packet and at least 30% consignee text response; otherwise shelve it.
ideas.why_now: Accessorials are the highest-value error class in his own research, incumbents cannot verify events, and NMFC and accessorial changes are raising billing friction; cheap SMS, parsing and imagery AI make per-shipment evidence economical for the first time.
ideas.founder_edge: He already shipped the cube-rule and invoice-checker tools and builds SMS-first flows fast; MHC's offices are real consignees to test on; MedFreight clients provide consignee lists.
ideas.first_10_customers: MedFreight clients get it bundled; one DME shop that delivers to homes; two brokers wanting a differentiator; MHC offices as test consignees.
ideas.path_to_big: An API licensed to freight-audit firms, brokers and TMS vendors, priced per shipment, built on a growing address-truth and dispute-outcome dataset. Unproven: carriers may not budge, and consignee response rates are unknown.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nobody found sells consignee-confirmed event evidence. Warp's free tool flags suspicious accessorials by rule; address-classification vendors only classify addresses; SMC3 RateWare Plus (industry-association owned) covers published accessorial rates, not events; the big freight-audit firms check invoice vs rate file.

ideas.title: ProofPack: Medicare proof-of-delivery packets for shipped DME and pharmacy orders
ideas.one_liner: Auto-build the proof-of-delivery file Medicare auditors demand (full carrier tracking, signature, date, recipient) for every shipped order and flag gaps before billing.
ideas.customer: DME/HME suppliers that ship resupply (CPAP, diabetic, wound care) and small pharmacies, starting with any DME or pharmacy arm of MHC; peers through HME buying groups (VGM cites about 3,500 providers and 9,000 locations).
ideas.who_pays: The supplier's owner or compliance lead pays $149-499 a month per location; budget line is audit exposure and recoupments.
ideas.problem: For shipped DMEPOS items the record must trace the item from supplier to beneficiary and be kept 7 years; without it claims are denied and overpayments requested. With 79,000+ enrolled suppliers and an active DME fraud crackdown, small shops with paper tickets and screenshots are exposed.
ideas.solution: Connect to carrier tracking feeds plus an order CSV; generate a per-claim PDF packet; add e-signature delivery tickets for direct deliveries; answer documentation requests in minutes; later monetize the same tracking data with 25% parcel-refund recovery. Sign a BAA, use HIPAA-eligible hosting, minimum-necessary fields keyed by order ID, and get an attorney review.
ideas.why_now: Federal DME crackdown and enrollment moratorium (Feb 27 to Aug 27, 2026) raise audit intensity; carrier tracking APIs make packet assembly cheap.
ideas.founder_edge: Fast build of tracking-to-packet pipelines; MHC as a possible pilot (only if it has a DME or pharmacy arm, which is unverified).
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC's DME or pharmacy arm if any; three HMEs from the family circle; six from a talk to a state association or VGM-type group.
ideas.path_to_big: Evidence layer for every payer that demands proof of delivery, plus refund recovery; 10,000 locations at $250 a month is $30M, but that is a large share of buying-group networks, so it is heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ParcelShield (predictive tracking plus proof-of-delivery audit; Walmart Specialty and UNC Health named), practice-management vendors (Brightree, WellSky workflows), VGM Fulfillment for outsourced fulfilment, parcel refund firms (Refund Retriever, ShipScience). Small shops are underserved but incumbents are well funded.

ideas.title: Advisor-Embedded Leak Check: a white-label spend-leak scan advisors give their business-owner clients
ideas.one_liner: A CPA, RIA or fractional CFO hands a business-owner client a branded leak check (freight, supplier surcharges, duplicate fees) run by the engine; the client pays only on recovery.
ideas.customer: Advisors and CPAs with business-owner clients (channel); the business owners are the end buyers.
ideas.who_pays: The client pays 15-20% of recoveries; the advisor pays nothing at first and later a flat annual license (not per-referral commissions).
ideas.problem: Advisors want retention hooks and cannot see accounts-payable leaks; owners rarely audit freight or supplier surcharges. Referral commissions are a compliance trap (AICPA limits for attest clients, fiduciary conflict disclosure), so the structure must avoid per-referral pay.
ideas.solution: White-label intake portal where the client uploads 12 months of freight bills and supplier invoices; engine runs freight audit and the surcharge ledger; advisor sees a co-branded summary. Use a flat license or no fee so no commission rule is triggered.
ideas.why_now: The tariff-refund and surcharge disputes (idea 1) give advisors a timely reason to call business-owner clients.
ideas.founder_edge: Ron's 24 years in financial services and a network of pre-screened flat-fee advisors; MFA built compliance technology for advisors, so Ron understands how they vet vendors.
ideas.first_10_customers: Three advisors Ron introduces, each bringing two or three business-owner clients, plus three CPAs from the same circle.
ideas.path_to_big: A distribution channel rather than a product; only worth building if ideas 1 or 2 work. Advisors are cautious endorsing third-party vendors, so scale is slow.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FreightWise pays referral commissions to brokers and fulfilment firms; cost-reduction consultancies run franchise-style CPA channels (not verified in detail); tariff-refund firms court CPAs. No white-label leak check for advisors found.

ideas.title: Baygrass Buying Club: an event-production co-op for independent festivals
ideas.one_liner: Independent festivals share anonymized vendor quotes and invoices; the club benchmarks staging, sound, fencing, sanitation and trucking prices, runs pooled bids, and audits invoices against contracts.
ideas.customer: Independent festival directors, starting with bluegrass and Americana festivals, later fairs, races and municipal events.
ideas.who_pays: Festival pays $49-199 a month; vendors pay an administrative fee on pooled deals (the model CAHSAH's purchasing group uses with vendor royalties).
ideas.problem: Stage, sound, lighting, labor and insurance costs jumped. Okeechobee paused future editions after its 2026 return, Michelada Fest cancelled again in 2026 citing production, labor and insurance costs, and UK independent festivals fell from roughly 800-900 to 592 in 2025.
ideas.solution: Shared price database and benchmark per unit (stage hour, fence foot, porta-potty), quarterly pooled RFPs for supplies and rentals, and invoice-versus-contract audit for overages and delivery or fuel fees.
ideas.why_now: Cost squeeze is forcing independents to cancel; pooled buying is the obvious survival tool but no US festival co-op was found.
ideas.founder_edge: Ron co-founded Annapolis Baygrass (IBMA 2026 Event of the Year nominee) and knows the bluegrass circuit; Baygrass is a ready pilot.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass first; then five to nine festivals Ron names through IBMA and regional associations.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest: bluegrass festivals are a small market. Reaching $10M needs a broader temporary-events co-op (fairs, races, municipal events) with about $300M of pooled spend at a 3% fee; plausible only if the first festivals show real savings. The '15-30% pooled discount' claim is an undocumented ticketing-vendor blog claim.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No US festival buying co-op found; UK Association of Independent Festivals offers member benefits; home-care GPOs (HPSI, IMCO, MED Group) prove the GPO model in a neighboring sector.

ideas.title: Broker Audit Drop-In: the audit engine white-labeled to freight brokers, 3PLs and parcel consultants
ideas.one_liner: Brokers with 50-300 small shippers each add 'we audit your bills' as a feature run by his engine and pay per enrolled shipper.
ideas.customer: Independent freight brokers, 3PLs and parcel consultants serving small shippers.
ideas.who_pays: The broker pays $100-300 a month per enrolled shipper or gives a 30% share of recoveries.
ideas.problem: Small shippers do not audit, brokers want differentiation, and building an audit engine is beyond a small broker. Weakness: brokers earn on volume and may not want carrier errors surfaced; no family tie.
ideas.solution: Hosted engine with broker-branded intake, per-shipper reports and a claims queue; brokers keep the client relationship.
ideas.why_now: The engine is built and tested; the NMFC density rewrite and accessorial growth create audit demand; one broker equals many shippers.
ideas.founder_edge: Finished engine and call sheet; speed to onboard; MedFreight results can serve as proof points.
ideas.first_10_customers: Three brokers from the existing call list; any broker serving a MedFreight client; four from freight-association contacts.
ideas.path_to_big: Scale is multiplied by the broker's book, but still capped by small-shipper recoveries; only meaningful if idea 2 proves the engine finds real money.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Freight-audit-and-payment firms (Cass, nVision and others), TMS-embedded audit modules, and FreightWise, which pays referral commissions to brokerages, audit and fulfilment firms.

ideas.title: Cold-Chain Claims Desk: reship and refund recovery for independent specialty and infusion pharmacies
ideas.one_liner: Track every temperature-sensitive overnight parcel, file the carrier's late-delivery refund inside its roughly 15-day window, and document reships and excursions for claims.
ideas.customer: Independent specialty, compounding and infusion pharmacies; any MHC pharmacy or infusion arm as pilot (unverified).
ideas.who_pays: The pharmacy owner pays 25% of refunds and claims recovered.
ideas.problem: Reships after late or distressed cold-chain parcels cost real money; FedEx and UPS money-back guarantees now cover only overnight and 2-day AM services, request windows are about 15 days, and late-eligible volume is about 3.5% of shipments, so monitoring must be continuous. Carrier liability for temperature-sensitive pharma may be limited by tariff (not verified).
ideas.solution: Ingest carrier invoices and tracking, match each late or distressed parcel to its refund eligibility, file inside the window, build excursion evidence for claims, and benchmark packaging and lane failure rates.
ideas.why_now: Direct-to-patient specialty shipments keep growing and carriers narrowed guarantees, so pharmacies leave money unclaimed.
ideas.founder_edge: Fast build of the tracking and filing loop; pharmacy contacts through the family if any.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC-linked pharmacy if one exists; three independents via a state pharmacy association; six via cold outreach.
ideas.path_to_big: Folds into ProofPack (idea 4) as monetization of the same tracking data; standing alone it is small.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ParcelShield (tracking and intervention, Walmart Specialty and UNC Health), Refund Retriever, ShipScience and LateShipment (refunds), sensor vendors such as SpotSee. Generic parcel refund recovery is crowded.

ideas.title: CareFund: the paying-for-care desk at the home-care front door
ideas.one_liner: A 12-minute family intake that turns 'how do we pay for Mom's care?' into a Care Funding Map plus a flat-fee advisor or elder-law consult, handed out by home-care agencies at admission and discharge.
ideas.customer: Owner-operated home-health and private-duty agencies (administrator or owner signs), plus fee-only or flat-fee advisors and elder-law attorneys in the same county (principal signs). Later: LTC carriers, credit unions, employers.
ideas.who_pays: Agencies pay a flat license of about $300-900/mo for the intake tool and handouts. Advisors pay about $299/mo for an exclusive county or $200-350 per qualified consult (SmartAsset leads reportedly cost advisors $150-300+). Per-start fees to agencies are the Caring.com model but may be restricted by state patient-brokering law, so default to flat fees.
ideas.problem: Agency private-pay care runs about $35/hr, so 40 hr/wk is roughly $6,000 a month. Families learn this in a crisis, often do not know a parent holds an LTC policy or how to claim it, and do not know VA Aid & Attendance or Medicaid-waiver rules. They cut hours or never convert from a Medicare episode to private duty. Agencies lose the conversion and advisors meet the family only after the damage is done.
ideas.solution: A non-advice, software-first funding map the family fills in via QR or link: local cost and months of runway; LTC-policy lookup and claim-start checklist; VA, Medicaid waiver, Medicare Advantage extras and state programs screened against a live rules database kept current by his multi-agent research pipeline; family cost-sharing; then a booked 45-minute flat-fee advisor or attorney consult as the paid next step. The agency receives only 'completed and consented', so no PHI flows and no BAA is needed at the start.
ideas.why_now: CY2026 Medicare home-health payments were cut about 1.3%, and the CY2027 proposal keeps a 3% temporary cut. A May 13, 2026 CMS moratorium bars new agencies and branches for six months (extendable), so growth must come from existing census and private pay. LTC insurance paid $16.9B in 2024 and Milliman projects a $42B peak by 2041. There are 63M family caregivers (+45% in a decade). Genworth's CareScout shows carriers and providers fund navigation. SEC 2026 exam priorities spotlight older investors.
ideas.founder_edge: Dad's flat-fee advisor roster and compliance toolkit (he already lives under the SEC Marketing Rule promoter regime); agency intake workflows he can shadow at the family company; his freight-audit pattern of cheap diagnostic first, paid action second; AI-speed build of the intake and the 50-state rules database. Depends on what MHC actually is (unverified): if Medicare-only home health, the pilot is the discharge-to-private-duty conversion.
ideas.first_10_customers: 3-5 advisors from Dad's roster at a $99 founding rate, then $299. The family agency pilots the QR handout at admission and discharge, free for 60 days then a flat fee. 2-3 peer agencies via grandfather's introductions and Home Care Association of Florida events. 2 elder-law attorneys. 2 ALF discharge planners as free referral sources. A county 'Money and Care' lunch hosted jointly by agency and advisor is the lead engine (the only place the workshop idea survives).
ideas.path_to_big: Agencies and advisors are the wedge; the big money is carriers (CareScout proves they pay to steer claims), credit unions (Carefull/CSI show they distribute caregiver tools) and employer caregiving benefits (Cariloop and Wellthy raised $20-25M rounds). Bottom-up: about 200k consults a year at $250 plus 100k agency starts at $400 is about $90M, which is heroic share. Realistic 8-year outcome is $20-60M unless one carrier or bank channel lands. Legal premises to clear: Rule 206(4)-1 promoter agreement and disclosures, Florida patient-brokering statute (from my recollection, verify with counsel), no VA claim-prep fees unless accredited.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Genworth CareScout (provider matching, nurse assessment; providers pay placement fees; 1,100+ locations, about 2,950 matches in H1 2026); A Place for Mom and Caring.com (lead sale); Wellthy and Cariloop (employer-paid concierge); NCOA BenefitsCheckUp (free, benefits only, about 2,000 programs); Carefull and ElderFi (finance apps); Everplans (document vault for advisors). No one found combining a funding map, advisor fulfillment and agency-intake distribution.

ideas.title: Day-90 Bench: pre-health campus caregiver pipeline with a retention guarantee
ideas.one_liner: Pay-per-retained-hire recruiting of 18+ pre-health college students into part-time caregiver roles at agencies, with a free replacement if they quit before day 90.
ideas.customer: Home-health and private-duty agencies (administrator, HR director or owner signs).
ideas.who_pays: $1,000-1,500 per hire who reaches day 90, which is below the $2,304 average aide sign-on bonus (HCS 2025) plus the $2,600-5,000 replacement cost (vendor-sourced).
ideas.problem: Aide turnover is 34% in the HCS survey of 1,100 agencies and 75-79% in vendor blogs, with about 80% of departures in the first 90 days (vendor claim). Interviews no-show about half the time. Agencies spend over $2,000 a head on bonuses alone and still churn.
ideas.solution: Student ambassadors at pre-med, nursing, PA, PT and OT clubs run short-form recruiting; same-day interview booking; text-based onboarding through day 90; a verified patient-care-hours letter for school applications; exam-aware scheduling. The agency employs, trains and runs competency evaluation; Bench only recruits and retains, so it is not an employer or nurse registry (confirm with Florida counsel). 18 and older only.
ideas.why_now: Medicare cuts and the enrollment moratorium make labor cost and census-led growth the only levers. 2025 HCS data show agencies already paying up on wages and bonuses.
ideas.founder_edge: He is the target demographic and is about to be a college freshman, so Gen Z distribution is the product. The family agency is a ready first customer. He can ship onboarding and texting automation in days. The same campus network feeds idea 3.
ideas.first_10_customers: The family agency (Riverview/Tampa, Boca Raton and Fort Lauderdale branches if confirmed) at $1,000 per day-90 hire. 3-4 peer agencies in the same metros via grandfather's introductions. Recruit from UF, USF, UCF, FAU, Nova and FIU pre-health clubs. Then 5 private-duty franchise owners.
ideas.path_to_big: 12,234 Medicare-certified agencies at an assumed 25 aide hires a year is about 300k hires before non-medical agencies. A 10% share at $1,200 is about $36M from certified agencies alone and roughly $100M with private duty. Then add a shift marketplace and retention SaaS. Risks: seasonal student churn, thin margin per placement, low switching cost.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Papa (Gen Z companionship, health-plan paid, about $1.4B valuation, relaunching direct to consumer); Fountain Frontline OS and Paradox (generic frontline hiring automation); Indeed; Clipboard Health, CareRev and ShiftKey (shift marketplaces); Home Care Pulse content. No pre-health campus channel with a day-90 guarantee found.

ideas.title: Advisor Residency: Gen Z paraplanner and associate pipeline for independent RIAs
ideas.one_liner: A 10-week cohort that trains finance and econ students and career changers as paraplanners and associates, placed with independent RIAs for a fee, plus fractional paraplanning to the same firms.
ideas.customer: Independent RIAs and fee-only planning firms (managing partner signs).
ideas.who_pays: $6-12k placement fee after a 90-day hold, or $1.5-3k a month for fractional paraplanning by residents supervised by a lead planner.
ideas.problem: About 106k advisors retire over a decade, McKinsey sees a 100k shortfall by 2034, 72% of rookie advisors fail, 64% of new-advisor recruiting is word of mouth, and independent RIAs are invisible on campuses. The one matching tool, Schwab/TD RIAConnect, only serves firms it custodies.
ideas.solution: Campus recruiting, a structured curriculum in planning software and client-meeting prep, optional SIE, supervised first-client prep, and a placement guarantee. Residents do support work, not advice, so there is no license wall for Asher.
ideas.why_now: The retirement wave, rookie failure rates, and SEC 2026 priorities that raise the supervision burden on thin teams.
ideas.founder_edge: Dad's 24 years of peers; XYPN's partner program (2,200+ fee-only advisors) as a non-family door; the same Gen Z campus engine as idea 2; he is the recruit's peer.
ideas.first_10_customers: 3 RIAs in Dad's circle take summer-2027 interns as the pilot. Then XYPN-adjacent firms, FPA chapters and Dad's introductions.
ideas.path_to_big: About 5,000 placements a year at $10k is $50M, plus 2,000 fractional-paraplanning firms at $24k a year is $48M, so about $100M if it becomes the default pipeline. That is roughly 10% of hiring, which is heroic. Risks: incumbent free tools, recruiter relationships, outsourcing client data under Reg S-P.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Schwab RIAConnect NextGen; Kitces and FPA career centers; specialist recruiters; exam-prep vendors; outsourced paraplanning shops; AI notetakers like Jump and Zocks are adjacent, not this. No Gen Z residency-plus-placement model found.

ideas.title: Heir Onramp: a next-gen program advisors give clients' adult kids, run by an actual heir
ideas.one_liner: A white-labeled 6-session cohort plus a play-money family-wealth simulator for 18-35-year-old heirs of an advisor's best clients, capped by an in-person Heir Day in festival hospitality.
ideas.customer: Independent RIAs and trust companies serving business-owner families (principal or head of client experience signs).
ideas.who_pays: $6-15k per firm per year; Heir Day hospitality is $2.5-5k per advisor, shared with the festival.
ideas.problem: In the 2025 Harris poll 43% of heirs plan to leave the parents' advisor and 42% stay; 26% of leavers do not personally know the advisor, and 82% of under-40 heirs prefer in-person. Advisors know this but today the fix is consultants and workshops, not a product.
ideas.solution: Educational, non-advice modules on family-business ownership, trusts, taxes and what the advisor actually does, hosted by Asher as a real third-generation business-family heir. A play-money family-office simulator built on the economy engine he already shipped in House Money. Heir Day is a VIP tent at Baygrass or a partner festival, which gives the festival hospitality revenue while festival costs run about 40% above 2019.
ideas.why_now: Heir-attrition data, SEC 2026 fiduciary and older-investor focus, and festival cost pressure that makes hospitality revenue valuable.
ideas.founder_edge: He is the target user; his family's second generation already works in the family business; he has built playable economy apps; Dad's Baygrass access supplies the venue and Dad's advisors are the buyers.
ideas.first_10_customers: 2-3 RIAs from Dad's network for a paid pilot cohort with Baygrass as the first Heir Day, then 5 RIAs from XYPN and FPA events.
ideas.path_to_big: 3,000 firms at $10k is $30M; enterprise trust-company and custodian licensing could add $10-20M. Honestly a $20-50M business unless a custodian licenses it. Festival hospitality alone is small and is only the hook.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Legacy Capitals and Cannon Financial workshops; Nitrogen and Hearsay client-engagement tools (general); in-house programs at large wealth managers. No productized heir cohort plus simulator found.

ideas.title: Open Door: a financial-safety layer for in-home care
ideas.one_liner: A 5-minute protocol and mobile checklist that lets agency staff in clients' homes flag financial-exploitation red flags to a consented trusted contact, with escalation packets for the client's bank, advisor and Adult Protective Services.
ideas.customer: Agencies (owner or director of nursing) for the pilot; later credit unions, banks and LTC carriers (head of fraud or member experience).
ideas.who_pays: Agencies $3-6 per active client a month as a risk-management and differentiation tool; institutions $1-4 per enrolled member a month. Whether agencies pay is unproven.
ideas.problem: CFPB found non-family caregivers were the perpetrator in 1 of 9 known-perpetrator exploitation cases, with an average loss of $57,800. Banks see transactions but not the stack of past-due mail or the new 'friend'.
ideas.solution: Micro-training, an observation checklist, consent and trusted-contact capture compatible with FINRA Rule 4512, a bank and advisor handoff, and exploitation-reporting workflows. Non-clinical and HIPAA-authorized per client; counsel needed for Florida mandatory-reporting duties.
ideas.why_now: Banks are adopting Carefull and EverSafe; FINRA Rules 2165 and 4512 push firms to build workflows (2165's safe harbor requires documented training); the moratorium and fraud task force make 'clean agency' signaling valuable.
ideas.founder_edge: Family agency shadowing for the protocol; Dad's advisor and trusted-contact conversations; AI-speed build of the checklist app.
ideas.first_10_customers: The family agency pilot, 2 peer agencies, 1-2 advisors via Dad, and one local credit union reached through those advisors.
ideas.path_to_big: 3M enrolled members at $4 a month is $144M, but that needs bank and credit-union channels with 6-12 month sales cycles. First revenue is slower than ideas 1-4.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Carefull (consumer $12.99/mo; Synovus and CSI bank channels); EverSafe (Sompo); AARP BankSafe (free training, 1,500 institutions); consumer monitoring apps. Nobody uses in-home staff as the sensor.

ideas.title: Cash Desk: contingency recovery for LTC-insurance and private-pay home-care claims
ideas.one_liner: His freight-invoice-audit playbook applied to home-care billing: compare each LTC-insurance and private-pay claim to the policy schedule, find short-pays, rejections and missed benefit days, and recover them for 15-25%.
ideas.customer: Agencies with private-duty or LTC-insurance billing (owner or controller signs). Depends on whether the family agency has such a line.
ideas.who_pays: Contingency of 15-25% of recovered dollars, or a monthly SaaS tier after a flat diagnostic.
ideas.problem: ADL documentation gaps, elimination-period math and slow insurers leave money uncollected. Existing tools mostly submit claims rather than recover underpayments.
ideas.solution: Ingest claims and EOBs, parse each policy schedule, flag underpayments and fixable rejections, and prepare appeal packets. Flat diagnostic first, as in his freight offer. BAA required and minimum-necessary claim fields only.
ideas.why_now: LTC insurance payouts of $16.9B in 2024 rising toward $42B in 2041, and agency margins squeezed by Medicare cuts.
ideas.founder_edge: He already has a built audit service with a flat-diagnostic-plus-contingency structure; the family agency supplies real claim data under a BAA.
ideas.first_10_customers: The family agency if it bills LTC insurance, then peer agencies via grandfather's introductions.
ideas.path_to_big: If 45% of LTC benefits flow to home and community care (my assumption, unverified), a 4% recovery fee on about $7.6B is a roughly $300M fee pool, but $100M would need heroic share. Realistic outcome is $15-40M, and it also feeds idea 1's cost and claim data.
ideas.who_does_it_today: AssuriCare LTCfastpay (used by large LTC insurers), AxisCare and AlayaCare (agency billing), in-house billers, generic medical-bill advocates. No recovery-first player found, but only a light check.

ideas.title: Dementia-Ready Advisor: clinician-built senior-client training and trusted-contact workflow
ideas.one_liner: Scenario-based, AI role-play training written by home-health clinicians that gives broker-dealers and RIAs the documented training FINRA Rule 2165's safe harbor requires, plus ready-to-use trusted-contact and escalation templates.
ideas.customer: Broker-dealer and RIA chief compliance officers or heads of training.
ideas.who_pays: $50-200 per advisor per year, or $3-10k per firm per year, from the compliance and training budget.
ideas.problem: Rule 2165 Supplementary Material .02 requires documented training for firms relying on the safe harbor, and the SEC 2026 priorities scrutinize recommendations to older investors, yet most training is generic.
ideas.solution: Clinician-written dementia and capacity-concern scenarios, a voice role-play practice tool, and quick-reference scripts. Education only, not legal advice.
ideas.why_now: SEC 2026 priorities, FINRA's senior-investor focus (May 2026 conference) and heightened fraud enforcement.
ideas.founder_edge: Access to clinical subject-matter experts at the family agency and Dad's compliance contacts; he builds role-play tools quickly.
ideas.first_10_customers: Dad's compliance-officer contacts, 3 RIAs for a $2-5k pilot, then XYPN and FPA webinars.
ideas.path_to_big: 300k advisors at $150 is $45M if it wins, but free substitutes cap pricing. Honestly a $10-30M business, better as a module inside ideas 1 and 4 than as a standalone.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FINRA and SIFMA materials; AARP BankSafe (free); the Certified Senior Advisor credential ($395 exam, $180 a year); generic compliance-training vendors.

ideas.title: Age-in-Place Funding Navigator: from the home-safety evaluation to a funded modification
ideas.one_liner: When the agency's PT or OT recommends grab bars, ramps or a bathroom change, the family gets a funding stack and a vetted bid from a remodeler who pays a flat membership, never a success fee.
ideas.customer: CAPS-certified remodelers and accessibility contractors (owner signs); the agency's PT/OT director is the channel.
ideas.who_pays: Contractors $300-900 a month flat, not per sale. The agency receives nothing and seniors pay nothing.
ideas.problem: Medicare covers no modifications, grants are narrow (VA HISA $6,800 service-connected or $2,000 otherwise; some Medicare Advantage plans about $500), and families stall. Third-party lead sites charge contractors $150-600 per lead shared among 3-5 bidders.
ideas.solution: A funding-first checklist reusing the idea 1 rules database, exclusive qualified projects for a monthly fee, and a published ethics code against high-pressure stairlift-style selling.
ideas.why_now: 63M caregivers, the Joint Center's $13B aging-in-place renovation market, and Medicare cuts pushing more care into the home.
ideas.founder_edge: The multi-agent rules database from idea 1 and the family agency's PT/OT access. Family consents and initiates because evaluations are PHI; Florida patient-brokering and kickback rules require that the agency gets no remuneration.
ideas.first_10_customers: 3 local remodelers from Dad's and grandfather's contractor networks, the family agency's PT/OT team, and 2 senior-center partners.
ideas.path_to_big: 50k projects a year at $400 equivalent revenue is about $20M. It is more a feature of idea 1 than a standalone company, and the ethical risk of selling to older adults needs hard guardrails.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Angi and HomeAdvisor lead sites; stairlift and walk-in-tub direct-response sellers; Rebuilding Together and local Area Agencies on Aging (grants and free help). Nobody uses the PT/OT evaluation plus funding-first as a channel.

ideas.title: Contract Truth: managed-care underpayment and authorization-leak audit for home health
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee diagnostic plus contingency audit that checks what Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed-care plans actually paid against the signed contract rates and the authorized visit units, then recovers the gap.
ideas.customer: Owner or CFO of a Medicare-certified home health agency with at least $2M revenue and 25%+ managed-care mix (Florida has many). The family agencies come first, then peers and third-party billing companies.
ideas.who_pays: The agency, out of recovered dollars: $2,500 flat diagnostic on 12 months of remits, then 20-25% of recovered underpayments, then $500-1,500 a month for an authorization watchdog. Self-funding, so no existing budget line is needed. The owner or CFO signs.
ideas.problem: The biller's secret: denials are visible so agencies chase them, but underpayments are invisible. Every MA and Medicaid managed-care plan pays off its own rate sheet, the contract is a PDF nobody re-reads, remits are posted as paid-vs-billed rather than paid-vs-contract, and visits past authorized units or dates are silently written off. MA volume has passed fee-for-service in home health (Trella, vendor analysis) and MA often pays below traditional Medicare by a large margin (HHCN).
ideas.solution: Ingest 835/ERA remits (patient names stripped), contract PDFs (LLM extracts rate tables) and an authorization-log export. Flag paid not equal to contracted rate, visits outside authorized units or dates, and appeal or timely-filing windows about to close. Deliver a claim-level recovery file with dispute letters. Phase 2 is a real-time watchdog that tells schedulers a visit is unauthorized and to request an extension today. It reuses the freight-invoice audit engine he already built.
ideas.why_now: MA now outweighs fee-for-service in home health; federal scrutiny of MA denials is up (OIG reports June 2026, Senate letter July 2026); CY2027 proposed rule gives +2.4% but LeadingAge says strain remains; the May 13, 2026 CMS moratorium on new agencies and branches means incumbents must protect margin instead of expanding.
ideas.founder_edge: His freight-audit system (rate contract vs invoice vs recovery, flat diagnostic plus contingency) is the same engine, built but not yet selling. Mom inside MHC can introduce the biller and CFO on day one and get real 835s. Pure AI-speed build, no license needed.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Ask Grandfather for one MHC agency, sign BAA and NDA, run a free 90-day look-back on one MA plan. 2) Convert to contingency once the recovery file is real. 3) Add the other MHC provider numbers (the directory lists Areas 6 and 10). 4) Two peers via Grandfather's owner circle and the state home-care association. 5) One third-party billing company serving 20-100 agencies is a channel worth 20+ customers: free look-backs plus revenue share.
ideas.path_to_big: Bottom-up (assumptions, verify): about 11,000 Medicare-certified agencies, managed-care share 40-50% of revenue, typical revenue $3-5M, leakage 2-5% gives $25-100k a year recoverable per agency, fee 20-25% gives $5-25k per agency-year. $10M needs roughly 700-1,500 agencies, which is 6-13% of all agencies, a stretch not a given. $100M needs the same engine pointed at every post-acute and ancillary provider billing managed-care plans (therapy, DME, behavioral health, SNF Part B, infusion). The authorization watchdog makes revenue recurring; cross-agency payer-behavior data is the asset (watch antitrust if shared). If MHC is hospice-only the idea shrinks because MA hospice is carved out to fee-for-service.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nearest is Claim Health (YC X25: AI billing, denial appeals, claims to recover denied or underpaid revenue). Also Aegis and Covered Health (generic appeals), outsourced billing companies paid on percent of collections that chase denials not contract compliance, and hospital-side underpayment vendors (general knowledge, none verified for home health). I found no contract-compliance-first home health product, but not finding it is weaker than it not existing. Legal check: Medicare and Medicaid restrict agents paid a percentage of collections they receive (42 CFR 424.73, 447.10; verify with counsel), so stay off fee-for-service claims and never touch the money.

ideas.title: Agency Integrity Report: claims-integrity diligence and sell-side readiness for the moratorium deal wave
ideas.one_liner: A five-day, AI-assisted chart-to-claim integrity audit that tells sellers what a buyer will find and tells buyers what overpayment liability they would inherit, delivered through counsel.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators weighing a sale of a Medicare-certified home health or hospice agency, regional operators and PE-backed platforms buying agencies, plus M&A advisors, healthcare counsel, lenders and R&W insurance brokers.
ideas.who_pays: Sellers pay $5-10k for a pre-sale audit, funded from expected proceeds; buyers pay $10-25k inside a diligence budget that every deal already has (price is my estimate). Owner (sell-side) or deal lead and counsel (buy-side) sign.
ideas.problem: The enrollment specialist's secret: buying an agency means buying its past. CMS can offset a prior owner's overpayment against the new owner (Vernon Home Health, 5th Cir.), the 36-month rule can void a provider-agreement transfer, and R&W insurers treat billing, coding and hospice cap as heightened-concern or excluded areas depending on diligence depth. Buyers sample thirty charts and call it diligence; sellers go in blind and get repriced late.
ideas.solution: Standardized package: random chart-to-claim sample tested against OASIS, face-to-face, orders and PDGM grouping; extrapolated error rate and repayment range with a confidence interval; Review Choice affirmation trend; ADR and TPE history; star-rating trend; payer concentration and MA contract exposure; 36-month-rule check; clone-note screen. Engaged through the seller's or buyer's healthcare counsel so findings sit in privilege and the 60-day overpayment clock is handled by a lawyer.
ideas.why_now: CMS imposed a nationwide six-month moratorium on new home health and hospice enrollments, branches and some ownership changes effective May 13, 2026, with an extension decision due about mid-November. That made existing certified agencies scarce. Braff Group annualizes 134 home-based-care deals in 2026 (certified home health pacing +41%, hospice +57%). Adaptive Innovations just raised $50M to buy small agencies.
ideas.founder_edge: Multi-agent research pipelines map directly onto chart-review agents; text-forensics skill from his detector; the mentor built and sold a roll-up-heavy company and can intro M&A advisors; the family company is either a prospective buyer or knows who is selling.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) Run a free mirror-test integrity pass on one MHC agency (useful to MHC, yields an anonymized case study). 2) Ask Grandfather who in his circle is buying or selling. 3) Take the case study to three or four home-health M&A advisors and healthcare law firms, first deal free for a reference. 4) Mentor intros to deal people. Expect 2 family-circle deals, 3 via advisors, 5 via counsel.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest: home-based-care deals run in the low hundreds a year, so alone this is a $2-5M boutique. It is only big if it generalizes to healthcare-services M&A broadly (physician groups, DME, labs, behavioral health, SNF, thousands of deals a year at $10-25k) and becomes a standard that R&W insurers, lenders and PE accept as an Integrity Score; sell-side owners also become warm leads for wealth advisors and attorneys (advisory referral compensation must follow SEC Marketing Rule promoter requirements). Needs a credible partner because enterprise buyers will not trust an 18-year-old cold. If no partner, call it a boutique and kill it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Big-4 and regional accounting firms, healthcare compliance consultancies (SimiTree-style), law-firm compliance reviewers, and billing and coding auditors, all human-sampled and slow. I found no standardized AI-native integrity product for agency deals. Legal premise to guard: a report that creates a known overpayment the client ignores defeats its own privilege, so use counsel-directed engagement and state it is not legal advice.

ideas.title: One Inbox: cross-agency physician orders network with text-link batch signing
ideas.one_liner: One phone-friendly queue where a certifying physician signs every pending home health, hospice and DME order from every participating agency, with turnaround dashboards for the agencies.
ideas.customer: Administrators and billing managers at home health agencies, hospices and DME suppliers; the second side is certifying physicians and their office staff.
ideas.who_pays: The agency pays $300-900 a month or $1-2 per signed order. Cash math (assumption): a $5M agency that cuts 10 days off its collection cycle frees about $137k once, and cutting write-offs 0.5% is about $25k a year. Budget is the A/R and write-off line; owner or billing manager signs.
ideas.problem: The intake coordinator and biller secret: unsigned orders are typically the number one cause of held final claims. Medicare final claims wait for signed orders, the window is roughly 37-40 days after period end, and aged orders turn into days sales outstanding and write-offs. Staff chase the same forty doctors by fax while every agency, hospice and DME company has its own portal that the doctor ignores.
ideas.solution: The doctor gets one text link that opens a single queue of every pending order across all participating agencies, batch signs with identity verification and a full audit trail. Agencies get turnaround by physician and claim-hold dollars. No deep EHR integration at the start: orders arrive as forwarded PDFs or CSVs and AI parses and routes them. Phase 2 helps doctors capture care plan oversight (G0181) and certification billing so they earn something. Phase 3 extends to hospice, DME written orders, SNF and payer notices.
ideas.why_now: The moratorium makes each existing agency's cash cycle more valuable; AI fax and PDF parsing is now cheap; physicians are drowning in portals; the CY2027 rule environment keeps agencies cash-conscious.
ideas.founder_edge: Fast build and mobile-first Gen Z UX. Mom can say which doctors are slowest. Starting inside the MHC provider numbers gives density on day one because the same doctors sign for all of them.
ideas.first_10_customers: The MHC provider numbers as one network (3 if the directory is right), then agencies in the same markets (Tampa Bay, Broward, Palm Beach) that share referral doctors. Make it doctor-led: any physician already using the inbox gets their other agencies added free, so peers get pulled in by their own referral sources.
ideas.path_to_big: About 11,000 agencies plus about 6,500 hospices (verify) at roughly $6k a year; 15% penetration is about $16M. $100M needs the network to extend to DME, labs, SNF and payer notices as the order-exchange standard for post-acute. Network effects are the moat; chicken-and-egg physician adoption is the main risk. Works for hospice (G0182) and DME if MHC is not pure home health.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Each EHR's own physician portal (Axxess, HCHB, WellSky; general knowledge), Enzo Health's order-management module inside its EHR, DocuSign plus fax, and staff paid to chase signatures. I found no neutral multi-agency physician network, but EHR vendors can block integrations or copy it. Verify Medicare e-signature authentication requirements and sign BAAs with every agency.

ideas.title: Note Forensics: clone and AI-authorship integrity audit for home health and hospice documentation
ideas.one_liner: Monthly monitoring that finds copy-paste notes, template saturation and likely machine-authored text across a chart set before a Medicare reviewer does.
ideas.customer: Compliance officers, administrators and DONs at home health and hospice agencies inside the Review Choice Demonstration; PE-backed multi-agency platforms; later AI-scribe vendors and payer fraud units.
ideas.who_pays: $2,500 flat diagnostic on 200 charts, then $750-2,000 a month monitoring; $50-150k a year for multi-agency platforms (my estimate). Budget is the QA and compliance line, which already funds a QA nurse. Administrator or owner signs.
ideas.problem: The RCD specialist's secret: the day a reviewer sees the same sentence in hundreds of visit notes, it is over. Florida agencies face a 90% affirmation bar every six months, note cloning is a named auditor red flag, and AI scribes make notes polished and look-alike with unclear authorship.
ideas.solution: Apply the detector method he proved (read the gestalt, normalize formatting, compare drafts): cross-patient and cross-clinician similarity, within-chart copy-forward, template saturation, vocabulary-drift signals suggesting machine authorship, missing visit-specific facts, impossible timestamps and visit-length vs mileage mismatches. Output is a chart integrity score and a per-clinician coaching list.
ideas.why_now: HCHB (with Stenohealth) and Enzo are shipping AI scribes; audit targeting is data-driven; the CY2027 proposed rule adds enrollment-revocation grounds; moratorium raises the value of every existing license. I could not find an OIG or UPIC statement specifically about AI-written home health notes, so this is an inference.
ideas.founder_edge: His AI-text detector beat commercial tools in his own blind tests and compare_drafts.py already handles human-draft vs AI-rewrite. This is the rarest asset in the lens.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC pilot framed as coaching and readiness, not an overpayment audit; peers through Grandfather; PE-backed platforms through the mentor; billing and QA outsourcers as resellers.
ideas.path_to_big: Provider-side is a few thousand agencies and hospices at $5-30k each. The real prize is a cross-vertical authenticity layer for clinical documentation sold to payer special-investigation units, hospital systems, PE portfolios, behavioral health and ABA. Venture-shaped but needs enterprise credibility he lacks today.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Brellium (AI documentation auditing for home health, hospice, behavioral health), Enzo's QA tool, EHR audit modules, SimiTree-style QA outsourcing. This is the most crowded home-health idea; the differentiator is authorship and clone forensics rather than completeness checking, and I did not verify that nobody offers forensics. Legal premise: a retrospective audit that finds overpayments starts the 60-day clock, so offer prospective coaching and route sensitive findings through counsel.

ideas.title: Heir Apparent: next-gen onboarding for business-owner families, sold through RIAs
ideas.one_liner: A parent-invited, advisor-branded family wealth room plus a ten-session family-meeting kit that gets an advisor's clients' adult children engaged before the inheritance, with an engagement score that flags heirs about to leave.
ideas.customer: RIAs and multi-family offices whose clients are business-owning families (healthcare-agency owners like his own family). End users are adult children, 21+ by design.
ideas.who_pays: The advisory firm: $2,500 pilot for three to five families, then $3-8k setup plus $100-300 per family per year (my estimate). Budget is client retention, marketing and next-gen programs; an advisor with $100M under management earns about $1M a year at a 1% fee, so one retained heir household justifies the spend. Firm owner signs.
ideas.problem: The RIA founder and CCO secret: we lose the kids at the funeral. Heir attrition estimates vary (66% in an InvestmentNews survey of 544 advisers, 70%+ quoted second-hand from Cerulli, lower recent figures for ultra-wealthy heirs under 40), but advisors rarely know the kids, cannot text them casually under recordkeeping rules, and cannot market to them under the Marketing Rule. 82% of heirs under 40 prefer in-person meetings, so the product must support the meeting, not replace it.
ideas.solution: Interactive education (how the family's structure works, compounding and drawdown, inheritance taxes, business-ownership scenarios), simulators built from his Strategy Lab and play-money economy mechanics, compliance-reviewed content, archived communications, and a ten-session family-meeting kit the advisor runs. Education only; the advisor gives advice. Parent consent before any heir data is used.
ideas.why_now: The multi-trillion-dollar intergenerational transfer is under way (Cerulli cited at $84T through 2045, second-hand), advisors are openly worried, and I found no dedicated heir-engagement platform in search.
ideas.founder_edge: He is a third-generation heir in a business-owning family and an actual 18-year-old, which no incumbent can fake; Dad has 24 years in the advisor world; the family's own succession is a live test case; he builds simulators fast.
ideas.first_10_customers: Dad's peers who run wealth practices; the family's own advisor; Maryland RIAs through the Annapolis network; FPA and NAPFA chapter events. One free pilot for a case study, then $2,500 pilots.
ideas.path_to_big: About 15,000 SEC-registered RIAs plus multi-family offices, trust companies and bank wealth units. 1,500 firms at $20k is $30M; $100M needs about 5,000 firms, over 20% of RIAs, which is heroic unless banks and trust companies buy. Risks: advisors buy slowly and education is hard to price.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Next-gen consultants and in-house programs at large firms, client portals from eMoney and Envestnet, and Savvy Wealth competing as an advisory firm for heirs. My search did not surface a dedicated heir-engagement platform, but absence in search is not proof. Guardrails: adults only, no investment advice from the platform, Reg S-P consent.

ideas.title: Festival Buyers Club: group purchasing with savings-share for independent festivals, then every community event
ideas.one_liner: A free-to-join buying club that autopsies a festival's biggest invoices, rebids them with multi-event vendor deals, and keeps 20% of verified savings.
ideas.customer: Directors of independent music festivals (start with bluegrass and roots via the IBMA world), then fairs, races, markets, and school and college events.
ideas.who_pays: Free to join; the club takes 20% of verified savings, then a 2-5% supplier admin fee on pooled volume once volume exists. Purchasing lines (production, rentals, sanitation, security, insurance, printing) already exist. The festival director or board signs.
ideas.problem: The production manager's secret: I pay retail for toilets, fencing, power, wristbands, cups and insurance because I am one five-thousand-person event; five bluegrass festivals buy from the same three vendors in the same months and never compare notes.
ideas.solution: Members send last year's ten biggest invoices; AI normalizes line items, benchmarks against regional bids, rebids the top categories with multi-event vendor agreements, and negotiates pooled insurance, payment-processing and ticketing rates. A shared vendor scorecard (no-shows, quality) and a certificate-of-insurance and permit vault ride along.
ideas.why_now: Festival alliances pooling orders are being written up as a cost-cutting model (Ticket Fairy, Oct 2025, which claims 15-30% discounts as its own estimate) and no dedicated independent-festival co-op turned up in search.
ideas.founder_edge: The savings-share mindset from the freight audit; Dad's Annapolis Baygrass (IBMA Event-of-the-Year nominee) is the first customer and door-opener; AI invoice normalization is easy for him.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass plus four or five Mid-Atlantic festivals Dad knows, then contacts from IBMA's World of Bluegrass and Folk Alliance. Offer the free invoice autopsy; take 20% only of realized savings.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest: about 3,000 mid-size independent festivals at roughly $250k addressable spend (assumption) is about $750M of purchasing; at 3-4% that is $22-30M with total penetration, so festival-only realistically tops out at $2-3M (about 35% share needed for $10M). It is only big if it widens to the whole community-events market (fairs, races, parades, markets, school and college events), where a 5% share of a multi-billion-dollar pool reaches $8-15M. If it cannot widen, it is a boutique.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nothing dedicated found. Neighbors: RedZone Group Purchasing (venues, claims 25-60% savings), informal festival alliances, Eventeny (software and vendor marketplace), and an IFEA National Event Services page I did not check, which may be a member-discount program. Sponsorship marketplaces (SponsorMyEvent since 2014, SponsorPark, HelloSponsor) have not broken out in ten years, which is why sponsorship is deliberately excluded.

ideas.title: Aide Pipeline: Gen Z creator-led caregiver recruiting plus first-90-day retention, paid per aide retained
ideas.one_liner: Short-form video recruiting from real young aides, an SMS funnel, and a 90-day retention coach, priced per aide still working at day 90 instead of per applicant.
ideas.customer: Labor-constrained home health, home care and hospice agencies, starting with MHC.
ideas.who_pays: $250 on the aide's start date plus $500 at day 90, against typical recruiting cost of $2,600-5,000 per hire (vendor benchmarks). A 100-aide agency at 75% turnover spends roughly $225k a year on recruiting (illustrative). The owner or HR lead signs.
ideas.problem: The scheduler's secret: about 80% of turnover happens in the first 90 days, annual turnover sits near 75-79%, only 12.8% of applicants are hired, median pay is $16.78 an hour, and after the hire nobody checks in during week two.
ideas.solution: Creator-style short videos built with real aides aged 18 and up, an AI SMS funnel (apply, screen, schedule, pre-boarding), and a shift-fit and check-in coach that warns supervisors before an aide quits. Outcome-based pricing is the point.
ideas.why_now: Turnover has stalled near 75% even as shortages eased; the moratorium means incumbents fight over the same labor pool; some agencies already test TikTok recruiting.
ideas.founder_edge: Gen Z distribution is the one thing the family cannot build in-house; Mom's HR contacts provide a live funnel and quick feedback.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC as pilot; nine more Florida agencies via Grandfather's circle, paid only on retained aides, with the first cash about 30 days after the first start.
ideas.path_to_big: Implied volume is over 2 million aide hires a year (assumption, verify BLS). A 5% share at $750 per retained aide is about $75M, which is heroic. Expansion to SNF and assisted-living aides widens the pool.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Indeed, ZipRecruiter, Joveo and EngineHire (recruiting marketing), Activated Insights / Home Care Pulse (benchmarking and engagement), and AI recruiting bots such as Paradox and Fountain. This is the closest to a cliche and survives only if outcome pricing and creator distribution beat job boards on cost per retained aide. Legal: recruiting is not staffing, he must not employ or place aides, and I did not verify whether Florida regulates fee-based placement.

ideas.title: Claim Check: Marketing-Rule claim substantiation and honest-backtest verification for advisors
ideas.one_liner: Extracts every factual or numeric claim from an advisor's website, posts and decks, builds the substantiation binder automatically, alerts when claims go stale, and checks hypothetical performance against an honest-backtest method.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size RIAs and the outsourced-CCO firms that serve them; strategists, TAMPs and ETF sponsors that publish backtests.
ideas.who_pays: $200-600 a month per RIA; consultants pay a platform fee per client firm; strategists and TAMPs $20-60k a year for backtest verification (my estimate). The compliance line exists because the Marketing Rule is a standing exam priority. The CCO or owner signs.
ideas.problem: The CCO's secret: the examiner asks for support behind every number on the website and every post, there is no folder, and the post says clients average 9% with no proof. Examiners keep finding policies not reasonably designed, books-and-records gaps and performance not presented fairly.
ideas.solution: Map each claim to Marketing Rule categories (performance, testimonials, third-party ratings, hypothetical), capture source, as-of date and calculation into a binder, flag stale claims, and test hypothetical-performance presentations for net-of-fee figures, 1/5/10-year periods, benchmark and holdout, using methodology from his Strategy Lab.
ideas.why_now: Marketing remains a 2026 SEC exam priority, off-channel and Reg S-P deadlines are crowding CCO calendars, and AI-washing is a rising exam topic.
ideas.founder_edge: Strategy Lab (honest, pre-registered backtesting is his proven edge) plus Dad's compliance-tech platform as potential day-one distribution, if it is still active (unconfirmed; public sources are dated).
ideas.first_10_customers: Advisors already on Dad's platform, three outsourced-CCO firms with 50-200 clients each, Maryland RIAs through the Annapolis network.
ideas.path_to_big: About 15,000 SEC-registered plus about 17,000 state-registered RIAs (verify). Even at $4k a year, $10M needs about 2,500 firms. Likely a $5-15M ceiling unless it becomes a recognized verification standard for strategists and fund sponsors.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Saifr (Fidelity-backed AI marketing compliance), Smarsh, Global Relay, Hearsay, Red Oak and ACA. This is the most crowded idea in the set, which is why it ranks last; the narrow slot is substantiation files and hypothetical-performance checks rather than general content review.

ideas.title: Contract Atlas: the independent home-health payer-rate network (Aledade for agencies that cannot negotiate alone)
ideas.one_liner: Port his freight-audit engine into a contract-versus-remittance auditor for MHC, then pool what independent home-health agencies are really paid by each Medicare Advantage plan into a peer rate benchmark, then a messenger-model contracting network, then an MSO.
ideas.customer: Owner, administrator or CFO of an independent Medicare-certified home-health agency (12,234 agencies nationally per MedPAC's July 2026 data book; about 1,079 in Florida in 2023) with a growing Medicare Advantage or managed-care book. First customer is MHC, if it turns out to be skilled home health (unverified).
ideas.who_pays: The agency. Stage 1: $500-1,500 flat diagnostic plus 20-25% contingency on recovered MA/managed-Medicaid underpayments (same structure as his freight product; check billing-agent rules before taking a percentage of Medicare FFS money). Stage 2: $600-1,500/month for member-only peer rate benchmarks. Stage 3: 2-4% admin fee on revenue contracted through the network, plus MSO fees. Budget line: managed-care contracting, billing and compliance; an analyst estimates agencies earn 30-40% less from MA than from traditional Medicare, so a 5-10% rate fix outweighs most software spend.
ideas.problem: Agencies sign MA contracts one at a time, cannot see what peers are paid, and rarely check remittances against the contract schedule. Insurers that own captive home-health capacity erode independents' leverage (LeadingAge, analysts). With the nationwide moratorium on new HHA enrollment (since 2026-05-13, expires 2026-11-13 unless extended) every existing Medicare number is scarce, so protecting its cash flow matters more.
ideas.solution: Stage 0 (Monday): LLM-extract MHC's MA contract PDFs into a rate table, ingest 835 remits, flag short-pays, wrong rate tiers, late payments and missed timely-filing windows, deliver a recovery packet. Stage 1: pooled anonymized benchmark (percent of Medicare by plan and market). Stage 2: with antitrust counsel, a messenger-model network (Home Care Iowa and a DOJ business-review letter are precedents; competitors cannot agree on prices) or a clinically integrated network. Stage 3: MSO services, in-home visit capacity sold to MA plans, value-based contracts. Aledade (3,000+ practices, 3M+ patients) proves the independents-network model, but I found no Aledade program for home-health agencies.
ideas.why_now: MA is 55.4% of beneficiaries (flat, Jan 2026) and MA home-health volume now exceeds fee-for-service; a 3% temporary Medicare cut continues in the proposed CY2027 rule; the moratorium makes each existing certificate scarce and no extension decision had been announced as of late October; insurers are building captive home-health capacity; no payer-rate benchmark vendor for independent agencies was found.
ideas.founder_edge: The freight-audit engine already does rate-table-versus-invoice with a flat-plus-contingency model, so the port is weeks not months. The family firm supplies real remits under a BAA, a founder-owner whose name opens doors with peer owners, and a mother inside the company. No licence is needed for software and audit work.
ideas.first_10_customers: (1) MHC. (2) Grandfather and Mom introduce five owner friends; offer a free 90-day one-payer diagnostic for a contingency on recoveries. (3) Present anonymized 'what Humana really pays agencies like you' findings at one state home-care association meeting reached through the same introductions. (4) Ask each paying agency for two intros. Expect the first paid recovery within 60-90 days once remits are in hand.
ideas.path_to_big: Value created: roughly $14B of MA/managed-care home-health revenue (assumption; FFS alone was $16.0B in 2024) times a 10% uplift is about $1.4B/year; capturing 5-10% is $70-140M. Bottom-up: 1,500 member agencies (12% of the nation, a stretch) x $1.6M contracted revenue x 3% = $72M, plus about $7k/year software each = roughly $10M. Florida alone at 20% share is only about $10M, so national expansion is required. Exit candidates: Waystar, Axxess, Trella, Enzo, an Aledade-type operator or a PE platform. Sibling lenses list narrow versions (Payer Truth, PayerProof, MA Rate Truth), so expect contest; the network and MSO stages are what the narrow versions lack.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No independent HHA payer-rate network found. Adjacent: Trella (referral analytics), Strategic Healthcare Programs (cost/clinical benchmarks), Enzo (contracting glossary, not a rate base), Claim Health (YC) and Amperos ($16M Series A) on denials and appeals, eCapital on financing, Aledade for primary care only. Precedent: Home Care Iowa (ten visiting-nurse associations, 1994 messenger model). Antitrust risk is real: messenger only, firewalls, counsel first.

ideas.title: Ground Truth Guild: a vetted expert bench that sells graded evals to AI companies
ideas.one_liner: A bench of working professionals (CFPs, CPAs and advisors from his father's 24-year network; RNs, OASIS coders and billers from the family company) that sells expert-graded eval sets and rubric grading to AI companies, starting in home-health operations and money-advice AI where no independent tests exist.
ideas.customer: Heads of product, ML or clinical quality at home-health-operations AI startups (OASIS review, scribes, denials, intake) and at advisor-tech and fintech AI startups; later AI labs and larger vendors.
ideas.who_pays: The AI company's eval and data budget. $2,500 for a 100-chart blind eval; $10-50k for an eval pack; $3-10k/month for regression-eval retainers. Expert hours billed at expert pay plus 35-50%. Mercor's contractors keep roughly 60-70% of gross, so a 30-40% take is the market norm.
ideas.problem: Healthcare AI vendors publish self-reported accuracy (Enzo about 95%, Olli 98% 'verified through internal audits') and no independent OASIS benchmark exists. Generic expert marketplaces are not vertical and have had breaches and contractor lawsuits (Mercor). Hippocratic AI hires nurses in-house, which is slow and costly. Startups need credentialed graders they can trust.
ideas.solution: Build synthetic gold sets with no PHI (experts write realistic charts and client emails). First packs: OASIS/chart review, advisor marketing-rule review, and consumer money questions graded to CFP standards. His multi-agent pipelines pre-grade; experts adjudicate; deliver inter-annotator agreement and an error taxonomy. Then monthly regression subscriptions, then adjacent licensed roles (tax, insurance, billing).
ideas.why_now: Expert data is the hottest line in AI: Mercor reported about $2B annualized gross run rate in June 2026 and was in talks at $20B; Handshake about $1B gross. Healthcare-ops AI raised heavily in 2026 (Enzo $20M Series A, Brellium $23M, Basalt $20M, Arya $18.2M) with no independent test of their accuracy claims.
ideas.founder_edge: His AI-text detector beat commercial detectors in his own blind tests, which is exactly eval design. Fast tooling. The family supplies pre-vetted experts who trust the name: his father's pre-screened advisors and MHC's clinicians and coders.
ideas.first_10_customers: List 60 healthcare-ops AI startups and 30 advisor-tech AI startups. DM founders a one-page offer: blind eval of your model on 100 expert-graded synthetic charts, $2,500, results in 10 days. Use his father's advisor-tech peers for fintech introductions. Seed the bench with MHC coders and five advisors. Target two paid pilots in 60 days.
ideas.path_to_big: $50M of gross billings at a 35% take is $32.5M of expert pay, about 340,000 hours at $95, roughly 2,000 part-time experts at 3 hours a week. That is plausible only if the bench spreads across regulated professions or becomes an eval standard; honest base case for the home-health-plus-advisor vertical alone is $5-15M. Mercor and Handshake prove the category is huge but lanes are won on trust.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Mercor, Surge AI, Scale/Outlier, Handshake AI, Turing; healthcare-specific Centaur Labs (50,000+ experts, Series B of $16M+ in Oct 2024); in-house nurse annotators at Hippocratic AI. No home-health-operations or advisor-specific independent bench found. Risks: worker classification, expert-data security, trust in a young founder.

ideas.title: Proving Ground: the first measured bake-off of home-health AI tools
ideas.one_liner: Run the same blind test on every AI tool agencies are being sold (OASIS review, scribes, denials, intake), publish a scorecard, and sell it to operators and PE platforms as a buying guide and to vendors as private regression reports; it shares the bench and synthetic charts with the Guild.
ideas.customer: Owners, COOs and quality directors at home-health agencies, PE-backed platforms, state associations and consultancies choosing AI tools; secondary customer is the vendors themselves.
ideas.who_pays: Operators and associations $1,500-3,000/year; PE platforms and consultancies $10-25k reports; vendors $5-15k private reports, with publication rules fixed in advance and no pay-for-rank. Budget: software selection and consulting.
ideas.problem: Every accuracy claim is vendor-reported, and buyers are told to run their own pilot with their own coders. Surveyors will not accept 'the software made a mistake' as a defense. KLAS ranks home-health EHRs by customer-reported satisfaction, not measured performance.
ideas.solution: A quarterly Home Health AI Scorecard: 300 synthetic charts graded by credentialed coders, per-error results (missed PDGM driver, wrong functional score, hallucinated visit), cost per chart, and BAA and data-use checks. Operator edition sold by subscription; vendors invited but results published either way.
ideas.why_now: At least six funded vendors compete in one workflow (Enzo, Olli, Brellium, SimiTree SARA, Basalt and others). CMS proposes cutting the OASIS submission deadline from 4.5 months to 45 days, which pushes adoption and buyer anxiety. No independent measured benchmark exists.
ideas.founder_edge: His detector-versus-GPTZero-versus-Pangram blind tests are the same method. MHC's owner can sit on a small operator advisory panel, which lends credibility a teenager lacks.
ideas.first_10_customers: Publish a free 'five tools, 100 charts' blind test on LinkedIn and home-care groups. Ask MHC to forward it to five owners. Sell ten operator subscriptions at $1,500 and two private vendor reports at $5-10k.
ideas.path_to_big: KLAS-style: 3,000 subscribers x $2,000 = $6M, plus PE and vendor work of $4-8M. $50M would need to become the standard across all post-acute and then hospital procurement. Honest ceiling $10-25M; best used as the trust layer that feeds the rate network and the expert bench.
ideas.who_does_it_today: KLAS (satisfaction surveys, Best in KLAS home-health EHR rankings), vendor self-reports, a SimiTree 'questions to ask your AI vendor' blog, a QAPIplus webinar. No measured independent benchmark found.

ideas.title: Care Navigators: his father's flat-fee marketplace model applied to elder care
ideas.one_liner: Families pay a flat fee for an independent care navigator who compares options and plans costs, takes no commissions, and no money passes to or from any home-health provider; MFA's pre-screened, flat-fee playbook moved to elder care.
ideas.customer: Adult children of aging parents, among 63 million US family caregivers (AARP 2025). First: clients of his father's advisors and families leaving hospital stays. Later: employers.
ideas.who_pays: Families, $295-495 for a care-and-cost plan and provider shortlist, versus Aging Life Care managers at $150-350/hour. Caregivers already spend about $7,200 a year out of pocket. Later: employers at an assumed $4-8 per employee per month.
ideas.problem: A Place for Mom is free to families because facilities pay referral fees, and conflicts are documented; it raised $175M at a $1B+ valuation (Dec 2024 report). Independent geriatric care managers are expensive and scarce. Families choose agencies with no neutral guide.
ideas.solution: AI intake plus a contracted human navigator (care managers, social workers, retired discharge planners, pre-screened the way MFA screens advisors) producing: care level needed, three vetted options including agencies other than MHC, what Medicare/MA/Medicaid/VA cover (information with pointers to official sources), and private-pay costs. No medical, legal (Medicaid planning goes to elder-law attorneys) or investment advice.
ideas.why_now: AI answers are eroding SEO lead-gen incumbents (NerdWallet tied Q4 2025 revenue drops to organic-search headwinds); caregiver numbers rose 45% in a decade; the moratorium on new agencies makes choosing among existing ones the decision.
ideas.founder_edge: The 24-year playbook (pre-screening, flat fee, consumer demand) lives in his father. The family company supplies domain intelligence and trust, not payments. He builds the AI intake in days.
ideas.first_10_customers: Offer ten of his father's advisors' clients with aging parents a $295 'parent care plan'. Mom has MHC social workers hand a neutral flyer to private-pay families (no payment either way). Post in two local caregiver Facebook groups.
ideas.path_to_big: 50,000 families a year x $400 = $20M. Beyond that the employer channel: 1M covered employees x $6/month x 12 = $72M (assumption). Direct employer-benefit rivals probably include Wellthy, Cariloop and Ianacare (unverified, from memory). Consumer CAC is the main threat.
ideas.who_does_it_today: A Place for Mom, Caring.com and Seniorly (provider-paid referral); Aging Life Care managers (hourly); Area Agencies on Aging (free, public); employer caregiver-benefit vendors. I found no flat-fee startup. Legal: Anti-Kickback Statute means never accept payment from a provider that bills Medicare or Medicaid, and disclose the family tie to MHC; check whether Florida regulates senior-care referral agencies (unverified).

ideas.title: Advisor Front Door: the compliant 'talk to a human' exit for AI assistants
ideas.one_liner: Expose his father's pre-screened flat-fee advisors as a tool that AI assistants, newsletters and fintech apps can call when someone needs a human for a money question.
ideas.customer: (1) Flat-fee and hourly advisors who want AI-era client flow, starting with the MyFinancialAdvice roster. (2) Distribution partners: fintech apps, newsletters, alumni groups, employers.
