ideas.who_pays: Advisors pay a flat $99-299/month listing, not a per-lead success fee, because compensated referrals are 'endorsements' under the SEC Marketing Rule and some states require solicitors to register (counsel decides). For scale: WiserAdvisor charges $1,000-2,500/year plus per-lead fees and Broadridge about $1,899/month.
ideas.problem: NerdWallet's credit-card revenue fell 24% and SMB revenue 12% in Q4 2025 on organic-search headwinds, so lead-gen incumbents are bleeding. Advisors report prospecting that now starts with a prompt to a chatbot. No standard, vetted way exists to hand someone from AI to a human fiduciary.
ideas.solution: A weekend build: an MCP server, a ChatGPT-style app and a web embed. It collects a structured non-advice brief (goal, asset range, state, complexity), matches against the verified roster (CRD/IAPD checks), and books a 20-minute consult. The assistant never recommends products.
ideas.why_now: ChatGPT app submissions opened Dec 2025 (monetization narrow; I found no financial-services policy). The SEC's Dec 2025 risk alert on promoters and refer-a-friend programs makes unvetted lead-gen riskier, so pre-screening becomes a selling point. NY Life (Sept 2026) found 40% of Gen Z say AI makes them more likely to want a human.
ideas.founder_edge: He ships MCP and app integrations in days. MyFinancialAdvice has the roster, the 24-year screening process, social-media compliance tech and the consumer brand.
ideas.first_10_customers: Ten existing MFA advisors at $149/month (three months free in exchange for case studies). Then list the app in the ChatGPT and Claude directories and pitch five finance newsletters for embeds.
ideas.path_to_big: 5,000 advisors x $200 x 12 = $12M. $50M needs about 20,000 paying advisors or a counsel-approved per-consult model plus employer channels. Main risk is platform dependence: AI assistants can add their own handoff, and OpenAI's monetization rules were narrow. Direct rivals are funded: Zoe ($45M raised), Range ($60M, Feb 2026), Facet.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Zoe Financial, Facet Wealth, Range, SmartAsset, WiserAdvisor, Wealthtender. None found as an AI-assistant-native handoff; the sources I found are commentary only. Sibling lens CFP-Checked and Launch Season are adjacent.

ideas.title: Founder Transfer Kit: turn an owner's head into what a buyer pays for
ideas.one_liner: An AI interviewer converts an aging owner's knowledge into a transfer binder, owner-dependence score and regulatory calendar, starting with his grandfather and sold through advisors, CPAs and bankers.
ideas.customer: Owners aged 55-75 of founder-led businesses. First: his grandfather as design partner. Then owner-clients of his father's advisor network, plus CPAs, bankers and brokers.
ideas.who_pays: The owner at $2,500-7,500 per kit, or the advisor at a $1,500 white-label price and resells. Budget: exit and succession planning.
ideas.problem: About 6 million US private businesses are expected to change hands by 2035 (McKinsey, as cited by IQExit). Owner-dependent firms are discounted. In home health, the moratorium makes certified agencies scarce, and buyer diligence reads like a compliance audit.
ideas.solution: Weekly 30-minute voice interviews structured into SOPs, vendor and referral maps, key-person risks, a 12-month licenses/enrollment/contract calendar and a buyer-ready data room. A healthcare edition adds CCN and payer-concentration facts.
ideas.why_now: Certified home-health deal pace is up about 41% in 2026. Seed-funded entrants prove demand but are generic: Rowan ($3.3M seed, March 2026) and IQExit (launched Feb 2026, sells through banks, wealth firms, CPAs and attorneys).
ideas.founder_edge: His grandfather is the founder-owner and an authentic case study; advisors in his father's network are the channel; he is the plausible next generation, which lends credibility.
ideas.first_10_customers: Grandfather (free, for a testimonial and introductions). Five advisors from his father's network offering two owner-clients each a $1,500 pilot. Three CPAs.
ideas.path_to_big: 600,000 transfers a year x 1% x $3,000 = $18M; add data room, buyer matching and financing referrals toward $50M. Long sales cycles, funded competitors and fee compression cap it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Rowan, IQExit, exit-planning firms and business brokers; Sugarwork/Rumi sell enterprise knowledge capture. None found specific to certified-healthcare owners.

ideas.title: Cash Radar: payer-level cash forecasting for post-acute, then a working-capital marketplace
ideas.one_liner: Use remittance data to tell each owner which payer will pay what on which day, then connect the forecast to a licensed lender; the financing stage of the rate network.
ideas.customer: CFO or owner of a home-health agency or hospice with 30-300 employees, especially after an ownership change or with a heavy MA book.
ideas.who_pays: Agency $300-800/month; lender partners pay origination fees where state licensing allows (check). Lender appetite is real: eCapital announced a $10M facility (Sept 2026) and a $30M facility (Aug 2026) for post-acute providers.
ideas.problem: About 52 days in accounts receivable and a 13% denial rate (vendor benchmark); aides are paid biweekly. Lenders may take a security interest in Medicare receivables but cannot receive Medicare payments directly (double-lockbox structures); Medicare Advantage assignment depends on each contract (unverified).
ideas.solution: Train payer-specific pay-time models on 835s; deliver a 13-week cash forecast with alerts; later an Advance Desk with a licensed lender; later a family-capital facility for peers, under counsel.
ideas.why_now: Pre-claim review in Florida slows cash; the moratorium raises a certificate's value as collateral; post-acute lenders are active.
ideas.founder_edge: The audit data from the rate network feeds the models; the family's investment connections are the capital partner; the family firm is customer zero.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC (free), then the rate network's member agencies at $300/month; open lender-partner talks through family connections.
ideas.path_to_big: $50M of revenue at an 18% yield needs an average loan book near $280M (assumption), which requires a licensed lender entity and institutional credit. A multi-year option, not a start; the software alone is a $3-8M business.
ideas.who_does_it_today: eCapital and other specialty healthcare lenders and factors; Care.fi (India, $8M Series A, hospitals). I found no tool forecasting cash by payer for home-health agencies.

ideas.title: Roots Circuit: a shared audience and sponsor network for independent roots festivals
ideas.one_liner: Run first on Annapolis Baygrass: a consented fan database, sponsor reports, and volunteer and vendor workflows, then a co-op of neighboring festivals that sells regional sponsors an audience no single festival has, plus live-set archive sales.
ideas.customer: Independent roots, bluegrass and folk festival producers and their sponsors. First: Baygrass, nominated for IBMA 2026 Event of the Year.
ideas.who_pays: Festivals $200-600/month plus 5-10% of sponsorship they close; sponsors $5-25k packages across several festivals. A veteran organizer says corporate sponsorship is the only way festivals survive long term; an old blues-festival source puts sponsorship near 25% of revenue (both soft).
ideas.problem: Sponsors are sold one at a time with no audience data; festivals patchwork Eventeny, Etix, Tixr and volunteer tools; audiences are aging and weather-exposed.
ideas.solution: Weekend build for Baygrass; invite ten neighboring festivals into the co-op; regional sponsor packages; optional live-set recording and archive in the style of nugs.net (rights are complicated).
ideas.why_now: Eventbrite sold for about $500M (Dec 2025), so ticketing alone is a low ceiling and the value moves to audience, sponsorship and payments; IBMA's convention gathers festival promoters in one place.
ideas.founder_edge: His father co-founded Baygrass and sits in the IBMA world; he builds in days.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass (free pilot), then five festivals met through his father's contacts and the next IBMA convention.
ideas.path_to_big: About 283 US bluegrass festivals (listing-site count) x $6k/year of software plus sponsorship take is $2-5M. Adding roots, folk and Americana festivals and food festivals might reach $20-40M. Venture scale is unlikely; the realistic exit is to a ticketing or festival-software company. Ranked last because it is the weakest on size, but it is the cheapest to run and a real testbed.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Eventeny (all-in-one festival software), Etix (1,800 venues), Tixr, Eventbrite (now owned by Bending Spoons), nugs.net (live recordings, self-financed until 2017). No sponsorship co-op found.

ideas.title: Lien Curve: collection curves and law-firm payment scorecards for treat-on-lien injury clinics
ideas.one_liner: Turn a clinic's closed-case history into a weekly collections plan, a per-law-firm payment scorecard and a diligence-grade collection-curve report; build it on MHC's 38 years of data, then sell to peer clinics, PE sponsors and receivable funders.
ideas.customer: CFO or head of revenue cycle at multi-site injury-clinic groups and lien-heavy ortho, pain, imaging and surgery-center practices; second buyer is the PE sponsor, lender or M&A adviser valuing letter-of-protection (LOP) receivables or a PI-law-firm MSO.
ideas.who_pays: The clinic's revenue-cycle budget (it already pays collectors: Surgery Partners 'Litigation Collector', a New Jersey spine group, a Las Vegas 'Lien Specialist', Morgan and Morgan lien roles). Assumed price: $3-5k/month per group or 5-8% of cash above a baseline; diligence reports $15-40k each. Signer: the CFO (MHC's CFO is a CPA).
ideas.problem: Money sits for years: KFF says LOP providers often wait years 'if at all' and some sold liens for 10-25 cents on the dollar; VMG Health says A/R in these businesses can approximate a full year of revenue and that buyers demand historical claim-level collection curves. Clinics cannot say which law firms pay, how fast, and after what reduction, so collectors work by habit and receivables are under-priced when sold.
ideas.solution: Weeks 1-2: take a 12-month closed-case export from MHC (hashed case ID, date of service, CPT, billed, law-firm ID, payer type, settlement date, amount paid, reduction; no patient names, under a BAA) and build firm scorecards with honest confidence bands. Weeks 3-6: per-case expected cash and timing (survival-style curves) turned into a ranked weekly call list. Weeks 6-12: a billing-policy view for intake (which financial arrangement fits), billing only, never clinical triage. Months 3-6: one-click diligence report for M&A and lenders, then a de-identified pooled benchmark once 3+ groups contribute.
ideas.why_now: PE is buying PI law firms (Bloomberg Law, May 2026: one adviser did 10 law-firm MSO deals last year and has 20 this year), so open-case inventory and liens need valuing. Florida (2023) and Georgia SB 68 (2025) made LOP terms, factoring-sale price and referral source discoverable and the sale price admissible, so receivable values are now argued in court; 2026 bills in Nebraska, Utah and Oklahoma copy it. Funders securitize these pools, which needs claim-level data.
ideas.founder_edge: CORRECTION to the brief: mhcorp.com shows MHC HealthCare is a 130+ location auto-accident/personal-injury clinic network (founded 1987 by Dr. Semyon Friedman; Owings Mills MD; DE, FL, MD, NC, VA, DC), not home health; his mother (inferred: Julia Friedman-Peremel) is a patent co-inventor and officer. That gives him a data asset no startup can buy, a CPA CFO and an A/R team to reach through Mom, and an attorney portal already used by law firms. His Strategy Lab (pre-registered tests, holdout checks) is the right discipline for small-sample modelling; he ships dashboards in days.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) MHC pilot via Mom to the CFO: free scorecard on closed cases, then pay-for-performance on lifted collections. 2-3) Two outside clinic groups from Mom/Ron intros to owners who sponsor Maryland Association for Justice, NC Advocates for Justice and Trial Lawyers Association events alongside MHC. 4-6) Lien-heavy ortho/pain practices from the MoveDocs directory (10,000+ listed providers); offer 'free benchmark of your last 200 closed cases'. 7-8) Two healthcare M&A advisers (VMG Health, Health Capital Consultants write on this diligence) as white-label channels. 9-10) Two receivable funders (Alleon, Libra/Key Health) paying for data-backed screening.
ideas.path_to_big: Bottom-up with flagged assumptions: if 2,500 of the ~10,000 PI-accepting providers are lien-heavy (assumption) and 16% (400) pay $30k/year = $12M; add 20-40 diligence reports at $25k ($0.5-1M) and a pooled receivables index licensed to 50-100 funders, lenders and insurers at $50-250k ($2.5-25M). $10M needs the clinic layer plus a few index licences; if lien-heavy practices number under 1,500 the ceiling is about $8M. End state: the credit bureau for medical liens.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Searched and found: funders' internal underwriting (Libra Solutions/Key Health, Alleon); Cherokee's Gain Servicing (staff plus software for LOP receivables, since 2018); in-house collection teams; PI EMRs that track liens but show no collection-curve or firm-scoring product (Ambula at $300/provider/month, ADSC); law-firm side tools (Lido ledgers, MoveDocs free to firms, ChartRequest); attorney-side AI (EvenUp $2B+, Eve $1B, Supio) which do not serve the clinic's cash. ideas.title: Fast-Pay Ladder: pre-approved discount schedule and one-link payoff for LOP balances
ideas.one_liner: The clinic sets a discount ladder (for example 12% off within 7 days of disbursement, 8% within 14, 4% within 30); the attorney opens one link, sees the balance and ladder, e-signs and pays, so cash arrives in days and the record shows the amount actually paid.
ideas.customer: The clinic's head of collections (payer); paralegals and lien negotiators at plaintiff law firms use it free.
ideas.who_pays: Clinic pays 1-3% of cash moved through the ladder or a flat SaaS fee (assumption). Budget line is the same collections/lien staff payroll shown in the job postings.
ideas.problem: Reductions are negotiated by phone one case at a time; postings literally say 'negotiate final resolution within company guidelines'. An attorney source says firms aim for 10-15% off, funders buy at roughly 20-40 cents on the dollar, and providers wait years. After Florida s.768.0427 and Georgia SB 68, 'amount actually paid' is evidence, so a clean payoff record has new value.
ideas.solution: Payoff link from the portal or statement; finance sets guardrails by case type and balance; auto-approve inside the ladder, route exceptions to a human; payment through a regulated payments partner (e.g. Stripe Connect with the clinic as connected account) so Asher never holds funds; auto-post to the clinic ledger. Attorneys only, no patient contact, and the tool only makes offers; it never tells a lawyer how to disburse (ethics opinions exist on LOP disbursement).
ideas.why_now: The same Florida/Georgia/2026 LOP-law wave makes documented paid amounts matter, and PE-backed PI firms want faster, cleaner closings.

I found no PI-specific early-payment ladder; generic B2B early-payment platforms exist but I did not search them. Check state billing rules and ethics language with counsel.

ideas.title: Festival Cost Desk: contingency-fee procurement and invoice audit for independent festivals, growing into a buying group
ideas.one_liner: Audit a festival's last-year invoices, run competitive bids on each major cost line (staging, sound, fencing, toilets, generators, shuttles, security) and keep 15-25% of verified savings; later pool demand across festivals for vendor-paid volume fees.
ideas.customer: Independent festival producers with $0.5-5M budgets, starting with roots, bluegrass and Americana events.
ideas.who_pays: Contingency on verified savings (no savings, no fee), so no budget fight. Insurance is excluded from scope because it needs a licence; a licensed event broker can partner. Later, vendors pay volume admin fees.
ideas.problem: Costs and insurance are crushing independents: FestivalPro (Jan 2026) reports renewal premiums up by a factor of 5 or more even with clean records; AIF counted 78, 43, then 20 independent UK festivals cancelled or postponed in 2024, 2025 and by mid-2026; Okeechobee paused citing costs. A UK collective projects up to 40% savings from shared staging, marketing and talent (organiser projection); I found no US buying group.
ideas.solution: Week 1: collect last year's invoices and contracts. Week 2: flag overbilled days, duplicate fees and fuel surcharges. Weeks 3-6: AI-normalise quotes from 3-5 alternative vendors per category, negotiate and document savings. From month 4: where several festivals share a region or weekend, bundle demand and ask vendors for a volume rate with the fee paid by the vendor. Publish an anonymised price index.

Asher already built a freight-invoice audit with a flat diagnostic plus contingency; this is the same machine on a new invoice type. Reaching $10M+ needs widening to fairs, races, parades and outdoor concerts (an assumed 30,000+ events). Treat the ceiling as $5-10M unless it widens.

Ticket Fairy publishes content on resource-sharing alliances but sells ticketing and financing (Ticket Fairy Capital, $10k-$3M+); a UK collective (Where It All Began) exists; Eventeny, Marketspread, LocalStalls and FestivalPro manage vendor applications, not production procurement; specialist event insurance brokers exist (excluded).

ideas.title: Insurer's-Eye Audit: run the insurer's fraud-pattern analytics on your own PIP clinic billing, privileged through counsel
ideas.one_liner: A monthly report that shows a PIP or no-fault clinic what an insurer's special-investigations unit would see (templated notes, repeat service patterns, missing medical-necessity and 14-day documentation, ownership and supervision gaps) and a fix list, delivered to the clinic's lawyer.
ideas.customer: Owners and compliance counsel of Florida PIP clinics first, then New York, New Jersey and Michigan no-fault clinics.
ideas.who_pays: Legal/compliance budget: $2-5k/month per group or $10-25k per audit (assumption). Signer: owner or outside healthcare counsel.
ideas.problem: GEICO filed three federal suits against Florida clinics between 2026-07-06 and 2026-08-19 alleging $3.6-5.9M schemes each, one on ownership and licensing theory; defending one costs six figures. Florida PIP was not repealed in 2026 (bills died), so the exposure continues.
ideas.solution: Detectors built from the public allegations in these complaints (identical treatment protocols, same-day multi-service patterns, 14-day-rule and emergency-medical-condition documentation, medical-director supervision records) plus a cloned-note detector. Output is a documentation and training fix list; the product refuses any feature that helps evade detection rather than fix practice. Reports go to counsel to preserve privilege.
ideas.why_now: The suits are fresh, the Florida PIP fee-schedule and peer-review fights continue, and tort reforms in 2023 and 2025 put more weight on records.
ideas.founder_edge: CORRECTION: MHC is a PI/auto-injury network with Florida clinics, so there is a pilot inside the family (if executives agree). His AI-text detector beat commercial detectors in his own blind tests; cloned or templated clinical notes are the same signal, and his multi-agent pipeline can turn public complaints into detector specs.

ideas.path_to_big: If 1,500 high-exposure clinics in no-fault states pay $30k a year (assumption) the pool is $45M; 20% share is $9M. Expansion to hospital-based outpatient groups and ASCs raises it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Searched and found: insurer-side SIU vendors sell to insurers; Brellium (AI chart audit) targets home health, not PIP; compliance consultants and law firms do it by hand. I found nothing selling this self-audit to PIP clinics. Risks: bad actors may self-select as buyers; keep reports privileged; family executives may dislike an audit by a relative.

ideas.title: Disclosure Pack: one-click LOP disclosure packets that meet state law
ideas.one_liner: Generate the packet Florida requires and Georgia makes discoverable: the letter of protection, an itemized coded ledger, any receivable-sale identity and price, insurance-availability facts and the referral source, state-specific, logged and ready for the law firm.
ideas.customer: Clinic records and billing teams (subscription) and plaintiff firms' litigation support (small per-packet fee).
ideas.who_pays: Clinic group subscription $200-500/month, or $30-75 per packet charged to the requesting firm (assumptions).
ideas.problem: Florida s.768.0427 makes the LOP, itemized ledger, factoring buyer identity and referral source disclosure items before claiming LOP medical expenses; Georgia SB 68 (signed 2025-04-21) makes LOP, coded charges, receivable sale and price, and referral relationship discoverable for claims arising on or after that date; Nebraska, Utah and Oklahoma had 2026 bills. Packets are assembled by hand from different systems with varying formats.
ideas.solution: Pull from EHR/billing exports, apply a state rule matrix kept current by a research pipeline, flag missing items (for example unknown health-insurance status), log what was sent and when, and export to the firm. Built to preserve records under legal hold, never to hide anything.
ideas.why_now: Georgia's first covered cases are maturing now, Florida cases are litigating the referral-discovery change, and three more states are copying.
ideas.founder_edge: CORRECTION: MHC is a PI clinic network with a patented report-generation module and an attorney portal already handing records to law firms, plus Florida sites. Asher's multi-agent research pipeline keeps a multi-state rule matrix cheap to maintain.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) MHC Florida sites and the firms they work with. 2-5) Florida ortho groups and surgery centers (the KFF Broward cluster shows many LOP providers). 6-10) Attorneys met through MAJ/NCAJ and Georgia firms newly exposed to SB 68.
ideas.path_to_big: If 5,000 providers in disclosure states pay $3-4k a year that is $15-20M (assumption); it depends on how many large states beyond Florida and Georgia adopt similar laws. Treat as $5-15M, regulatory-diffusion dependent.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Searched and found no LOP disclosure-packet product. Adjacent: Lido (lien ledgers), ChartRequest (records requests), Ambula and ADSC (bills and attorney portals), EvenUp/Eve chronologies. Ambula could add it as a feature, so speed matters. Packets surface markups, so the defence bar may use them.

ideas.title: Narrative and Testimony Desk: fixed-price treating-physician narratives and testimony slots
ideas.one_liner: Attorneys book a narrative report (AI-drafted from the chart, signed by the treating physician within five business days) or a testimony slot at published prices through the portal.

Fees stay fixed because AMA policy treats contingent physician fees as unethical.

ideas.title: Verified Vendor Sales: POS-checked revenue share for festivals and fairs
ideas.one_liner: Vendors connect Square, Clover, Toast or Stripe read-only; the festival sees real sales during the event window, the percentage fee is computed, invoiced and collected, and insurance and permit expiry is tracked.
ideas.customer: Festivals, fairs and markets that take a percentage of vendor gross sales.
ideas.who_pays: The organiser: $300-1,500 per event or 0.25% of verified vendor sales (assumption).
ideas.problem: A Square community thread has an organiser saying they have always used the 'honor code' for vendor sales; Tulsa State Fair requires percentage vendors to self-report gross by 8am daily; Marketspread's percentage tool relies on vendor-submitted sales. LocalStalls describes managers who cannot recall whose insurance expired.
ideas.solution: OAuth read-only connections to vendor processors, daily pull of sales for the event window, automatic percentage and minimum-fee calculation, invoicing, certificate-of-insurance and permit expiry tracker, and a variance flag when self-reported and processor totals differ.
ideas.why_now: Cost pressure on independent festivals makes every leaked percentage point matter, and processor APIs make verification cheap.
ideas.founder_edge: Ledgers, accounts and reconciliation are what his casino app is built from. Ron can confirm whether Baygrass takes vendor percentages (unknown; verify).
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass if it applies; the four other IBMA nominees by Ron's introduction; Maryland fairs and farmers' markets; city event offices that run percentage concessions.

result.teen_blockers: Age: not a legal wall. He is an adult and can form an LLC, sign contracts and take payments. Credibility is real but mitigated: Dad's 24-year name and grandfather's introductions can land about 5 customers; cold-pitching Florida elder-law attorneys or agency owners without a warm intro is weak. Licenses: none needed while the product stays non-advice and non-brokering. Legal walls that are real but clearable by design: (1) Fla. Stat. 817.505 patient brokering covers AHCA-licensed home health agencies and carries felony penalties ($50k up to $500k), so per-start fees to agencies must be dropped; a flat fair-market fee to a non-steering consumer information service fits exemption (3)(i). (2) Florida Bar Rule 4-7.22 makes CareFund a 'qualifying provider' for lawyers: no fee-sharing, a panel with lawyers from at least 4 firms, annual list to the Bar, 15-day written response; this conflicts with the '2 attorneys' start and the 'exclusive county' offer. (3) SEC Marketing Rule 206(4)-1: any advisor paying per referral makes CareFund a paid promoter (written agreement, disclosure at referral, eligibility checks); SmartAsset shows it is workable and Dad's compliance toolkit is a real edge. (4) HIPAA marketing rule: an agency handout promoting a third-party advisor funded directly or indirectly by that advisor likely needs patient authorization; keep no remuneration to agencies and no PHI. (5) VA: no claim-prep fees unless accredited. Capital: legal review pushes cost to about $6-10k, not $4k. Unverified and load-bearing: nothing public confirms what MHC Healthcare is (only an unverified 'MHC Area 6 LLC' Riverview listing on a low-quality directory), and MyFinancialAdvice looks like a small Boulder CO firm founded 2001 (about 8 employees per one profile, last detailed coverage 2004), so Dad's 'advisor roster' may be thin. A family pilot is weak proof to non-family peers.

The HCAF HomeCareCon was July 21-24, 2026, so the next one falls outside the 6-month window; use regional meetings and webinars until then. First 10 named customer types or communities: (1) MHC itself as family pilot agency; (2-3) two peer Medicare-certified or private-duty agency owners from grandfather's circle; (4) a local home-care franchise owner (Visiting Angels, Home Instead, Comfort Keepers or BrightStar) who already publishes 'how to pay' content; (5) 3-5 advisors from Dad's MyFinancialAdvice roster (after confirming it is active); (6) Florida flat-fee planners from XY Planning Network or Garrett Planning Network chapters as the low-cost tier; (7) hybrid or AUM RIAs with an eldercare niche (FPA Elder Planning Specialist graduates) under promoter agreements; (8) Florida elder-law attorneys via NAELA and the Florida Bar Elder Law Section, 4+ per county panel; (9) ALF discharge planners as free referral sources; (10) hospital discharge planners and Aging Life Care Association care managers as free referral sources.
result.deciding_reason: The payer math does not close as written. A flat-fee advisor consult earns about $270-300, so a $200-350 per-consult lead fee is roughly 100% of revenue, which makes Dad's flat-fee roster the wrong payer. The payers who can afford leads (elder-law attorneys with $3-15k engagements, AUM RIAs) sit behind the Florida Bar 4-7.22 four-firm panel rule and SEC promoter rules. Agency marketing budgets are only about 1-2% of revenue, so a $300-900/month license against about 2-5 consults per agency per year is a hard sell. The $90M bottom-up needs about 2M completed intakes plus per-start agency fees that Florida patient-brokering law (817.505) makes felony-risky. The free funding map is commoditized by NCOA BenefitsCheckUp, and the big channels (CareScout/Genworth, Carefull with banks, Cariloop and Wellthy with employers) are already taken or out of an 18-year-old's reach. It is not dead because the family-agency wedge, Dad's compliance tooling and an empty exact combination are real.

sharpened.title: CareFund Rail: the compliant funding-and-referral desk for home care
sharpened.one_liner: A free 12-minute care-funding intake that home-care agencies hand out at admission and discharge, paid for by flat-fee, rule-compliant sponsorships from elder-law attorneys and advisors, with the compliance rail (promoter agreements, disclosures, Bar-panel rules, no per-start fees, no PHI) as the moat.
sharpened.pitch: Families learn private-duty care costs about $6,000 a month in a crisis; most then cut hours or never convert from a Medicare episode. Agencies lose the conversion, and attorneys and advisors meet the family late. CareFund is a non-advice intake agencies hand out at admission and discharge. It produces a funding map (LTC policy claim checklist, VA Aid and Attendance, Medicaid waiver, state programs, family cost-sharing) and a booked consult with a vetted professional. Three changes from the original. First, the payers change: elder-law attorneys (a rotating panel of four or more per county, flat monthly sponsorship) and hybrid or AUM advisors under written promoter agreements pay, because a roughly $300 flat-fee consult cannot carry a $200-350 lead fee; flat-fee planners become the low-cost tier. Agencies pay a small flat fair-market license, with no per-start fees. Second, the family-agency pilot is instrumented, together with three or four free peer pilots using de-identified aggregates, to produce the one number peers will pay for: private-pay conversion and length-of-stay lift. Third, the product that scales is the compliance rail itself (SEC promoter agreements and disclosures, Florida Bar 4-7.22 panel rules, HIPAA marketing guardrails, built from Dad's compliance tooling), which carriers, banks and caregiver-benefit vendors need more than another lead list. Kill criteria: by April 2027, if fewer than 3 of 10 peer agencies would pay $300 a month after seeing pilot data, stop.

result.teen_blockers: Age and legal form are not blockers: he is 18 and can form an LLC, sign contracts and take payments. No license wall exists, because grading AI outputs on synthetic prompts is not giving regulated medical or financial advice. The blockers that are real: (1) Credibility. Vendors will ask who the clinical lead is. He needs a named credentialed lead, such as an MHC director of nursing or an HHCS-O auditor, and fixable. (2) Independence conflict. If MHC is a customer or affiliate of a vendor he grades, 'independent' is compromised. MHC Area 9 LLC is registered as doing business as Choice Health At Home, which is acquiring Accentra, whose CEO created the Apricot AI tool. This is unverified and the single biggest unknown. (3) Bench existence. The family company may have sold its agencies to Choice, in which case the RN/coder bench may not be his to recruit. The only exact-name search hit for MHC Healthcare was an unrelated Arizona nonprofit, and MyFinancialAdvice shows only 2004-era press, so the advisor network's current state is unverified. (4) HIPAA. Low while everything is synthetic, but it becomes real if experts write charts from memory of real patients or if retainer evals run on production traces. (5) Worker classification. Minor at under 10 project-based experts, but a real wall at scale: Mercor (Texas), Handshake (N.D. Cal., July 2026) and Scale (SF) are all being sued over AI-trainer misclassification. (6) Expert-data security. The Mercor breach (March 2026) led to at least 4-7 class actions. (7) Advisor side-gigs. FINRA 3270 requires registered reps to give prior written notice to their firm, so flat-fee RIAs are lighter. (8) Capital at scale: experts are paid weekly before clients pay, so a $50M-billing marketplace needs a multi-million float, but the pilot needs under $10k.
result.first_customers_channel: Cold founder DMs with a one-page offer, backed by one family and one clinician introduction. Home-health AI vendors, all named in the search results: Enzo Health ($20M Series A), Olli Health ($10M Series A), Brellium ($16.7M), Apricot (Insight Partners Series A), Lime Health AI, Healthorbit.ai, and SimiTree's SARA. The better payer is the agency or advisor firm choosing a vendor, not the vendor itself: only 1.3% of 160 agency respondents were 'very confident' in their OASIS accuracy, and CMS leaves coding liability with the agency.
result.deciding_reason: The wedge is real but too small, and the only big path is a fight with Mercor. I found no independent accuracy benchmark for AI OASIS vendors and no home-health-specific bench, and there is no license or age wall. But the vertical is about 80 named AI vendors, which bottoms up to $1-3M a year, not the pitch's $5-15M. The generic expert-eval lane is occupied: Mercor now sells Enterprise Evals to application-layer companies (Ramp, Cognition) from a 30k-expert, $2B-run-rate base, and Centaur and Vals already own the healthcare and independent-benchmark niches. The vendor-pays model has a structural problem: vendors want badges, not honest scores, in-house clinical teams do it today (Hippocratic, Ada), and CHAI's assurance-lab plan failed partly because nobody settled who pays. The $2,500 price is below the roughly $5-6k build cost of a defensible 100-chart gold set, so the first pilots lose money. The idea survives as weak, not dead, because the buyer side (agencies, with 1.3% confidence in OASIS accuracy and liability under CMS) is unserved and KLAS shows a $40M-scale vendor-funded ratings model exists, but that path takes years and needs a verified MHC bench.

sharpened.title: Ground Truth Ledger: the independent accuracy scoreboard for back-office AI in regulated services
sharpened.one_liner: A small credentialed bench grades back-office AI (home-health OASIS first, advisor communications second) on hidden synthetic gold sets, sells blind diagnostics and buyer-side vendor bake-offs, then turns the accumulated rubrics and an anonymized index into a subscription standard that vendors license a verified badge from.
sharpened.pitch:
The weak point of the original idea was the payer and the scale model. Vendors will not pay for honest independent scores, and a 2,000-expert marketplace is a head-on fight with Mercor, which now sells enterprise evals from a 30,000-expert, roughly $2B-run-rate base. The sharpened version keeps the expert bench but changes who pays and what is sold.

Step 1, days 0-90: build one 100-chart synthetic OASIS gold set with a hidden test split, graded by three credentialed coders with inter-annotator agreement and an error taxonomy. His pipelines pre-grade, cutting expert time by roughly 60-70%. Sell a $5,000 blind diagnostic to vendors. The first two go for $2,500 as design partners, with testimonial and anonymized-publication rights, since a defensible set costs about $5-6k to build.

Step 2: sell a buyer-side bake-off to agencies choosing among AI vendors, at $3-10k. Only 1.3% of 160 surveyed agencies were very confident in their OASIS accuracy, CMS leaves coding liability with the agency, and no independent benchmark exists. This is the payer with the mandate and the pain.

Step 3, months 6-24: publish an anonymized industry accuracy index. Vendors that score well license a verified badge, and gold sets and rubrics are sold as subscriptions. KLAS, at roughly $40M of revenue, shows that vendor-funded independent ratings can last, so the moat is a data asset and a standard, not a take-rate on hours.

Step 4: advisor-AI marketing-rule and client-communication review only after a signed design partner from his father's network.

Gate zero, before spending a dollar: confirm what MHC Healthcare actually is. Its Florida entities appear to operate under Choice Health At Home, which is tied to Apricot, a vendor he would grade. An independence conflict, or a sold company with no bench, changes the plan. Keep the bench to 10-20 people on per-project contracts through a payroll partner.

result.teen_blockers: Age: not a blocker. He is 18 and can form an LLC, sign BAAs and fee agreements, and take payments. License: I found no license required to audit remits or file payer disputes on an agency's behalf, but a healthcare attorney must confirm. That is a roughly $2-3k check; the estimate is mine. Credibility: real for non-family owners and not real for the family pilot. Strangers will want a result from the family agency, so the first 3 peers must come through the grandfather's calls. A cold 18-year-old pitching contract audits to owners will not close. Legal wall 1, Medicare billing-agent rule: 42 CFR 424.73(b)(3) bars an agent's pay from being tied to dollars billed or collected, but only for agents who receive Medicare payments. It is not triggered if all cash goes to the agency's own accounts and he never touches funds. Real but avoidable. Legal wall 2, Florida Medicaid: Fla. Stat. 409.913 (subsection number unconfirmed) reportedly bars percentage pay to billing agents on Medicaid claims. Medicaid managed-care work must be flat-fee. Real but avoidable. Legal wall 3, anti-kickback: OIG treats percentage billing pay as a risk because it can encourage upcoding. A pure contract-rate audit has less of that risk, and a lawyer must sign off before any fee agreement. Real but clearable. HIPAA: a BAA with every customer and a sub-BAA with the model vendor. Anthropic offers an API BAA and zero retention, but one June 2026 secondary source says its newest 'Covered' models require 30-day retention and cannot run under zero-retention. Verify directly before touching PHI. Real but manageable. Scaling blocker: beyond the family and 3-5 friendly owners, chains will demand SOC 2, cyber and E&O insurance. That is real and costs money and months, but it does not block the first 60-90 days. Biggest unverified premise: MHC Healthcare as an owner-operated home-health company. Directory listings show 'MHC Area 6/9/10 LLC' as Medicare-certified Florida agencies (Riverview, Boca Raton dba Choice Health At Home, Fort Lauderdale) with no owner named. Nothing I found ties Peremel to MHC. If the family firm is not a home-health operator with Medicare Advantage revenue, the pilot and the trust advantage vanish.
result.first_customers_channel: Channel: the grandfather's owner-to-owner calls, backed by a pre-registered 30-day free scan. The January 2027 rate-change window is a talking point only, because I found no source that plans load rates late. Associations are too slow for the 6-month goal. HomeCareCon (Home Care Association of Florida) was July 21-24, 2026 and the next is July 2027. The Alliance for Care at Home webinar series is policy-focused with no revenue-cycle session found. First 10: (1) the family group (the MHC Area N agencies, if verified). (2-4) Three Florida owner-peers the grandfather calls personally, preferably multi-location groups. (5-6) Two Home Care Association of Florida member groups reached through a grandfather or mentor introduction, using a short written scan offer. (7-8) Two healthcare CPA or attorney firms serving agencies, as referral channels only, with no referral fees until counsel reviews. (9) One PE-backed regional operator via the mentor's network. (10) One billing company or EHR reseller that wants a premium add-on. Target groups with $10M+ of non-FFS revenue, not $3M single agencies.
result.deciding_reason: The idea reaches a first paying customer and clears the legal walls, but the home-health-only fee pool is too small for $10M a year and the leakage rate is unproven. Size: MedPAC reports $16.0B of fee-for-service home health spend in 2024 across 12,234 agencies. Using SimiTree's 26% MA revenue share (2022) and a growing MA share since, MA home-health revenue is about $8-10B. That is well below the idea's $12-16B. Public leakage anchors are 0.5-1% of net patient revenue (R1, hospitals) and 1-3% (a vendor webinar, commercial payers). Applying 1% leakage and 60% recoverable, with a 25% fee, gives a national fee pool of about $12-15M. Even the idea's own 3% leakage gives only about $40-50M. $10M a year therefore needs 70-80% of the base pool, or 20-25% of the optimistic pool. An agency with $3M of MA revenue yields only about $4-9k a year in fees. A realistic median is about $0.4M a year by year 3. Only a pooled payer benchmark, or expansion into hospice, SNF and outpatient lines, gets near $6M. Those lines are crowded with funded rivals (Fuse, Trek, R1, Aspirion, Ensemble). The January rate-reset premise is also thin. No source supports plans loading rates late. The payer with budget is the vendor, who pays only if it wins, which is the pay-for-rank conflict the pitch forbids. Bottom-up, home health alone is about $0.8M in the median case and about $6M at best, below the $10M bar. The 'why now' is also overstated: the 45-day change is the HH QRP measure-data deadline, not the 30-day OASIS rule, and it is still only proposed. Add real tool-access and ToS walls (SARA is not standalone, Olli and SARA are human-in-the-loop) and an unverified MHC. It works as a trust and lead-gen engine for a bigger business, not as a standalone company.

sharpened.title: Post-Acute AI Proving Ground
sharpened.one_liner: A locked, versioned test of chart-coding AI (OASIS first, then SNF MDS and hospice) that starts with a public, vendor-free baseline of plain frontier LLMs, then lets vendors opt in to beat it, funded by vendor testing and PE and payer bake-offs, not operator subscriptions.
sharpened.pitch: The original idea fails on who pays: providers get KLAS free, so a 3,000-subscriber operator base is fantasy, and vendors who pay only when they win create a pay-for-rank problem. This version fixes both without shrinking. Phase 1 is a public leaderboard that needs nobody's permission: plain frontier LLMs (Claude, GPT, Gemini) graded on 100 to 300 synthetic OASIS charts, scored against double-coded gold labels from credentialed HCS-O and COS-C coders, with the full protocol published. It answers the question every operator can now ask a vendor: do you beat a plain LLM, and show me the per-error breakdown (missed PDGM driver, wrong functional score, hallucinated visit). Phase 2: vendors opt in under pre-agreed publication rules, with results published either way. Vendors pay for what only they need: a private regression harness, per-error diagnostics, and re-tests after each model update. A written firewall keeps payment from ever changing rank, the way Vals AI works with model labs. Operators get the scorecard free and contribute de-identified pilot results under BAAs, which grows the gold-label set. PE platforms, payers and consultancies pay for custom bake-offs on their own charts. The same bench extends to SNF MDS and hospice, which is where the $10M+ lives, with Vals AI, CHAP and KLAS as the real competitors. Gate before any build: Olli plus two more vendors sign participation terms, five operators pre-pay a $750 charter membership within 3 weeks, and MHC's type is confirmed. If not, kill it.

result.teen_blockers: Age and contracting: NOT real. At 18 he can form an LLC, sign contracts and take payment; selling software and fixed-fee documentation needs no license. Credibility with owners 55-75 and with CPAs: REAL but partly mitigated. CPAs and advisors put their own reputation and E&O exposure behind a white-labeled kit from a teen vendor, so expect 'come back with five case studies'; the grandson-interviews-the-founder story, the mentor and family introductions help. Licensing: REAL for the big path only. Florida treats selling a business for another as real estate and requires a real estate license (law-firm summary; statute number not confirmed), and the 2023 federal M&A broker exemption does not preempt state law, so the idea's 'buyer matching and financing referrals' step toward $50M is license-walled (also broker-dealer finder exposure). The kit itself (software plus fixed fees, no success fees, no referral splits) is clear. Valuation and legal-advice labels: moderate, avoid calling anything a valuation and have a healthcare attorney review the regulatory-calendar templates and disclaimers ($2-5k). HIPAA: manageable and avoidable, design the kit to hold zero PHI; if referral or billing data is touched, sign a BAA with the family company, use minimum-necessary data and an LLM vendor with a BAA or zero retention; Florida is an all-party recording-consent state so get written consent. Capital: NOT real, about $1,500 to first revenue. Unverified premise: REAL, I could not confirm what MHC Healthcare is or that the grandfather is actually planning a transition (directory listings show MHC Area 6/10 LLC as Medicare-certified home health, but name collisions exist); the 36-month rule plus the May 2026 enrollment moratorium may block a sale if the agencies are young. Family pilot is free and proves nothing about willingness to pay.
result.first_customers_channel: Channel: warm introductions to sell-side people whose deals die in diligence, plus a paid family design partner. Named first 10: (1) MHC Healthcare as design partner, insist on a $1,500 paid token invoice; (2) the CPA who prepares MHC's taxes; (3) two more CPAs from the family's circle; (4) two home-health M&A advisors or healthcare transaction lawyers reached through his grandfather and mother (Braff Group, Mertz Taggart, Ad Astra Equity, CT Acquisitions and AGG are the active firms in this space); (5) two other Florida home-health or hospice owners from grandfather's and mother's peer circle (state home-care association and NAHC members, verify names); (6) two advisors from Ron's network who actually serve owner-clients 55+ (ask Ron for these by name; his flat-fee MyFinancialAdvice network is likely the wrong segment); (7) one founder-owned AV integrator via the mentor (AVI-SPL founder). Second payer to test: search-fund and roll-up buyers (about 850 search funds) buying a 90-day post-LOI knowledge handoff. Gen Z distribution is not an edge here.
result.deciding_reason: The generic kit is already sold: Rowan ($3.3M seed), IQExit (same banker/CPA/advisor channel, free to owners), Sell Ready AI (data room plus SOPs), VDR.ai and Value Builder (CPA channel, 46,000 owners, owner-dependence score) all exist. The one open gap, certified home health, is only about 92 home health plus hospice deals a year (the '+41%' is an annualized half-year count off a four-year low, and a second tracker shows a flat count). Ron's flat-fee advisor network is probably the wrong segment, a kit is bought once per owner lifetime, and the $18M path uses the 6M 'transitions' figure rather than the roughly 110k annual sales (about $3.3M at 1% share). Reachable and legal for a first pilot, but crowded, small where unoccupied, and unproven on willingness to pay.

sharpened.title: Sale-Ready File: the regulator-aware diligence file for owner-run care businesses
sharpened.one_liner: An AI interviewer plus a regulator-aware calendar that builds the buyer-ready file for owner-run Medicare-certified home health and other regulated care businesses, sold through the sell-side advisors and lawyers whose deals die in diligence, and kept as an annual subscription.
sharpened.pitch:
Generic exit-readiness is taken: Rowan ($3.3M seed, March 2026), IQExit (same banker, CPA and wealth-advisor channel, free to owners), Sell Ready AI (data room plus SOPs), VDR.ai, and Value Builder (CPA channel, 46,000 owners scored). So do not compete on the generic kit. Compete where diligence reads like a compliance audit: owner-run Medicare-certified home health and hospice first, then dental, vet, behavioral and therapy practices that roll-ups buy.

Weekly 30-minute AI voice interviews, designed to hold no PHI, produce a sale-ready file: SOPs, a referral-source and payer-concentration map, key-person risks, an enrollment, license, accreditation and change-of-ownership calendar (including 36-month-rule status), and a staged data room. An annual refresh subscription makes revenue recur instead of one payment per owner lifetime.

Who pays: the owner at $2,500-5,000 (up to $7,500-15,000 for agencies with $1M+ EBITDA, where one turn of multiple dwarfs the fee), or the sell-side advisor or healthcare transaction lawyer at $1,500-2,500 wholesale, because letters of intent now close only about half the time. Test a second payer: search-fund and roll-up buyers purchasing a standard 90-day post-LOI knowledge handoff.

Start with MHC as a paid design partner, then home-health advisors and lawyers through his grandfather and mother, three CPAs, and the advisors in Ron's network who actually serve owners 55+. No brokering, valuation, buyer matching or financing referrals (Florida real estate license and broker-dealer exposure). Kill gate: no paid non-family pilot by week 10.

result.teen_blockers: Age is not a blocker: he is 18 and can form an LLC, sign BAAs and take payment. Real but clearable: (1) HIPAA. Every agency needs a BAA and the LLM vendor needs a sub-BAA; dates of service are identifiers, so an index must compute durations locally and ship only non-identifying intervals. About $1.5-3K counsel plus $1-2K a year cyber and E&O. (2) Standing. Under 42 CFR 422.574 and 422.578 the treating physician, not the home health agency, has the right to request a pre-service reconsideration on the enrollee's behalf, and plans can dismiss non-party filings, so the auto-draft appeals promise needs a physician signature or the plan's peer-to-peer and provider-dispute routes. This is real and weakens the appeals feature. Contracted-provider payment disputes also run through the contract. (3) Contingency fee. I found no guidance either way on 20-25% of overturned dollars for MA appeals; general billing companies charge 4-10%, so it will draw pushback and needs counsel and a flat-fee fallback. (4) Credibility. Cold, an owner-operator will not buy from an 18-year-old; warm intros from the grandfather cover the first 5-10 customers, but the chain is thin after that and the mentor's AV network has no home health overlap. (5) MHC Healthcare is unverified: low-quality directory listings show MHC Area 6 and Area 10 as Medicare-certified home health agencies; if it is FFS-heavy or another type the pilot loses its data. (6) Publishing a plan scorecard carries defamation and payer-contract confidentiality risk; needs a lawyer's read of the first release.
result.first_customers_channel: Channel: the family agency (MHC Area N LLCs, if confirmed Medicare-certified; a multi-site pilot) then grandfather-introduced peers, then the Home Care Association of Florida (HCAF) member base and its annual HomeCareCon (next likely mid-2027; the 2026 edition was 21-24 July). Opener: free 30-day clock audit of the last 90 days of authorizations. First 10 customer types: (1) the family agency, ideally all its MHC entities (Riverview, Boca Raton, Fort Lauderdale) as one pilot; (2-4) three owner-operator peers of the grandfather with MA-heavy Florida census; (5-8) four HCAF member agencies in Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach and Hillsborough with high MA mix; (9-10) two non-agency data buyers reached through the mentor and family investors: a hospital system post-acute network team or ACO/MSO, and a home health investor or PE roll-up, who would pay for the index, not the tool. Avoid Interim HealthCare franchisees at first (Claim Health already lists Interim as a customer).
result.deciding_reason: Four funded startups (Claim Health, Silna, Enzo, Adaptive; about $100M combined) plus HCHB and outsourcers already sell MA home-health authorization and denial work to the same buyer, and at realistic overturn rates (1-3% of about $14B MA home-health revenue, 25% fee) the national fee pool is only about $35-105M, with roughly $5-8K a year per average agency, so $10M needs 10-30% of the pool or 1,250-2,000 paying agencies. The founder can reach the first customers and no license or age wall exists, which is why this is weak rather than kill, but the only unclaimed piece (home-health-level plan and UM-contractor clock and denial measurement, which OIG says CMS lacks) is a feature a funded rival can ship in a sprint unless it becomes a data network.

sharpened.title: Clock Index: the first home-health Medicare Advantage authorization benchmark
sharpened.one_liner: Free clock audits that turn agencies' own authorization logs into the first public, pre-registered index of how fast and how often each Medicare Advantage plan and its UM contractor decides home health requests, sold as data to the hospitals, ACOs and investors who have the budget.
sharpened.pitch: Lead with measurement, not appeals. The funded rivals (Claim Health, Silna, Enzo, Adaptive) already sell authorization tracking and appeal drafting to agencies, and an agency is not even a party to a pre-service MA denial (the treating physician is, under 42 CFR 422.578). So appeals become a physician-signed, flat-fee upsell or a partner integration, not the core. The core is the gap nobody has filled: KFF's 12% denial and 67% overturn figures are aggregated across all services, and OIG's June 2026 reports found denial rates from 0.4% to 23% across plans and contractors but said CMS collects no request-level data by service or contractor, and none of it covers home health. Opener: a free 30-day clock audit of an agency's last 90 days of authorizations, computed locally into plan-by-UM-contractor decision times against the 72-hour and 7-day clocks, visits requested versus approved, and denial reasons. Only non-identifying intervals leave the agency, which keeps HIPAA exposure small. In return each agency gets its own benchmark against peers. The aggregate becomes a quarterly index with a pre-registered method (his strategy-lab discipline), published to the Home Care Association of Florida and sold to the buyers with real budgets: hospital post-acute network teams, ACOs and MSOs, home health investors, and associations, with the agency benchmark as a paid tier. Five-week gate: confirm what MHC actually is; audit the family agency plus four peers (kill if fewer than three can export submit and decision timestamps); kill if clock misses are too rare to tell a story; kill if none of ten data-buyer calls will name a price. Base case is about $0.4M a year; $10M needs the index to become the standard reference across roughly a thousand agencies.
